The engine of the plot is four siblings concealing their mother's death and improvising a family structure once all adult authority disappears - a real, nameable idea about what a household regresses into without structure - and the incest is the endpoint of that regression rather than the reason the book exists, so filter 6 does not fire. That puts it near the territory of Promena 58, a book with a real idea undercut by a hard-to-root-for lead and bleakness that arrives from the start rather than gradually - Jack here is similarly controlling and unsympathetic, harassing his younger brother throughout. Unlike Promena, this book also carries a real sexual-content cost: moderate volume, explicit depiction at the climax, and a coarse register several reviewers flagged directly, which compounds further below that anchor.

The book is a manoeuvre: run a warship past a blockade, hold an alliance of convenience together, get a stranded colony fed. Those are problems, not ideas, and I would put ideas in the risk column rather than the support column, which is what usually decides whether a book of this kind clears the 65 line here - Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 are both competent novels whose scores were not carried by anything they left behind. It does not fall further because the shape is safe: one narrator, one concrete objective at a time, no confusing fan-out of the kind that ended three books at 30, no occult, no investigation, and sexual content that is understated rather than crude. Against that, it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien. The set-piece emphasis is the other drag - set-piece action with no character revelation reads as dead weight for this reader, which is why Golden Son 92 sits under Red Rising 95 despite the same author and cast.

It does start clean: four years of peace, one ship, one reconnaissance objective, and a reader who knows within a page what the situation is and what is wanted from it. A single concrete starting situation is the strongest positive available in this log, since the three books that ended at 30 all failed on exactly its absence. What I cannot do is name an idea beyond 'the enemy was not finished after all', which is a plot turn rather than something to think about, so ideas go in the risk column - and that is the most common reason a perfectly readable book settles in the 60s here, as with Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien. No filter fires - one first-person narrator throughout, no occult, no investigation, and sexual content handled without crudeness.

Reviewers agree the draw is the politics and not the fighting - one warns outright that a reader after non-stop bloodshed will not find it here - and that the friction between an honourable hot-head and a self-made climber is the vehicle for what a voting city could and could not bear. That is page time on what men want and why, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and it leaves one idea nameable in a phrase: a free city will vote out the man who saved it. Both leads are interesting and worth rooting for, the pairing whose failure cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87. It opens on one concrete situation, the field at Marathon, so the several-plot-lines-at-once start that put Guards Guards and The Gunslinger on 30 is not the danger here. Capped in the high 70s because historical fiction has not cleared The Count of Monte Cristo 75 in this log, and because three to five rotating viewpoints dilute the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89. One review reports the Delphic oracle prophesying Leonidas' fate appearing in the text; divination enacted on the page is a hard filter, and the Greek pantheon is what held Percy Jackson to 57, so that is a risk that could sink the number rather than trim it. Leaned on motives and ideas rather than on the battle writing, because set-piece action with no character revelation is what docked Catching Fire 83. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: the Delphic oracle prophesying Leonidas' fate - enacted in a scene, or reported?

The structure is a sequence of standalone nighttime-Tokyo character vignettes whose fates barely intersect, using sex and violence as the connective texture for a critique of consumer alienation and loneliness rather than the plot itself being a sexual relationship, so it clears the sex-as-the-plot filter, if narrowly. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The correction changes nothing here: graphic explicitness plus a crude, joyless treatment is the Ready Player One charge at sustained length, so the sinking dimension is present at full strength and volume compounds it. The episodic structure also gives no single protagonist to invest in, unlike the mythic scope that let The Silmarillion score 80 despite lacking one; here nothing offsets it.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography, and the printed contents list is a run of destinations - Marianske Lazne and Sumava, the Cote d'Azur, the Loire chateaux, Britain - which makes it a travel-anecdote collection rather than a book with a subject. There is no premise whose consequences could be worked out and no plot to hold together, so the whole weight falls on what the observations leave behind, and the stated message that attitude matters more than age is a sentiment rather than an idea. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. A sequence of holidays attempts neither. Description with little story is a named penalty term for this reader, and a chapter per destination is mostly description. For scale: The Chronicles of Narnia stalled at 67 for lacking higher things to think about while still having a plot and an invented world; this has neither, so it sits under that. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk.

There is a real question at the centre and it is a declared price with consequences: crossing the place outside space costs memory, so the heroine spends the self she is trying to defend in order to defend it, and the same journey is how the book finally answers what the enemy actually is. Working a stated cost through to its second-order effects is the thing that put Project Hail Mary at 92, and the first-person voice that carries it is the tight single-POV shape of The Hunger Games 89. The shape of the book is the risk, and it is a well-documented one: reviewers consistently report a slow first half, a quest that reads as a detour from the war framing the story, and the familiar cast replaced almost wholesale by new faces. This log punishes that combination specifically - Lord of the Rings 84 was docked because the story is thin for the number of pages, Catching Fire 83 because the second set piece existed for its own sake rather than to reveal anyone, and Unfinished Tales 69 because the pieces did not connect to each other. A sequel is also not a safe bet here: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on the memory premise and the narrator rather than on the worldbuilding, which is inventive but is mostly new scenery rather than a consequence of anything declared earlier.

Nine short pieces about children and adolescents keeping hold of their dignity in the transports and the camps, written out of the author's own years in Terezin, Auschwitz and a Buchenwald satellite. What is genuinely there is moral seriousness: the stories are built on borderline situations and refuse the consolation that the right choice always wins, and examining what is actually true is what earned the Qureshi memoir 91 rather than the form it was written in. Three things cap it below the line. Short fiction has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points - and separate stories with no single premise leave no worked-out idea to lean on, only glimpses, which is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s here. The protagonists are children observed from inside, and that pairing produced the log's lowest entry of all, a first-person child testimony abandoned at 40, and dropped Narnia to 67 partly for the same reason. And it is unrelieved: sustained bleakness is the mildest recorded objection but a real one, 1984 at 60 for being too depressing, with none of the companionship that lifts a grim book. Leaned on the dignity-and-motive thread rather than on the historical weight of the subject, because weight of subject has never by itself scored well for this reader.

t: Den, kdy padla noc (A Day of Fallen Night)
why: The declared question is a good one and the book is genuinely built on it: an order of warrior sisters has trained for five hundred years against an enemy that never came, the younger ones have started saying out loud that their whole institution is pointless - and then the enemy wakes. Set beside a princess whose only recognised function is to bear an heir she did not choose, it leaves behind the thought that institutions and dynasties outlive their reasons and go on collecting the same sacrifices anyway. That is a premise with consequences rather than a backdrop. The stronger asset is the lead: a woman of about fifty, the kind of character normally parked in a mentor's chair to hand a sword to somebody younger, carried here as the actual heroine, and reviewers consistently name her the standout of the book. Interesting and worth rooting for is what separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by twenty-two points, and it lands on the right side here, which is why the number leans on her rather than on the setting. The deductions are structural. It is 868 pages and there is broad agreement that the central plot only properly starts after a long stretch of buildup - thin story for the page count is the penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 and Les Miserables to 71, and it bites harder in a book that is slower still. One of the four viewpoints is reported as the weak one, spread across four separate continents. Two life-phase pushbacks, a woman of fifty and a girl of fifteen, are worth a couple of points between them and nothing more, since The Little Prince 82 shows the rule bends when the ideas carry. Magic is invented, drawn from a tree and from the stars, and the gods prayed to are the book's own inventions, so the occult filter does not engage. Not leaned on worldbuilding: the world is inherited rather than newly worked out, and Artemis 69 is what leaning that way costs. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: prayer to the book's invented gods - is a prayer or offering shown in a scene?

One premise declared precisely and then followed: take a species whose cognition is nothing like ours, uplift it, and work out what it actually builds. The answer here is a civilisation of octopuses whose thought is distributed through their arms and which therefore settles disagreements by broadcasting emotional state rather than by argument, set against an alien on a neighbouring world that cannot be negotiated with at all because it has no concept of a separate self. Second-order consequences genuinely explored is exactly what put Project Hail Mary 92 eight points above The Martian 82 by the reader's own account, and coming to understand an alien culture from the inside is what put Speaker for the Dead 90 above Ender's Game 87; this book is built on both at once, which is why the range sits in the A band. Structure is legible rather than confusing. Two strands - a terraforming crew in the past, a joint expedition in the present - kept apart by tense as well as by heading, each opening on one concrete situation, and reviewers describe the interleaving as tension-driven rather than withholding. That is not the several-plot-lines-at-once failure that ended Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic at 30, though three protagonist groups is more than the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89. The ceiling is set by the lead. Attention is split across humans, spiders and octopuses with no one person to root for, and while The Silmarillion 80 proves that can survive, Artemis 69 is the recorded failure of predicting a book up on its world while the lead was visibly thin - so the high is deliberately capped rather than pushed into the high eighties. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 fell to 70 for the ones that followed, the steepest decline recorded. Bleakness arrives as dread rather than sustained misery, closer to Animal Farm 78 than 1984 60, and a stretch of roughly sixty pages without dialogue is the density risk. No occult and no investigation.

Naming the idea is the problem: rebuilding a fleet and training replacements is a situation, not something the book leaves behind, and I would list ideas as a risk here rather than as what carries the number. That is the usual reason a readable book settles in the 60s for this reader, as with Narnia 67. Worse, the specific complaint reviewers make is the one this reader has actually walked out on a book for: a chase whose stated scarcities - fuel, food, exhaustion - are announced but never felt. Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned in its first chapters purely because a declared resource did not behave like a scarce one, so a book that names its constraints and then ignores them is exposed at exactly the point where this log is least forgiving. It stays in the 60s rather than lower because the narration is a single legible first-person line with no confusing opening, no occult, no investigation and no crude sexual treatment - the same clean profile that keeps Exodus 68 comfortably above the C band.

Two brothers meet over the mountain house their father left behind when he killed himself. One never left the valley and wants to raise a child in that house; the other has been felling timber in Canada for years and wants his share in cash; and a concealed ski-lift project makes the land suddenly worth a fortune. That is a declared premise whose consequences actually play out, and the book spends itself on what each brother wants rather than on what happens, the axis that lifts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Two things hold it down. It is 123 pages for a subject - inherited land, drink, fraternal violence - that Italian reviewers split hard over, one calling it short and forgettable and too slight for what it takes on. And it is unrelieved: a poacher father dead by his own hand, two sons who cannot stop once they start drinking, and someone shooting dogs along the river. Sustained bleakness is this reader's mildest recorded objection, but it is still the one that took 1984 to 60. I leaned on motives rather than on ideas because the fraternal motive is the thing the book demonstrably does, while whether the theme lands in that space is precisely what the reviews disagree about.

It opens on one concrete situation - a girl and her father waiting in a petrol station car park in early 1957 for the dragon they have hired - which is exactly the legible start this reader asks for and the opposite of the several-lines-at-once opening that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 in their first pages. It also has something to think about, and the fantasy is doing the thinking: a Japanese American family still not accepted after internment, a racist deputy, and an argument over whether dragons have souls all run on the same rails, so the premise earns its keep rather than decorating. Three deductions hold it here. The narration is spread over four perspectives, one of them a goddess, and reviewers report the point of view switching at unexpected places inside chapters - not the confusion filter, since the first chapters are grounded, but a legibility cost that runs the whole length. The prophecy is the engine rather than a background detail, driven by a worshipping cult acting on divine instruction, and that axis is graded on how reverently it is handled. Heaviest: the book declares its alternate 1957 in detail - a treaty, dragons as ordinary as cats, a Cold War - and then pivots to a parallel world where dragons never existed. This reader verifies declared worlds, and Divergent 58 sits in the C band precisely for a premise assembled from borrowed pieces that does not cohere. Leaned on ideas and motives rather than worldbuilding, because worldbuilding is the axis most likely to take this below the range, not above it. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: one of four POVs is a goddess - is she petitioned in a scene?

The engine is whether history can be steered at all once there are people who can read and quietly rewrite minds, and both halves are a contest of deduction in which the reveal is laid in fairly before it lands. Golden Son at 92 is scored up for exactly that quality, reveals that were logical and consistent with what came before rather than sprung, so a properly built twist is worth real points here. Each half also opens on one legible situation: a conqueror who cannot strike because he does not know where his enemy is, and later a girl secretly recording her father's visitor. The deductions are three and they accumulate. Two long sections sixty years apart share no cast, which is the Unfinished Tales complaint at 69 about pieces not connected to each other. A fourteen-year-old carries the second half, the small pushback Narnia at 67 records and that marked Ender's Game down to 87. And there is very little interior life, because most page time is spent reasoning rather than wanting, which is the reader's heaviest axis. Leaned on the idea, because the puzzle is what the book is, and not on the protagonist, who arrives late and loses agency once the plan needs her. Investigation-shaped but not a mystery: the payoff is where an organisation is hidden, not who committed a crime.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection at the same time, which is where this reader's returns are measurably thinnest: fifteen small episodes from the everyday lives of a city's inhabitants, most of them deliberately withheld from resolution. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and adds nothing. There is one idea and it can be named - lives that cannot move, stagnation taken for ordinary life - but it is atmospheric rather than a premise declared and then worked out, and the declared-and-worked-out kind is what earns the high scores here, so it belongs in risks rather than carrying the number. The closest read comparison is Unfinished Tales 69, marked down explicitly because the pieces are not logically connected to each other; fifteen unrelated casts with no continuous plot is more fragmented still. Sustained gloom costs a little on top - 1984 60 was too depressing. On the credit side the prose is legible, each story opens on one concrete situation, and nothing trips a hard filter. Leaned on the collection form and the mood rather than on the ideas, and did no further research.

One curse is declared precisely - it takes a man overnight, leaves him neither living nor dead, and every injury he suffers keeps hurting forever - and the book is largely its consequences: what a city of the uncured does to itself, and what a kingdom does with the neighbours it can no longer explain. The number rests on motive rather than action. The strongest thread is a priest sent to convert a kingdom under a three-month ultimatum who argues honestly against his own faith while doing it, and a foreign princess whose war is political manoeuvring rather than battle; that is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both score on, page time on what people want and why rather than on what they do. Faith runs as a thread inside a story instead of being the subject, which is the shape this reader accepts. Two deductions keep it under the top band. Three viewpoints rotate on a fixed one-chapter cycle from the start, and the author states himself that two chapters in three jump backward in time to overlap the third, so a reader is holding three situations early; legible rather than confusing, but every 30 in this log is a confusing opening, so it is the risk that could take the number below the range. And the lead is widely reported as the weakest of the three, near-flawless and relentlessly cheerful, so I did not lean up on the magic system however carefully built it is - Artemis 69 is the measured price of a thin lead beside sound world-logic. The ceiling is set by Hobbit 84 and Lord of the Rings 84: fantasy this reader liked without a protagonist he loved.

I cannot name an idea this book puts on the table. The war, the enemy and the narrator are all already standing, and what is added is a campaign, a famine on an ice moon and a standoff between human fleets - events rather than something left behind. That is the most common way a competent book stalls in the 60s for this reader: Narnia 67 was marked down for lacking higher things to think about and Ranger's Apprentice 74 for being easy with little to think about. It should stay out of the 50s, because one first-person narrator on one assignment at a time keeps the opening legible - the axis that ended three books at 30 - and there is no occult, no investigation and no crude sexual treatment to dock. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, and Catching Fire 83 was docked specifically for an arena that existed for its own sake, which is the risk when a war continues for its own sake. Leaned on the legible opening and the momentum; the ideas are the risk, not the support.

A gothic standalone that is mostly atmosphere. A girl with no voice inherits a house with a wall she is forbidden to cross, and roughly the first two thirds are her walking the corridors and reading her mother's journal while very little happens; reviewers put that stretch at a handful of story days. That is precisely the log's penalty term - a thin story spread over pages, plus description and digression - and it is what cost The Lord of the Rings 84 the tier its ideas would otherwise have reached, and what left Les Miserables 71 below The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Here there is less to offset it. The communication thread is real and is the best thing in the book, a mute protagonist whose signing and drawing are how she is known at all; but the central proposition amounts to choosing the living over the dead, which is nearer a mood than something left behind, and Quo Vadis 66 and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 are where well-made books without higher ground settle in this log. Reviewers also report the resolution arriving in a rush after that long build and the cousin relationship never developing, either of which would pull it under the range. No hard filter fires: the opening is one legible situation, a girls' school and then one house, and the death figure, the ghouls and the bone shards are the author's invention rather than anything drawn from real occultism. Leaned on story density and the shortage of ideas rather than on the prose, because beautiful writing is not an idea and this log has never paid for it.

t: Gentleman v Moskve (A Gentleman in Moscow)
why: One premise declared with complete precision - a man is sentenced in 1922 to spend the rest of his life inside a single hotel, and will be shot if he steps outside - and the whole book is its consequences. That is the shape Project Hail Mary 92 is praised for: a declared condition whose second-order effects actually get explored. It opens on one concrete legible situation, a tribunal transcript and then an attic room, so the confusion that put The Gunslinger and The Colour of Magic on 30 is absent. One protagonist, a third person extending only from him, and nearly all the page time on what he wants and why rather than on what he does - the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both top. It leaves an idea that can be stated in a phrase: how a person keeps purpose and dignity when his circumstances are fixed for good. The deductions are real but bounded. It is historical fiction, and historical fiction in this log settles between Quo Vadis 66 and The Count of Monte Cristo 75, chiefly where sprawl and digression cost - and the middle of this book leaps across three decades in widening episodes, which is thin story over many pages, the objection that cancelled the extra ideas in The Lord of the Rings 84. The Soviet backdrop adds mild bleakness, though the treatment is warm rather than grim. No occult, no crudeness, no investigation. Held under the high 80s on density rather than on protagonist, because the lead is the part of this book least in doubt.

The setup is worth something: two friends put on opposite sides of a siege with a captured sister between them, so allegiance and loyalty are in genuine conflict, and friendship is the thing that carried The Hobbit to 84 and The Lord of the Rings to 84 in this log. Against that, the mode is battle-forward military adventure whose outcome history has already fixed, and reviewers of this author's Punic-war writing praise the descriptive combat while granting the plot holds no real surprises. Page time goes to how a siege is fought rather than to what the men want, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 win on, and easy well-researched adventure with little to think about is what left Ranger's Apprentice at 74. I lean on the two leads and their competing loyalties, because that is the only thing here that can push the number toward the top of the range; I do not lean on an idea left behind, because I doubt there is one past the cost of war, and that doubt is what caps it. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70.

An orphaned, lame girl kept alive only because her hands are useful, in a village that discards the weak, set to embroider the robe on which the village's own history and future are stitched. The idea is nameable in a phrase - whoever holds the picture of the past owns what a people believe about itself - and that is the axis that carries short work in this log, since Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both scored on ideas rather than on plot. The lead is worth rooting for and interesting with it, the pairing that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points. It opens on one concrete situation, a girl about to be judged for existing, which is the opposite of the several-plot-lines-at-once start that put The Colour of Magic on 30. Nothing occult: the gift is invented, and an invented system is explicitly fine however elaborate. Held under the high 70s because the prose is spare and functional rather than a pleasure in itself, the lead is a teenager and that is a standing small pushback, and the society is the part most likely to break under thought - a village that culls the weak yet feeds and lies to three gifted orphans has to cohere, and an engineered society that does not is exactly what put Divergent at 58. Leaned on the idea and the protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding, because the world is the part I would not bet on.

The idea can be named in a phrase and it is actually worked out rather than gestured at: feed the world by herding whales like cattle, then let a religious leader argue that killing creatures of that order is murder, and make the man who runs the farms answer him - which he does, by changing his mind and losing the argument he was paid to win. A book that leaves an idea behind is what lifts a modest story in this log; that is how a short allegory reached Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 with no other advantage. Two further things fit this reader: the ending turns on going down for other people rather than on solo survival, which is the difference he named between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82, and the belief question is a thread inside the story rather than the subject of it. Deductions are real. Reviewers call the lead thin with only the religious leader standing out, and a flat protagonist is the whole 16-point gap from Project Hail Mary 92 to Artemis 69. The book is episodic in three parts with a mentor's death dividing it, so momentum breaks in the middle - the same objection that put Catching Fire 83 below The Hunger Games 89. The opening is a single clear thread, a man waking from a nightmare about space, so the failure that ended three books at 30 does not apply. Leaned on the idea and put the protagonist in the risks deliberately, since that is the axis that has misfired before.

The case for this one is payoff: long-built arcs close and characters who parted far back cross paths again, which is the kind of earned reveal that put Golden Son at 92 - consistent with what came before rather than sprung. The lead ends as someone worth rooting for rather than a figure in slow moral decline, and that single axis is worth 22 points here, the gap between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. The deductions are large and specific. Reviewers describe near-continuous duels, showdowns and battles across 717 pages, and action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader: Mockingjay took the top of its trilogy at 91 for showing the most motive and the least arena, and this is that trade run backwards. A book that is mostly battle is also a thin story over many pages, which is the named penalty term, not length. A sequel besides, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. I leaned on the lead rather than on momentum, because relentless fighting produces pace whether or not anything is at stake in it. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived pantheon - Source question, plus is any rite shown in a scene?

t: Inzerat na dum, ve kterem uz nechci bydlet (Inzerat na dum, ve kterem uz nechci bydlet)
why: Seven stories about people the 1950s pushed to the bottom - tradesmen, lawyers and philosophers shovelling ingots at the Kladno steelworks - and the strongest thing in its favour is the kind of understanding it offers: what it is like to be inside a group the state has written off. That is the axis that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, and here it comes with the wants and the talk foregrounded over the events, the axis behind Mockingjay 91. Two deductions. The tone is unrelieved - forced labour, discarded lives, and the author deliberately declines to turn it into criticism, so the misery is on the page without a conclusion drawn from it, and 1984 60 is the log's warning about exactly that. And two of the seven are described as barely narrative at all, closer to lyric bands than stories, so a reader wanting one legible starting situation gets prose poetry instead. I leaned on motives rather than on the testimony axis because this is fiction and the profile is clear that the memoir form earns nothing by itself.

t: Jak byt zenou (How to Be a Woman)
why: This is a broad-topic feminist memoir, not a book built around a sexual relationship or behaviour, so filter 6 does not apply. On the memoir-form axis, what earns points for this reader is examining what is actually true and giving insight into how another group experiences the world - the standard Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 set, against the counter-example of Anne Frank 40, the same form that failed to work. This book gives real insight into a woman's experience of body and work, but reads more as personal opinion and manifesto than the rigorous examination of truth that carried Qureshi, capping it well under the S band. Moderate volume and explicit content on the sexual-content axis (masturbation and body chapters) cost further, though the crude-humor register itself is not the objection per this reader's own rule, and reviewers largely call the treatment frank rather than crude.

t: Jak stvorit divku (How to Build a Girl)
why: The plot is Johanna's self-reinvention as Dolly Wilde across several threads at once - family poverty, a music-criticism career, class identity, and sexual exploration - so sex is one thread among several rather than the reason the book exists, and filter 6 does not fire. The protagonist is repeatedly described as witty, self-aware and sympathetic, and this reader's rule ranks a rootable lead above worldbuilding or plot mechanics whenever they compete - the clearest case in the log is Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, docked 22 points from Sunrise on the Reaping 87 purely on an unrootable lead, so a genuinely likeable teenage lead here is a real positive. Moderate volume and explicit content cost on the sexual-content axis, but the treatment is repeatedly described as comedic and self-aware rather than crude, which keeps the deduction from compounding as hard as it otherwise would.

t: Jasno lepo podstin zhyna (Spill Simmer Falter Wither)
why: A fifty-seven-year-old recluse adopts a one-eyed dog bred for badger baiting and talks to it through four seasons. The interiority is real and it is the whole book, which is the axis the log rewards most - Red Rising 95 tops it for spending more time on thoughts and motives than on action - and that is why this is the low 60s rather than the 50s. The problem is what the book leaves behind. Named honestly, the idea is loneliness rendered beautifully: a mood, not a thought, and reviewers agree the first half is close to plotless before an aimless road trip that slows again. A thin story spread over many pages is the standing penalty, the sparseness that held The Lord of the Rings 84 to a tie despite far greater ideas, and sustained bleakness is a mild further discount, as 1984 60 records. Because the idea is the part I would not bet on, no further research was done.

t: Jiskra v popelu (An Ember in the Ashes)
why: The opening is a genuine strength and worth saying first: one concrete legible situation from page one - a night raid on a house, grandparents killed, a brother dragged away - and two first-person narrators who each want one nameable thing. Tight narration and constant momentum is what makes The Hunger Games 89 the baseline favourite here, and both leads are interesting and rootable, which is the axis that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Ballad 65 by 22 points. What decides the number is the supernatural furniture. The author says in two interviews that the jinn, efrits and ghuls come from the Middle Eastern folklore her mother told her, and that the order of seers is modelled on the Pythia at Delphi; that is borrowed real-world material rather than an invented system, and it is the most expensive thing in this log - Percy Jackson 57, marked down because the Greek pantheon counts and not just witchcraft, and Harry Potter 51 for magic drawn from historical witchcraft. On top of that the themes stop at resistance and complicity with nothing worked out past them, and events with nothing to think about is what put Narnia at 67. Leaned on the occult axis rather than on the protagonist axis, because the protagonists are the part that would argue this number upward. Outstanding check: jinn and efrits from Middle Eastern folklore, Augurs modelled on the Pythia at Delphi - is the borrowed material enough to fail Source?

A curated selection of Bradbury's 1950-1964 stories, and what carries the number is the ideas: each piece declares one situation - a man who becomes afraid of his own skeleton, a house that goes on serving breakfast after its family is gone - and spends its length on the consequence rather than on plot. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score on, and it is why this sits in the 70s rather than the 60s. Two deductions hold it there. Seventy separate stories cannot pay the reader's heaviest axis at all: there is nobody to want anything for longer than twenty pages, and the log has already priced a book of disconnected pieces at Unfinished Tales 69, whose stated fault was that the parts are not logically connected to each other. Bradbury is also atmospheric by method, and description carrying little story is a standing penalty. Leaning on ideas rather than on the protagonist axis is deliberate, because the protagonist axis has nothing to grip here, and The Silmarillion 80 is the log's proof that a book with no continuous lead and dense prose can still land well when the ideas are large. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: seventy stories, not verified one by one; does any piece enact a real-world rite?

t: Klara a Slunce (Klara and the Sun)
why: Opens in a shop window with one narrator who never leaves the frame, and the case rests on her: a machine whose entire motive is another person's good, who spends herself for a sick child with nothing to gain. That is precisely what this log rewarded in Project Hail Mary 92 - companionship instead of isolation, and self-sacrifice to save others rather than personal survival - and the narration is nothing but motive and inference, the axis behind Red Rising 95 and Speaker for the Dead 90. There is a real idea to carry away: whether a person is an irreplaceable centre or a learnable set of behaviours, put to the one narrator who has to answer it in practice. Two things hold the range down. The world is asserted rather than worked out - gene-edited children and displaced workers are foregrounded as the subject and the society is never reorganised around them, the same breach that cost Harry Potter 51 its worldbuilding. And the narrator builds a private devotion to the sun, addresses pleas to it and destroys a machine as an offering, on the page; it is her own invention with no root in real occult practice, so the hard filter does not fire, but Percy Jackson 57 shows that a devotional frame aimed at a real object of worship costs points here. The plot is also quiet and thin for its length, the charge that held The Lord of the Rings to 84. Leaned on protagonist and ideas and deliberately not on the world, since the one recorded prediction failure in this log came from leaning up on worldbuilding.

Stopping early because the idea is the thing I would list as the risk, and that is the sharpest separator available. What the book is: a dying-Earth novel told as a written testament by a prisoner in a swamp penal colony below the last human city, working backwards through how he got there, episodic and non-linear. The Clarke Award shortlist assessment is that it is a series of events rather than an overarching concept, and that it reproduces the furniture of the subgenre without extending it. Measured against real scores that reading is unforgiving. A competent book with nothing to leave behind stalls in the sixties - The Chronicles of Narnia 67 was marked down in almost those words, for lacking higher things to think about - and an episodic story stretched over great length is the named penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 and Les Miserables to 71. Sustained bleakness adds a smaller deduction on top: a swelling sun, a prison, and an ending reviewers describe as fizzling out, with solo endurance rather than companionship, and 1984 60 is what unrelieved gloom costs here. The memoir frame earns nothing by itself either - the same first-person testament form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and a DNF at 40, so the form is neutral and only the examination inside it pays. What could lift it is invention and prose, and the range is set where it is because prose alone has never moved a number in this log. The number leans on length against a thin plot and on the bleakness, not on the idea, which is precisely the thing in doubt.

The reason this cannot be estimated high is its construction, not its author. The book is a montage that interleaves excerpts from two earlier prose texts, alternating chapter by chapter - the author himself described zipping them into each other by the pattern of an acacia leaf - so from the first pages a reader is tracking two unrelated strands, one a philosophising monologue that drifts and one a story about an artist. That is the log's single most reliable negative: Guards! Guards! 30, The Colour of Magic 30 and The Gunslinger 30 were all abandoned in their first chapters for several things starting at once with none of them legible, and this is that shape by design. The second deduction is that it was cleared for publication under normalisation and the philosophical, erotic and grotesque passages were cut, which removes the part that would have left an idea behind and leaves the mood. I leaned on motives - the artist strand does have a man with clear wants, and that is the axis behind Speaker for the Dead 90 - rather than on ideas, which the censorship is precisely what damaged.

t: Kocka a cert (The Cat and the Devil)
why: Graded, not excluded: the children's filter was retired on 2026-08-26 and this is now a question of how far toward a children's book it sits, which here is as far as it goes. Joyce wrote it on 10 August 1936 as a letter in deliberately simple language to his four-year-old grandson, retelling the folk legend of the bridge at Beaugency, and it has only ever been printed as an illustrated picture book; the Czech edition follows that form with a named illustrator. The positive case is real but small - a devil outwitted by a literal reading of his own bargain is an idea nameable in a phrase, and the short-form rule suspends the character and emotion tests. But that suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and The Little Prince 82 is the measure of what a children's book has to carry to score: an idea a grown reader keeps turning over. A ten-minute nursery anecdote carries nothing of that weight, which puts it below Anne Frank 40, the lowest completed score in the log, on reading experience rather than on subject. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the idea is present and simply too slight to lift the number, and the register is what decides it.

The religion and the power are invented, so the Source test passes, but failing Depiction alone is now a veto and this file's own flag had already named the devotions as the thing the Depiction test would catch.

Close third person anchored on one young man learning his trade under an older commander whose respect he wants: that is page time on what a character wants and why, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and it is far nearer the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89 than a rotating cast. The idea is stated by reviewers rather than invented by me - a generation that inherited a famous victory has to work out who it is now, personally and as a people - and the middle of the book deliberately is not battle: a marriage, an assembly, a man paying for a tragedy at a city festival. The lead is both interesting and worth rooting for, the pairing that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points on the protagonist alone, and his status is earned on the page rather than granted, so unearned competence does not bite. Held down by two complaints reviewers actually make: the cultural and military exposition is called explanatory even by the standards of the genre, and the middle is called slow - a thin stretch spread over many pages is what cancelled The Lord of the Rings 84 against The Hobbit 84 despite the larger ideas. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. Leaned on the lead and his motives rather than on the campaigns, because predicting a book up on spectacle while the interior is thin is the error that put Artemis at 80 against a real 76. Outstanding check: the Delphic oracle and Greek sacrifice - is divination or sacrifice enacted in a scene?

Chapter one is one concrete situation - an eighteen-year-old driven home from a work farm to a foreclosed farm, a plan to take his small brother west, and then two stowaways in the trunk who send him east instead - so the confusing-opening failure that put The Gunslinger and The Colour of Magic on 30 does not fire. The substance is motive: each perspective exists to say what that person wants and why, which is the page time this reader values above action, and the ten-day frame keeps events moving. The deductions are structural and specific. The book runs on eight perspectives, two in first person and six in third, with sections as short as three pages across nearly six hundred pages, and reviewers report the shifts reading as obtrusive and the whole as disjointed - that is the multi-POV cost plus a thin story spread wide, the objection that held The Lord of the Rings 84 down and that separates Les Miserables 71 from the tighter Monte Cristo 75. Worse for this reader, the one character kept at third-person distance is the central one, and reviewers say he is the hardest of the cast to feel connected to; a lead who is not interesting is the entire 16-point gap between Artemis 69 and Project Hail Mary 92. Leaned on multi-POV and protagonist rather than on ideas, because the journey-as-heroic-quest thread does leave something behind and is not what limits the number.

t: Mapa a uzemi (La carte et le territoire)
why: An artist photographs Michelin road maps and finds the map more alive than the land it stands for, and around that runs a quiet thread about work, fame and an aging father. There is a real idea in it - what a representation is worth against the thing represented, and what a life of work amounts to - and this reader rewards a book that leaves something behind, which is what puts Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 where they are. The cap is the lead. Reviewers describe Jed Martin as an emotional vacuum with almost no inner life outside his studio and his supermarket runs, and Artemis was docked to 76 purely because the protagonist was not interesting while the world logic was fine. Then the final third drops the artist novel for a police investigation with a new cast, which is the shape this reader avoids on principle, and several reviewers say the book never recovers from it. I leaned on protagonist rather than on ideas because ideas are the axis that shows up on both sides of this reader's line while a flat or unlovable lead has never been forgiven: 22 points separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 on rootability alone. The melancholy is priced in mildly, and the sexual material is clinical rather than juvenile, which the log says costs little.

Written and published for readers of eight to twelve, and it reads that way: a single twelve-year-old narrator, a haunting-of-the-week shape, and an idea I cannot state in a sentence beyond 'the dead linger and someone has to send them on'. The log is explicit that a competent book with nothing higher to think about stalls in the 60s, and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 is docked for exactly that combination - a child lead plus no higher ground - which is the closest thing in this reader's record to what is on offer here. Reviewers describe the narrator herself as flat, with the ghost sidekick carrying the personality, and that matters more than the world does: the rules of the spirit realm are reported as carefully built and consistently kept, but the recorded Artemis 69 miss came from predicting a book up on a solid world while the lead was thin, and the profile puts protagonist above worldbuilding when the two compete. There is also an occult deduction to price in. The mechanism is invented - a curtain between living and dead, a mirror pendant, a spoken phrase that releases a spirit - and no witchcraft, seance or divination is performed on the page, so no hard filter fires on the evidence I found. But the frame is real-world paranormal investigation at real haunted sites, and Percy Jackson 57 records how far this reader marks a book down when the supernatural is taken from what people actually believe rather than invented whole. Leaned on the thin idea and the flat lead rather than on the world; the range is kept wide low because that occult deduction could take it under.

Family, loyalty and honour are the declared subject here rather than decoration, and that is the axis The Lord of the Rings 84 scored on for this reader - with Tolkien's own drag removed, because 661 pages here carry a thick plot rather than the thin story that cancelled out those ideas. Roughly half the book sits with a blacksmith's son whose wants are legible and who is easy to root for: interesting and rootable at once, which is what put Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of the log. Deductions: the ideas are conventional good against evil, and thin ideas are what held The Chronicles of Narnia to 67 and Ranger's Apprentice to 74; the escalation into set-piece battle is the same drag that cost Golden Son 92 its three points against Red Rising 95. Sexual treatment costs nothing - what is reported is implicit rather than crude, and Red Rising 95 shows presence is not the objection. I leaned on motives and the lead rather than on the invented angelology, because predicting up on worldbuilding over a thin lead is the recorded mistake that put Artemis at 80 when it scored 76. The number is conditional on one thing: seven points of view spread over a continent are running by the early chapters, and a confusing opening is the only cause in this log that has ever produced a 30. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived names (Elyon, Asroth, Ben-Elim, Kadoshim) on an invented pantheon - does that make the Source real-world, and is any rite shown?

A collection of newspaper columns and interviews, so there is no premise to work out and nothing whose consequences can be followed; the axis that most often decides a number here is missing by construction. The form earns nothing by itself in this log - first-person non-fiction produced both a 91 and a walked-away 40 - and what earned the 91 was sustained examination of what is actually true, which weekly pieces on caffeine, celebrities, Twitter and a royal wedding do not attempt. Short pieces have the character and emotion rules suspended, but that suspension only removes penalties and never adds points, so what is left is a witty book with nothing to leave behind: the stall that put The Chronicles of Narnia at 67 for lacking higher things to think about, plus the fragmentation charge that took Unfinished Tales to 69 for pieces not logically connected to each other. Recorded rather than rejected, because nothing here trips a hard filter.

A ghost story written and published for readers of eight to twelve, and its idea is about as nameable as the form allows here: a girl who nearly drowned is hunted by an emissary of death, and the real question is what she owes the dead friend who only exists because she did not die. That is want-and-why material, and companionship plus self-sacrifice over solo survival is the axis that puts Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. But it is carried by a twelve-year-old narrator in a book built to the same city-plus-a-haunting template as the ones before it, and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 records what a child lead and limited higher ground cost together. The occult is the reason the range does not go higher and could go lower. The core mechanism is invented and no ritual drawn from real occultism appears in the chapter recaps I could reach, so no hard filter fires on the evidence I have; but the book states outright that voodoo is real, and where the plot goes for help is a secret society of practitioners with a medium, warded premises, protective amulets and an evil-eye pouch. Percy Jackson 57 is the log's record of what happens when the supernatural is taken from what people actually believe instead of invented whole, and that alone could put this under the range. It is also a sequel, which is not a safe bet here - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Leaned on the idea and the motive thread rather than on the world, which is the same one each time and which has never rescued a book in this log, as Artemis 69 shows. t: My ostatni tu proste zijem (The Rest of Us Just Live Here)
why: One premise declared exactly and then honoured: the apocalypse belongs to the Chosen Ones and is confined to an arch paragraph at the head of each chapter, while the book itself stays with four ordinary kids who want to graduate and are afraid of losing each other. That is the worked-out-consequences shape the log rewards, and it leaves an idea you can state in a phrase - an unremarkable life is not a lesser one - which is what separates a book in the 80s from a competent one stalled in the 60s, as The Chronicles of Narnia 67 was docked for having nothing higher to think about. The lead carries it too: the narrator's OCD is written from the inside as counting, looping and cracked hands rather than as a quirk, and the page time goes to what he wants and why, the interiority that puts Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91 at the top of this log. Deductions. Reviewers report the frame starving the real story of momentum and the Chosen Ones themselves staying flat, so the conceit may thin over the length. A late turn gives a friend inherited divine healing that could simply erase the narrator's condition - a capability declared and then not carried through, the breach that put Divergent 58 and Harry Potter 51 in the C band. And the arch tone puts weight on the prophecy axis, where a chosen-one plot played for ridicule costs and one played straight does not. High-school seniors sit a life-phase step from a reader of 28, worth a point or two and no more. Leaned on ideas and protagonist and not on worldbuilding, because the world here is deliberately thin and the recorded Artemis 69 miss came from predicting a book up on its world while the lead was thin; here the lead is the asset.

One question declared precisely and then paid for: may a court override a seventeen-year-old's religiously grounded refusal of the transfusion that would save him, and what does the court owe him afterwards. The book does not merely pose it - it settles the legal question at the halfway mark and spends the second half on the consequences, which is the premise-worked-out pattern that earns the top scores here. It is also the same rigour the reader singled out in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91: an honest examination of what is actually plausible and believable inside a belief, neither mocking it nor conceding it. Faith runs as a thread inside a story rather than as a subject in its own right, so no deduction falls there. A continuous novel rather than assembled stories, and its engine is motive: a councilman who believes he is being used, a mayor who is in fact using him, and a mentalist who believes a third power is quietly steering both of them. Almost all the page time goes to who wants what and why, which is the axis Mockingjay at 91 and Speaker for the Dead at 90 both top, and the question underneath it - whether a plan that predicts you leaves you anything to decide - is a real idea rather than a mood. Deducted because two plot lines start in parallel, one on a capital world and one on a hidden one, and run separately for roughly half the book. A confusing opening is the reader's one absolute filter, so that is named as the leading risk - but the books it actually ended, Guards! Guards! at 30 and The Colour of Magic at 30, failed on about six illegible lines at once, and two clearly signposted strands each opening on a concrete situation is a pushback rather than that failure. Docked further for talkiness and a slow convergence. Leaned on motive rather than on the setting, because the galaxy here is inherited rather than built, and Artemis at 76 is the reminder that a well-made world rescues nothing on its own. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's Guide fell from 83 to 70.

Held to the low sixties because the book declares a question and then does not answer it. The declared question is whether a galaxy merged into one shared mind is the right future, and the answer arrives as assertion: Kirkus calls the fade-out illogical and the finale artificial, and reviewers describe the argument between individual and collective as repeated rather than developed, across a planet-by-planet travelogue they call frightfully padded. A thin story spread over many pages is the deduction that cancelled out The Lord of the Rings' advantage at 84 and cost Les Miserables its tightness at 71, and Unfinished Tales at 69 records what disconnected episodes do. One day of a ceasefire, one airfield above Jerusalem, one pilot deciding on his own authority to avenge two comrades who did not come back: a concrete starting situation, and 246 pages spent on what a man wants and why rather than on what he does. The case is the idea, and it is stated plainly enough to name: a country taught to want everything on too grand a scale breeds men who chase vastness until it kills them, and a woman can spend a whole life tethered to one of them and still refuse him. t: Prevorstvi u pomerancovniku (The Priory of the Orange Tree)
why: The positive case is a doctrine declared precisely and then taken apart over the whole length. A kingdom's state religion holds that the unbroken bloodline of its queens is the only thing keeping the world's destroyer bound, the book follows what that belief costs the women who have to embody it, and then shows the claim was manufactured - the uncanny resemblance between the queens was a glamour, and the actual binding was a pair of jewels with a fixed thousand-year expiry that nobody had counted. That is a premise whose consequences are worked out rather than asserted, and it leaves an idea behind: the victor writes the history, and a state can rest for a millennium on a lie nobody alive is able to check. Rival accounts of one event, each partly self-serving, is the axis The Silmarillion 80 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. The court plotting also spends real page time on what people want and why rather than on set pieces, and the lead is competent and easy to root for, which is the combination behind Mockingjay 91. Two deductions. It runs past eight hundred pages and two of its four viewpoints do very little for the first few hundred - a thin story spread over many pages is the named penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 despite ideas the reader rated far above The Hobbit's, and that cost Les Miserables its digressions down to 71. And one viewpoint belongs to a self-pitying, resentful exile nobody roots for; that is the exact failure that put The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points under Sunrise on the Reaping 87, discounted here because he is a quarter of the book rather than the whole of it. Magic is invented - power drawn up through a tree and down from the stars - so the occult filter does not engage, and the romance between two women is treated seriously rather than crudely, which costs nothing in a log topped by Red Rising 95. Leaned on the idea and on motive-heavy politics rather than on worldbuilding, because the world here is wide rather than deep and Artemis 69 is the recorded price of predicting a book up on its setting. Three first-person narrators who genuinely want different things - a boy, a girl, and the branded survivor of the massacre committed against his own people - and the question the book is actually about is whether any of them can avoid becoming what they are fighting. Golden Son 92 stands high in this log precisely because its characters each think and want differently, and giving the wronged non-human species its own interiority is the Speaker for the Dead 90 move: an alien culture understood from inside by motive rather than observed from outside, which is the single axis that separates those two Card entries, 90 against 87. The idea states itself in a phrase - war makes monsters of men, and the live question is whether that is a description or an excuse - and the log is clear that having something like that to leave behind is what lifts a competent book out of the 60s, where The Chronicles of Narnia 67 stalled for lacking it. Deductions: three narrators who share most of their scenes means the same events arrive twice, and reviewers report exactly that repetition, which is a legibility and density cost rather than a filter. It is total war from early on with little relief, and 1984 60 records what unrelieved grimness costs, though the weighting is mild and the self-sacrifice that puts Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82 is here in quantity. And it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Leaned on the differentiated cast and the idea rather than on worldbuilding, because the recorded Artemis 69 miss came from predicting up on a world while the lead was thin, and what carries this book is the people.

The positive case is narrow but real: a narrator who is established, competent and easy to root for, carrying command responsibility for people other than himself - and self-sacrifice for others over personal survival is the axis that lifted Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. That is what keeps the number off the floor. Against it, I cannot name an idea the book adds; reviewers describe a long stretch of a tedious posting and a transfer, with little new ground covered. Ideas as a risk rather than a support is what puts a readable book in the 60s here, and a thin story spread over pages is a penalty in its own right - The Lord of the Rings 84 was held down by sparseness for its length and The Martian 82 by an ending that dragged. No filter is touched: a single legible first-person line, no occult, no investigation, no crude sexual treatment.

Both leads are introduced on the first page by what they want and then made to pay for it: one is desperate to be allowed to fight and cannot get anyone to let her, the other is strong enough to fight and has no heart for killing. That is page time on what characters want and why, the axis that put Red Rising at 95 and Mockingjay at 91 at the top of this log, and both are people to root for rather than a slide into ruin - the failure that held The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes to 65 against 87 for the reader's favourite of that author's prequels. There is a nameable idea as well: a minister who uses people as righteous tools, and what being a tool costs the person. The world is honest about itself - what the characters call elf-magic is salvaged technology and the gods are invented, so nothing is asserted that the book then has to fudge, and no real-world occult is practised. Deductions: two viewpoints instead of the tight single narration The Hunger Games got 89 for, an emphasis on romance that reviewers found slackened the tension, teenage leads as a small pushback, and it is a sequel - not a safe bet here, since Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I lean on motive and protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding, because Artemis at 76 is this log's warning against predicting a book up on a consistent world.

The argument of the book is stated out loud - a minister tells his apprentice that a blade in the right hands can be a righteous tool and the apprentice asks who decides whose hands are right - and the plot then tests that to destruction through three characters who have all sworn vengeance. Leaving an idea behind is what separates the top of this log from its competent middle, and vengeance and its price get real page time here, the axis Mockingjay 91 wins on. It opens on one concrete situation, a hall burned in the night with a single royal survivor, so there is something to be invested in immediately instead of the several-lines-at-once confusion that ended Guards! Guards! at 30. Magic is salvaged technology and the pantheon invented, so nothing on the occult axis. Deductions are real: three narrators are introduced early, and reviewers report they are overshadowed by returning power-players who make the actual decisions, which is the thin-lead failure that cost Artemis its whole gap to Project Hail Mary 92; one of the three thinks about little beyond fighting and killing, pushing on rootability the way The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes did at 65; and it is a sequel, never a safe bet here given the fall from 83 to 70 across Hitchhiker's. I lean on the idea and on motive rather than on the leads, because the leads are precisely what I am unsure of.

Sixteen sketches of the people in one weekend-cottage settlement, and the positive case is real: almost all the page time goes on what these neighbours want and why they want it so fiercely - two hunting clubs quarrelling over whose boar it is - which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and the wants are stated through the talkers themselves rather than through incident. Two deductions hold it under the 68 line. The chapters do not connect to each other, and Unfinished Tales 69 was marked down for exactly that - pieces that are not logically joined - while The Silmarillion 80 got away with the same shape only because a mythic frame held it together, and there is no frame here. And what it leaves behind is a mood of affectionate amusement rather than an idea; Narnia 67 stalled on precisely that lack of higher things to think about. I leaned on motives rather than on protagonist because no one recurs long enough to be rooted for, and rather than on ideas because I cannot name the idea in a phrase, which the profile says is itself the finding.

One concrete starting situation in a single first-person voice: a man stuck in a welfare tower with two ways out and a plain reason to want one. That is the structure this log rewards - The Hunger Games 89 is credited to tight single-POV narration and constant momentum, and the three books that ended at 30 all died on several plot lines starting at once, which does not happen here. It also leaves one real thing behind: a soldier recruited out of the underclass and ordered to fire on people who were his neighbours, reviewed repeatedly as the part that sticks. That is more to think about than Ranger's Apprentice 74 offers, which is why the number sits above it. Held under 80 because the book spends more page time on combat than on what people want and why - the same deduction that put Golden Son 92 under Red Rising 95 - and because the Earth half and the alien half read as two loosely joined stories. Leaned on the opening and the momentum rather than on the lead, because reviewers say he barely reacts to the worst thing he does, and predicting up on a possibly thin protagonist is how Artemis was called 80 and scored 76. Sexual content is understated and not crude, so no deduction there; the register is profane, which costs nothing.

t: Spisy 2 : Skrivanek na niti : povidky (Spisy 2: Skrivanek na niti. Povidky)
why: An editorial omnibus of the author's 1960s short prose, running to roughly 475 pages with a critical apparatus, and the good part is that the short prose is built on talkers whose wants are the whole subject - railwaymen, steelworkers, scrap-paper men - which is the motives axis that carries Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91. What keeps it low is the shape of the object rather than the quality of the writing. This is a great many pages with no continuous story anywhere in them, and story density is the recorded penalty term: The Lord of the Rings 84 was docked for a story too thin for its page count and Unfinished Tales 69 for pieces that do not connect, and an assembled reader's edition maximises both at once. A reader who wants one concrete starting situation and to be invested immediately gets a new one every fifteen pages and eighty pages of editorial commentary at the back. I leaned on motives because that is genuinely what the prose spends itself on, and not on ideas, because an assembly of separate cycles has no single premise to leave anything behind.

A short, spare, single-viewpoint novel that opens on one concrete situation - two girls running into occupying soldiers on the way home from school - and never loses that clarity, so the confusing start that put The Gunslinger and Guards Guards on 30 is not the danger. The girl at the centre is worth rooting for and her nerve is the whole book, the axis that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Against that, it is written for nine to thirteen year olds and its moral - ordinary people are obliged to be brave - is delivered plainly and completely, so little is left to work out afterwards; axis:ideas is the risk I would actually list, and that is the commonest reason a competent book settles in the 60s. The nearest comparable actually read is Exodus 68, a historical novel about Jewish survival, and the nearest structural neighbour is The Chronicles of Narnia 67, marked down precisely for child leads and for lacking higher things to think about. A child's inner life has cost a book badly here already, in the 40 given to The Diary of a Young Girl. Leaned on the protagonist rather than on the historical material, because the rescue of the Danish Jews is remarkable in itself and this book reports it rather than examining it - and examining what is actually true is what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91.

The positive case is narrow but real: one concrete military question - the legion against the Macedonian phalanx - carried through a campaign with the ordinary soldier's view of it kept in the foreground, and a well-researched world that behaves consistently costs nothing and adds a little, as it did for The Count of Monte Cristo 75. The deductions are larger. The subject as the book itself presents it is the fighting, the outcome is fixed by history, and manoeuvre described at length is exactly the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cancelled the greater ideas of The Lord of the Rings and left it at 84 rather than higher. Asked what it leaves behind, I can offer nothing better than how these two armies differed, and that is the finding: this is where a competent book stalls in the 60s, the band Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 already occupy. It is also a sequel dependent on a war begun elsewhere, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I lean on momentum rather than on the protagonist because I did not establish that any single lead carries enough interior life to raise the number.

Literary fiction in the form of a collection - one novella set in 1938 Hollywood plus six short stories - and that combination is where the returns are thinnest for this reader. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties; it never adds any, and a collection has no single premise whose consequences can be worked out, which is the thing that actually earns high scores here. The unifying device is formal, two people ending up across a table from each other, and a device is not an idea. The nearest read comparison is Unfinished Tales 69, marked down explicitly because the pieces are not logically connected to each other, and seven unrelated casts is more fragmented than that. The positive case is real, which is why the range is not lower: each piece turns on what one person wants from another, and page time on wants over deeds is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops the log on. Ideas would go in risks rather than carry the number, so no deeper research was done.

The best thing about it is structural: the narration alternates between a Roman centurion and the German chieftain hunting him, and reviewers report both stay three-dimensional and keep the reader's sympathy, with the Roman's quarrel with his superiors deliberately mirroring the German's quarrel with his fellow chiefs. It also opens on a mutiny over late pay and brutal officers rather than on a battle, so the early pages are about grievance and what men want, and that is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95 sit at the top of this log for. The deductions are what hold it under the line. The plot is a punitive campaign whose result is already settled by history, the viewpoint drops further down the ranks to several soldiers as well, and I would not be able to name what the book leaves behind beyond how legionaries lived and fought - which is the thin-ideas stall that left Ranger's Apprentice at 74 despite being an easy read, with historical novels in this log settling around Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66. It is a sequel and it opens years after events narrated elsewhere, and sequels are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70.

The taps stop on page one and the rest of the book is the consequence, hour by hour: a suburb, a queue, a highway, an evacuation. Declaring a resource scarce and then making the world behave as though it were is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 scores on, and it is the exact inverse of the failure that ended Mortal Engines 55 in its first chapters. The opening is one legible situation - a kitchen tap that gives nothing - so no filter fires, and the group that forms is companionship rather than solo survival, which is the difference the log records between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82. Two things hold it out of the 80s. Four narrators plus third-person interludes split the page time, where the log's highest scores are tight single-POV narration and The Hunger Games 89 is credited for precisely that. And the four read as functions before they read as people, where Golden Son 92 was praised because each character thought and wanted something different. So the number leans on the premise and the momentum, not on the characters, because the characters are the part most likely to disappoint. The catalogue summary's search for missing parents is a survival journey, not an investigation.

A ghost story written and published for readers of eight to twelve, and its plot is an identification puzzle: a poltergeist who cannot remember who he was, so the book is the work of finding out his name and how he died in order to release him. What holds it in the 60s is what held The Chronicles of Narnia at 67 - a twelve-year-old lead and very little to think about once the puzzle closes. One thread does reach further: the ghost friend's fear of what he is turning into and his refusal to say how he died is genuine want-and-why material, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95 at the top of this log, but it is a subplot in a children's book rather than its spine.
