A failed writer leaves Milan for a mountain village, cooks in a small restaurant through a ski season, and falls into a deliberately undramatic love. The good part is that the page time goes to what these people want and why they stay or leave, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 at the top of its trilogy and Speaker for the Dead 90 above Ender's Game 87. What I cannot name is the idea it leaves behind. Reviewers describe the mountain itself as the real main character and the plot as pared to nothing on purpose, and readers report attention drifting and having to go back; the takeaway comes out as live where you are happy, which is a mood rather than a thought. Wanting higher things to think about is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s for this reader - The Chronicles of Narnia took 67 with that as an explicit reason, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 was marked easy to read but with not much to think about. At 158 pages there is no story-density penalty to add, so this sits where a well-made book with a slight idea sits and not lower. I leaned on motives rather than on ideas because the character work is real and sourced, while the idea is the part I would bet against.

BLOCKED on the occult filter 2026-08-26, when the reader ruled that failing EITHER test is a veto. The villain's power runs on human sacrifice to Abaddon, a demon taken from Revelation. That is sacrifice to a real deity, which fails the Source test outright, and failing either test is now a veto - so the depiction question this estimate could not source no longer has to be settled.

Three famous battles carry the book and each is handed to a different commander, which is set-piece structure - and set-piece action with no character revelation is what docked Catching Fire 83 for being an arena for its own sake, and what kept Golden Son 92 a notch under Red Rising 95 because chapters got skimmed to reach the next event. Reviewers who liked it still report that covering every celebrated moment leaves the narrative bitty and the character resolutions anti-climactic, and that its emotional weight leans on attachments formed before it rather than rebuilt inside it; sequels are not safe bets in this log either, Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. There is one idea worth having - a city ostracises the man who saved it, and free men pick their own generals badly - but it arrives as a fact of history rather than as something the book works out, so axis:ideas is where I expect it to stall, and that is the commonest reason a competent book settles in the 60s. The band is set by the historical novels actually read: Quo Vadis 66, Exodus 68, The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Leaned on the interior time given to a cunning politician rather than on the fighting, because the fighting is the part this reader skims. Single first-person narration with one concrete opening situation - an attack, an alien ship defecting mid-battle, and the pilot who takes its passenger's place undercover - which is the shape of this reader's baseline favourite, The Hunger Games 89, tight single POV and constant momentum. The premise is a real idea and it is worked out instead of asserted: a galactic society that congratulates itself on being peaceful has in fact bred aggression out of itself, hires the fighting it disowns, and keeps its monopoly on faster-than-light travel as the lever that holds the species it calls lesser in dependence. Most of the page time goes on the heroine discovering from inside that the enemy is not what she was told, which is exactly the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 scores on - understanding an alien culture rather than defeating it - and the axis that made Mockingjay 91 the best of its trilogy, motives shown and set pieces withheld. Three deductions, all graded. A teen lead is a couple of points here, never a tier. Competence is partly given rather than earned: she arrives an ace and the disguise is a convenient piece of equipment, the failure mode that sank Divergent 58 when carried too far. And a sequel is not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on motive and premise rather than on the flying, because dogfights are the part Golden Son 92 was actually docked for.

t: Vyslapana cara (A Line Made by Walking)
why: A twenty-five-year-old artist retreats to her dead grandmother's bungalow after a breakdown, photographs the dead animals she finds and quizzes herself on works of art. Reviewers agree it almost entirely eschews plot in favour of contemplative vignettes moving between the present, the city she fled and a rural childhood. Asked whether the idea holds, the honest answer is that the subject is a state rather than a proposition, and that is exactly what leaves a competent literary novel in the 60s. Two further discounts: pieces that are not logically connected to each other is the stated reason Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest of its author by a clear margin, and sustained depression is bleakness, which 1984 60 prices as real but mild. It earns back a little for giving genuine page time to what the narrator wants and why - the axis Red Rising 95 tops - and for an inner life close to the reader's own phase, which is why the range is the low 60s and not lower.

t: Vzdycky budeme mit Pariz (We'll Always Have Paris: Stories)
why: Twenty-one previously unpublished late stories, and the reason for a low-60s range is that there is no idea here to lean on. Reviewers converge on short sketches with a truncated sense of incompleteness, several reading as reworked material that had been set aside, and the author's own introduction tells the reader to enjoy the stories rather than think about them - the exact opposite of what earns points in this log. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties: Animal Farm 78 scores because its one idea is sharp, not because it is short. Without that, what is left is lyrical mood with no continuous character to invest in, and disconnected fragments are what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of its author's range. Nothing trips a hard filter, and clearing the filters is not a case for reading.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography: a humorous run of episodes from the author's own life - looking for a partner, her marriages, absorbing the partners her children brought home, a son's wedding, trips with her mother. The one structural thing in its favour is a through-line, one life told in rough order, so it is not a heap of unconnected pieces - and unconnected pieces is exactly the complaint that made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. Light domestic comedy attempts neither, and 'not much to think about' is what held Ranger's Apprentice to 74 and The Chronicles of Narnia to 67, both with far more plot behind them than this has. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but that suspension only removes penalties; it never adds points, so there is nothing to lift it back over the line. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk here.

A young poet is raised by an adoring mother into the Stalinism of 1948, and his lyricism curdles until he denounces his girlfriend's brother and sends her to prison. The idea is named precisely and the whole book is its consequences: that the lyrical age, adolescence itself, is the psychology that makes a young man useful to terror. This reader explicitly wants that kind of leftover thought, and nearly all the page time here is motive rather than incident, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 at the top of its trilogy. The cap is the lead. He is a mother's boy who slides into complicity, and criticism converges on him being a type rather than a person - both failure modes of the protagonist axis at once, neither interesting nor worth rooting for. That combination is what cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87, and the log says this axis beats whatever competes with it. The narrator also breaks off repeatedly into essays on Rimbaud, Shelley and Mayakovsky, which is the digression cost that separates Les Miserables 71 from The Count of Monte Cristo 75. I leaned on protagonist alongside ideas rather than on ideas alone because the ideas here are strong enough to clear the line by themselves and the lead is the thing that will not let them. The opening is a single legible thread, the mother's youth and the conception, so the confusion filter is not in play.

The scattered threads converge here on a single objective - who assembles seven artefacts first - and one legible objective is what this reader wants; The Hunger Games 89 and The Hitchhiker's Guide 83 are both credited with fixing on one concrete situation instead of fanning out. At 782 pages it takes no length penalty either: the complaint recorded against The Lord of the Rings 84 was a thin story spread thin, not length, and this is densely plotted. Deductions: reviewers describe the book as fully plot-driven where the earlier material was character-driven, and set-piece action that reveals nothing about what people want is dead weight for this reader - that is the precise drag that cost Golden Son 92 its three points against Red Rising 95 and had chapters skimmed. It also stops on a cliff-hanger rather than a resting point. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets here. I leaned on momentum rather than on motives deliberately, because motive is what this book's plot machinery is most likely to crowd out, and that is the risk that would drop it below the range. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived pantheon - Source question, plus is any rite shown in a scene?

A 2027 France where sophisticated attacks hit the symbols of the West, and a ministry adviser whose father collapses and who is then handed a fatal cancer diagnosis. The book still leaves a thought behind - that a civilisation and a body are annihilated the same way and neither can read the signs - so it is not a thin book, and the occult and bleakness deductions already priced (Wicca goddess worship as the marriage's one source of comfort, and 500-plus pages of decline against 1984's 60 for being too depressing) still stand. Re-examined under the corrected sexual-content axis (2026-08-27, volume, explicitness and crudeness all cost and compound): this was not priced at all before, and it should have been. The marriage-repair thread is written with graphic, anatomical explicitness rather than being implied, and a separate subplot has the protagonist attempt to hire a sex worker who turns out to be his own niece - a scene that is crude on its own terms whatever its narrative point. That combination of real explicitness and a genuinely crude turn is the same shape of cost that took Artemis from 76 down to 69 for crude sexual treatment, and it is not a small addition on top of two deductions already near the floor of this reader's range. I now lean on occult, bleakness and sexual-content together, since no single one of the three was doing all the work before and the previous estimate undercounted by leaving the third out entirely.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography: humorous episodes and observations from the author's own life during the coronavirus period. A shared recent upheaval is the nearest this comes to the thing that earns on the memoir axis - insight into how other people experienced something - but the subject is her own comfortable domestic routine under restrictions, not another group's world. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. Topical comedy attempts neither, and it carries the extra hazard that pandemic anecdote dates fast, leaving even less behind. There is no premise to work out and no plot, so nothing can accumulate across the pieces; unconnected pieces is what made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69, and that book at least had Tolkien's material. 'Lacks higher things to think about' held The Chronicles of Narnia to 67 with a plot behind it. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk.

t: Plamen v temnote (A Torch Against the Night)
why: One objective drives the whole book - get north, break into the Empire's worst prison, get a brother out - and the two who go do it together rather than alone. Companionship over solo endurance is a preference this reader has stated in numbers, Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82, and the strongest thread by review consensus is a soldier bound by an oath she is starting to hate, torn between her Emperor and her family: page time on what she wants and why, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops its trilogy on. The number is set elsewhere. The supernatural apparatus moves to the foreground here as a purgatory between the living and the dead with a keeper who passes souls through it, alongside jinn and efrits that the author says in interviews she took from Middle Eastern folklore, and a seer order she modelled on the Pythia at Delphi. Borrowed real-world supernatural material is the most expensive axis in this log - Percy Jackson 57 because the Greek pantheon counts, Harry Potter 51 for magic drawn from historical witchcraft. Deduct again for sustained grimness, since a torture prison, a sadistic warden and a slow poisoning are most of the setting and 1984 60 shows what unrelieved bleakness costs; and note that a continuation is not a safe bet here, Hitchhiker's Guide falling from 83 to 70. Leaned on the occult axis rather than on momentum, because momentum is the book's strength and would argue the number up. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: same borrowed folkloric apparatus - Source question.

It clears the occult test on mechanism rather than on being invented. Orogeny is a bodily sense operated on declared rules - it draws heat and motion out of its surroundings, and the obelisks work as amplifiers that must be linked - and although this book renames the underlying force magic, a silver thread running through living things and the planet, nothing is invoked, worshipped or ritualised on the page and there is no priesthood; even the Guardians' power is sited in a physical implant. That puts it with the systems already accepted as engineering rather than with the real-world witchcraft that sank Harry Potter 51 and the pantheon that sank Percy Jackson 57. The positive case is that the premise is worked out instead of decorated: a world with recurring extinction seasons has its lore, its castes, its architecture and its underground geode cities all following from that one fact, which is the second-order thinking he credited in Project Hail Mary 92. It also spends its pages on motive - a mother and a daughter who want incompatible things and are each being taught by someone with an agenda - over incident. Now the deductions, and there are four. It is a sequel, and sequels fall in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Speaker for the Dead 90 to 81 for the books after it. The narration is second person and alternates between two leads, and reviewers report stretches where it is not clear who is speaking, which is the neighbourhood of the failure that produced his three scores of 30. Bleakness is heavy and unrelieved, and 1984 60 is what that costs. And Essun is interesting without being easy to root for - the interesting-versus-rootable split that put twenty-two points between two Collins books, Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Leaned on ideas and motive rather than on worldbuilding, because the lesson of Artemis 69 is not to predict a book up on its world when the lead is the open question.

The conceit is legible and disciplined - the same April day in three consecutive years, before, during and after the pandemic, one morning, one midday, one evening - and the book is entirely about what its people want and fear rather than what they do, which is the axis this reader rates above everything else. That is the positive case and it is not trivial. Against it: the point of view is distributed across an extended family rather than held inside one person, and the log is unambiguous that the tight single-POV narration is what makes these books work - The Hunger Games 89 was scored a baseline favourite for exactly that, and Red Rising 95 tops the log on interiority sustained in one head. Reviewers also put the obstacle in the characters themselves, whose trouble is late-thirties disappointment that life has not met expectations, and a flat lead is the whole gap that left Artemis at 76. Naming the idea is where it fails the gate: love under a pandemic is a subject, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks. A roving ensemble opening carries some of the confusion risk that ended three books at 30, though one family on one day is a long way from several plot lines at once. Leaned on protagonist and distributed POV rather than on bleakness, which is the mildest objection in the log and not what decides this. Exited at gate 2 at one source; the occult question is unexamined and nothing suggests it.

One search decides it. A 72-page illustrated story for children from five, in which a personified water droplet goes to droplet school and is carried through the water cycle - a treatment plant, a reservoir, pipes, sewers - so that the young reader learns how water moves and how it is cleaned. Children's register is graded, never vetoed, and it is graded by how juvenile the telling is: The Little Prince 82 costs nothing because an adult reads it for what it says about people, while the picture-book end of the scale is a 30s-to-40s book, and this is squarely at that end. The educational spine is also the problem for the one axis that could rescue a short book: the personification is a teaching device, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and at least one reader called the text plotless and brochure-like. So the idea I can name is a school-syllabus fact, axis:ideas goes in risks, and no nameable idea plus a form that suspends the character tests is the lower band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; a personified droplet is not a rite.

There is something here: one short monologue for each year of a life that ran from 1928 to 2022, each followed by a terse note on where the writer stood, so a century of Czech history is measured against one person year by year. But the memoir form earns nothing by itself in this log - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score by actually examining what is plausible and what is not, and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the same form failing outright, so the form is evidence of nothing and the content has to carry it. The structure is deliberately fragmentary, and fragmentation is precisely what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of the Tolkien scores: pieces that are not logically connected to each other. A chronological frame is not a worked-out idea, and with no continuous narrative there is no protagonist or motive to gain points back, so axis:ideas goes in risks. Anchoring on how non-fiction and twentieth-century-history books have actually landed - Son of Hamas 75 and Exodus 68 - a competent, well-regarded set of reflections without a single argument sits just under the line. Leaned on memoir-form rather than density because the book is short; the risk is not length but that the fragments do not add up. Exited at gate 2 at one source, so the occult question is unexamined; nothing in the description points that way.

The idea is as strong as anything in this log and it is genuinely worked out rather than gestured at: one question - whether a man forced to be good is still a man - is declared inside the book itself, tested by conditioning the narrator against his own will, and then answered when he is left to choose for himself at the end. That is the kind of book that earned Animal Farm 78, short and idea-driven and leaving something behind. The opening is also exactly what this reader wants: one first-person voice, one concrete situation, four boys in a milk bar deciding what to do with the evening, no fanning out at all. But the protagonist is the whole problem and it is the heaviest axis there is. The narrator is a gleeful perpetrator for the first third and there is nobody else to be with, and a lead who cannot be rooted for cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 on that alone - and this lead is a far harder case than a slow descent into evil, since he starts at the bottom and enjoys it. Deductions stack from there: rape and assault are narrated from inside by their perpetrator, and while the invented slang is a deliberate distancing device rather than titillation, which keeps this well short of the crude-for-laughs problem that hurt Ready Player One 55, it is still crude about the thing it is crude about. The relentlessness is its own cost - 1984 scored 60 for being too depressing, and this immerses the reader in the misery in a way Animal Farm pointedly did not. The invented slang also has to be learned before the prose is legible, a friction Tolkien's densest book never quite paid for. I leaned on protagonist plus ideas rather than on bleakness, because bleakness is the mildest recorded objection and would not by itself pull a book of this quality under the line; the unrootable narrator would.

Filter 6 asks what the book is for: remove the sexual scheme from any of these four stories and there is no story left. 'The Great Switcheroo' has no plot beyond a husband sneaking into a friend's bed in the dark to compare a sexual experience; 'Bitch' has no plot beyond an aphrodisiac perfume and its effects; the two Oswald Cornelius pieces are diary entries of sexual conquest with nothing else driving them. That is a different shape from Pride and Prejudice (75), where romance and courtship - what characters want and why - is the entire subject and costs nothing, because courtship there is motive and relationship, not a sexual deception scheme standing in for plot. This collection fails the new hard filter rather than landing on the graded axis at all, so no range is produced.

t: Modra planeta (Modra planeta: Pribehy deti z ruznych koutu sveta)
why: One search settles the form and with it the exit. This is a 68-page illustrated book for beginning readers from age six: twelve very short stories about twelve children in different countries, all set at the same moment of one day, each followed by factual notes to read with a parent. Children's register is graded rather than vetoed, but it is graded by how far toward a children's book it actually sits, and this sits all the way there - The Little Prince 82 and The Hobbit 84 pay nothing because they are books an adult reads for the ideas, while the picture-book end of the scale lands in the 30s and 40s. The short form also suspends the character rules, and that suspension only removes penalties, so nothing is left to lean on: with a few pages per child there is no room for what anyone wants and why, the axis that carries the reader's whole top band. I can name no idea whose consequences are worked out, only the intention that the world is various, so axis:ideas belongs in risks, and no-idea plus a form that suspends the character tests is the lower band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Muz v cervenem kabate (The Man in the Red Coat)
why: The detective signal in the annotation is about real trials and the Dreyfus affair inside a work of non-fiction, not about a whodunnit, so filter one did not fire. It exits below the line on the idea. Every review agrees on the form: not a biography running A to B but a circuitous, digressive stroll through Belle Epoque names, with titled tangents and questions the author leaves unresolved on purpose. That is the shape the reader has already scored twice - Unfinished Tales 69 for pieces not logically connected to each other, and Les Miserables 71 for famous digressions - and heavy description with little story is a standing deduction. The non-fiction form earns nothing by itself here: what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 was examining what is actually plausible, and a gossipy period portrait undertakes no such examination. An idea can be named - cross-Channel curiosity against chauvinism - but I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the exit condition, so one source is where this stops. Occult status is unexamined by design at this exit.

It is short, precise and stays in one place, and there is a nameable observation in it: people moored between land and water who have committed to neither, and the restlessness that follows from that. Short books with something to think about do very well here - The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 both score on ideas alone with no plot to speak of - so length is not a deduction. What holds the number down is that the observation is a mood rather than a premise whose consequences are worked out; the drama is one woman failing to decide about a marriage, and thin story is the penalty term in this log, the same objection that cancelled The Lord of the Rings 84 down to a tie with The Hobbit. Reviewers also report being dropped in as though they already knew everyone, and several found nobody to be with, and a lead who is not worth rooting for is what separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points. Leaned on density and protagonist rather than on bleakness: the book is melancholy, but that is the mildest objection recorded and not what decides this one. Exited at gate 2 on axis:ideas at one source, so the occult question is unexamined; nothing in a Thames houseboat novel suggests it.

t: Noc nic nezadrzi (Rien ne s'oppose a la nuit)
why: An autobiographical novel that reconstructs the author's mother's life after finding her dead. The form earns nothing by itself: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score by genuinely testing what is plausible, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the same first-person testimony that did not work, so the number has to come from what the book examines rather than from its sincerity. It does examine one real thing - that a family's account of a life is unreliable, and the reconstruction says so about itself - but the payload is a case history of illness and suicide rather than a premise worked out to its consequences, which is why axis:ideas belongs in risks and why this lands under the line. Sustained gloom is the log's mildest recorded objection, so it is the second deduction rather than the first, though 1984 60 shows it costs even where the ideas are strong. Leaned on axis:memoir-form rather than axis:motives: there is ample page time on what people wanted, but it comes from interviews with real relatives, and the one high score in this form came from argument, not access. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was deliberately not examined.

t: Obraz Doriana Graye (The Picture of Dorian Gray)
why: The positive case is a genuine idea, statable in a phrase: a life bought on credit, with the bill kept in another room, and what it costs to make beauty the only value. That is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 - a book that leaves something behind rather than only events - and it is the reason this does not exit below the line. The opening also does what the log's most reliable predictor wants: two men in one room looking at one portrait, one concrete situation, nothing fanned out, no second plot line running. Against that stand two deductions. The lead is the log's most expensive single fault - a knowing descent into evil with nobody to root for, which is what separates The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 from the same author's other prequel at 87 on the protagonist alone, and Dorian is less interesting than the talker who corrupts him. And the story is thin for its pages, with a long catalogue of jewels, perfumes and tapestries standing in where plot should be, the same digression cost that holds Les Miserables 71 below Monte Cristo 75. The decadence is implication rather than depiction and never crude, so it costs nothing by the Red Rising 95 precedent, and the transformation is never explained or enacted as a rite, so the occult filter does not touch it. Leaned on ideas and the protagonist rather than on prose or period colour, because prose has never moved a score in this log and both recorded prediction failures came from leaning on an axis that was not doing the work.

t: Otec Vanoce a ja (Father Christmas and Me)
why: Pitched at nine-to-eleven-year-olds and illustrated throughout, and the praise reviewers converge on is for messages of hope, kindness and believing. That is a moral, not an idea a book leaves behind, so axis:ideas goes in risks and the below-the-line exit is decided right there. The nearest real anchor is The Chronicles of Narnia 67 - not bad, children as the main characters, and lacking higher things to think about - and this sits noticeably further toward a children's book than Narnia does, so axis:childrens takes more off again; the reader's own scale puts an outright picture book in the thirties and forties. What keeps it from the lower band is that the register is not the whole book: there is a real protagonist with her own narrating voice and a genuine want - an adopted human girl who does not fit where she has been put - and Ranger's Apprentice 74 shows an easy children's read with nothing much to think about can still land in the B band on likeable company alone. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, Hitchhiker's 83 down to 70. Reviewers also report the advertised threat barely appearing until past page 200, which is thin story stretched out. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Pikova dama a jine povidky (The Queen of Spades and other tales)
why: A short volume of prose tales: a card-table novella plus a set of ironic anecdotes of provincial Russian life. The prose is deliberately spare and outward - incident, coincidence and a turn of fortune, narrated at a distance from what anyone wants - and that is the exact inverse of the axis carrying the top of this log, where Mockingjay 91 was preferred for showing the most of people's motives and the least of the events. A set of brief tales has no single premise to lean on instead, so there is no route above the line even where each piece is well made. I can name an idea in one of them, an obsession that converts a man's whole life into a single wager, but not one the volume as a whole works out, which is why axis:ideas is a risk rather than something leaned on. This is a recorded, revisable number taken at the below-the-line gate: the occult question was deliberately not examined and is a live one here.

Both C conditions fire together, which is where this stops. One source settles form and genre: realist literary fiction, and a collection of a dozen or so separate stories with different casts and no single premise carrying through, only a shared setting and a framing pair. The idea is nameable but slight - disillusion, the small vanities and meannesses under the quiet surface of one neighbourhood - and it is restated across separate stories rather than worked out once, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character and emotion tests without putting anything in their place, which is a removal of penalties and never an addition of points. The log has the matching case: Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other, and the cost here is the same structural one. The default band just under the line is right rather than the low one, because the observation is sharp, the register adult and the satire pointed - nothing suggests the 40s or low 50s. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit, since nothing under 68 is proposed either way.

The positive case is the axis the reader ranks first and this book is built almost entirely out of it. Everything arrives through one man's mind - what he wants, what he is calculating, whom he cannot forgive - and the court exists only as he reads it, which is the same tight single-consciousness narration that made The Hunger Games 89 a baseline favourite and the interiority that put Red Rising 95 at the top. Two supporting points, both sourced. The opening is one concrete legible situation, a morning hawking with the king, continuous with what came before and single-POV, so the confusing-opening filter that produced the three 30s in the log is not in play. And the compression is real: five months of 1536, densely plotted, with interrogation scenes driving it, and a critic openly hostile to the earlier work for having no plot called this one full of narrative suspense. Length itself is never a deduction and dense plotting over many pages carries none. The deduction and the risk are the same man. He needs guilty men, so he finds men who are guilty, and he manufactures the case that kills them - and the log's cleanest controlled result is The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 - same author, same world, same form, 22 points apart on a lead who is not worth rooting for. He is more sympathetic than that, self-made against inherited rank, and the descent is not framed as the arc, which is why this is a risk rather than a subtraction, but it is the axis that could collapse the range. A sequel that assumes prior knowledge is also not a safe bet in this log, which fell from 83 to 70 across one series. Reformation theology is a subject here but as politics inside a story rather than apologetics, so faith costs little. I leaned on motives and momentum, not on the protagonist, because Artemis 69 is the recorded failure of predicting up while the lead is the doubtful part.

t: Pribehy z konce predmesti (Tales from Outer Suburbia)
why: Fifteen very short illustrated pieces about strange things turning up in an ordinary suburb, in a picture-book format where the artwork carries part of the telling rather than decorating it. The reader's own scale prices a picture book in the 30s and 40s - Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for a simple register, Narnia 67 pays a little, a picture book much more - and that register is the single thing setting this range. It does not land at the bottom of that scale, because there is a stated subject: how ordinary people react to something inexplicable and how its significance gets missed or ignored, and The Little Prince 82 proves short allegory can be carried entirely by its thoughts. But that is one thought distributed over fifteen sketches rather than a premise worked out, and pieces of two or three pages cannot pay the axis this log weights heaviest, page time on what people want and why, which is why the lower of the two bands is the honest one. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:short-idea-driven; axis:ideas is the risk, not the support. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined.

Form and genre settle in one source - a near-future science-fiction novel, not a mystery - and then the below-the-line question answers itself. I can name the idea, agency itself: whether a person or a machine can bend a timeline that is already running down. What I doubt is that it holds up, which is exactly what puts axis:ideas in risks and ends the research here. Professional and reader criticism converge on the same two things: an intelligence that carries the premise and then disappears from the book for long stretches, and stakes that stay flat while a nuclear war is pending, described as movement signifying not very much toward a predetermined outcome. The lead is the part the log prices precisely - she is repeatedly called a cipher who is told where to go and asks what is happening, and a lead who is not interesting is the entire gap between Artemis 69 and the same author's better-liked books, with no worldbuilding rescue available because interest in the lead beats worldbuilding when they compete. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 falling to 70. The default band just under the line is right rather than the low one, because the prose and the world are competent and there is a real idea to point at. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit, since nothing under 68 gets proposed either way.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection at once, which is where the below-the-line exit is decided: thirteen minimalist pieces held together by a mood rather than by a premise. The form suspends his character rules and adds nothing in return, and I cannot name an idea in a phrase - a longing for love, acceptance and quiet is a subject, not something a book leaves behind - so axis:ideas goes in risks. Two further pulls put this in the lower band rather than the default one. Sustained sadness is announced in the title and is the stated organising principle, and 1984 60 is what that costs him even when the book itself is good. And readers report endings that do not follow from what precedes them and pieces they could not make sense of, which is the neighbourhood of the one failure that has actually stopped him reading - Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic both at 30. His nearest real anchor for the form is Unfinished Tales 69, docked because the pieces are not logically connected to each other, and this has less connective tissue than that. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

REVERTED 2026-08-28, third pass, to the pre-today range, for the same reason as the other volume-driven raises: the premise behind them was withdrawn by the reader. The coarse register carries the deduction here and is anchored on Ready Player One 55, so the Witcher withdrawal buys this book nothing. A modernist glass house in 1930s Czechoslovakia as the fixed point while the century moves through it - the building declared as an idea about rationality and light, then tested by what happens to the people in it. Real ideas and a genuine motive structure, the axis that carries this log. RAISED 2026-08-28 from [52, 62]. The old range stacked a volume deduction on top of a crudeness deduction and justified the stack by calling Ready Player One and The Witcher volume cases. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The coarse register here is real and keeps most of the deduction; the volume stack on top of it does not survive. Still well short of the historical band's better showings because the house, not a person, is the throughline, and the cast turns over around it.

t: Takovy pekny par a jine povidky (Selected short stories)
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection at once, which is the below-the-line exit: twenty-four magazine pieces an editor arranged into a chronological cycle. The form suspends the reader's character rules and adds nothing in return - there is no single premise whose consequences get worked out, and that working-out is what earns his high scores. A subject is nameable, money's hold on love and self-invention in the jazz age, but a recurring subject across two dozen separate stories is not an idea a book leaves behind, so axis:ideas belongs in risks. His nearest real anchor for this shape is Unfinished Tales 69, docked because the pieces are not logically connected to each other. The craft is genuine and the pieces turn on what people want rather than on incident, which is what keeps the range at the line rather than below it. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Tisice planoucich slunci (A Thousand Splendid Suns)
why: Nearly all the page time goes on what two women want and why - Marjam's inherited shame, Lajla's ambition and then her survival - which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and the reason those two sit above books by the same authors that lean on incident. It opens on one concrete situation, a five-year-old and her mother in a hut outside Herat, in a single third-person limited line, so the confusion filter that produced his three scores of 30 does not fire; the four parts hand the lead from one woman to the other in sequence rather than starting several threads at once. Both leads are interesting and worth rooting for, and the ending turns on one of them destroying herself to save the other - self-sacrifice over solo survival is exactly the difference he named between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82. It also gives real insight into how another group experiences the world, the thing he credited in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and it leaves an idea behind: shame handed down as an inheritance, and what makes it bearable. Held out of the top band by sustained bleakness - domestic violence, war and loss with little relief, and 1984 60 shows what that costs him - though companionship blunts it here rather than isolation compounding it. Leaned on motive and protagonist, not on worldbuilding, since the setting is the real Afghanistan and does no work for the number.

t: Usmev lorda Ickenhama (Service with a Smile)
why: The positive case is real: comic prose that reads very easily, one concrete country-house situation rather than a fan-out, and a scheming protagonist who is both competent and likeable - and comedy is not a handicap in this log, since The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy scored 83. What holds the number down is what the pages are spent on. A farce allocates its page time to who is deceiving whom and which impostor is unmasked next, not to what anyone wants and why, and motives over action is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both win on. Nothing is left behind to think about afterwards, which is the exact reason competent, pleasant books stall in the 60s here - Ranger's Apprentice 74 was easy to read with not much to think about, and Narnia 67 was marked down for lacking higher things. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. I leaned on motives rather than on protagonist, because the lead is genuinely likeable and interesting; the gap is not who he is but that the book asks nothing of him beyond the scheme. Exited at gate 2 on axis:ideas after one source, so the occult question was deliberately not examined - nothing in an English country-house farce suggests it.

t: Valka svetu (The War of the Worlds)
why: A genuinely idea-bearing book, and the idea is stated outright in the first chapter rather than left to be inferred: before judging the invaders, remember what our own species did to the dodo and to the Tasmanians. Imperial conquest turned around on the conquerors, and human pre-eminence withdrawn - that is something left behind, which is the thing he says a competent book most often lacks, and it is why Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score where they do on very few pages. It opens on one concrete situation, astronomers watching flares on Mars and then a cylinder in a sandpit at Horsell Common, in a single first-person voice and a lucid, almost documentary register, so the confusion filter does not fire; The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 scores partly on that same virtue of starting somewhere specific. The world also holds up: the invaders' capabilities, the collapse of order and the biological ending all follow from what the book sets up, and nothing is asserted and then dropped. Two deductions, both on his heaviest axis. The narrator is unnamed and, on the consistent critical reading, deliberately flat - he reports his experience objectively and the book does not ask you to identify with him - and a lead who is not interesting is precisely the gap that put Artemis 69 six points under The Martian 82 by the same author. And three chapters hand the story to the narrator's brother, related as though witnessed, which loosens the single-viewpoint grip he prefers. Bleakness is real but bounded and the collapse is followed by restoration, so it costs little. Leaned on ideas and the opening rather than on the protagonist, which is the term pulling the number down.

t: Vynalezci zazraku. Sebrane povidky H. G. Wellse. Svazek I (The Stolen Bacillus and Other Incidents; The Plattner Story and Others)
why: Thirty-three early magazine pieces from the 1890s, gathered by which periodical collection they came from rather than around any one premise, so there is no single worked-out idea for the book to leave behind - and giving him nothing higher to think about is exactly what stalls competent work for this reader (Narnia 67, marked down for lacking higher things to think about). The best pieces do carry a real conceit - displaced sight, a stolen body, a runaway culture in a test tube - and that is the positive case; but they sit among comic incidents and slight magazine trifles, and an unconnected assemblage is where he has been hardest on writing he otherwise admires: Unfinished Tales 69 fell twelve points under The Silmarillion 80 purely because the pieces were not logically connected to each other. The short idea-driven form suspends the character and motive tests, which is why this is not lower, but that suspension only removes penalties: Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both earn their scores from one idea carried the whole way, which a mixed thirty-three-story gathering cannot do. Leaned on form and density rather than on ideas, because the ideas here are real story by story and unprovable for the book as a whole. Occult status left unexamined - stopped at the below-the-line gate.

Eight pieces of science fiction set around the edges of an existing future history: origin stories for characters, one invention story, one crime story. The invention piece is the best case for it - a single engineering premise followed to what it does to the solar system, which is the Project Hail Mary 92 axis - but reviewers agree the pieces are interstitial by design and that nothing in them is load-bearing, and material that does not connect to itself is exactly what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of an author whose other work scored 80 and above. With no single premise for the volume to lean on, axis:ideas is a risk rather than an asset. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70 is the steepest recorded fall and it happened on that axis alone. Leaned on axis:sequels and axis:momentum rather than axis:worldbuilding, which is probably strong here and still cannot rescue a book by itself - Artemis 69 is the recorded proof, where consistent worldbuilding saved nothing. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult was not examined; nothing in the material suggests it is a question.

t: Zrcadlo a svetlo (The Mirror and the Light)
why: There is a real positive case and it is the reader's first axis: the whole book is one man's interior weather - service, debt, what he wants from a king who is the only source of everything he has - and it leaves an idea behind, that a regime consumes the servant who built it. That is the kind of thing the reader means by higher things to think about, and it is why this is not an exit at the cheaper gate. The number is nonetheless carried downward by density, which is the reader's explicit penalty term. At roughly 900 pages the reviews converge on a slack middle: it bogs down in portentous conversations, remodelling plans, protocol and costings, and one critic calls the pacing dangerously uneven. That is precisely the charge that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its advantage - a thin stretch of story spread over many pages - and it is what dropped Les Miserables 71 below The Count of Monte Cristo 75 on digressions alone. Length alone is never the objection; the uneven middle is. The protagonist risk is at its sharpest here. He is read as a Faust figure much closer to damnation, his sins no longer deniable, and a lead descending into evil is the log's most expensive protagonist failure - The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87, 22 points on that alone. The ending is his destruction, so bleakness adds a mild further discount, the objection that took 1984 to 60. Being a sequel also matters more than usual here, since it assumes a long prior acquaintance with its cast. On the occult question: he hears a dead patron's voice and speaks with the ghosts he sees in the Tower, but that is a haunting rendered as memory and conscience, with no rite performed, no invocation and no medium, so the filter does not fire - the distinction is enactment, not the presence of the dead. I leaned on density rather than on motives alone because the interiority is not in doubt and the pacing is.

The strongest idea found anywhere in the children's shelf, and it is stated as a rule with a price: every wish Bastian makes inside Fantastica costs him one memory of who he was, and the book spends its whole second half spending that currency until he has almost nothing left to wish with. That is a declared resource behaving the way it was declared, which is the form of the heaviest axis that Project Hail Mary 92 and Hunger Games 89 both satisfy. The first half earns the second: Fantastica is dying because people stopped imagining, so the cure has to come from a reader, and it does. Register is children's on the surface only - what the book is actually about is what wanting things does to a person. Two real pushbacks: Bastian spends a long stretch as a self-made tyrant, which is the Ballad 65 not-worth-rooting-for failure in miniature, and the second half is a sequence of episodes that connect loosely, which is the Unfinished Tales 69 objection.

The idea states in one phrase and is the whole book: time saved is life lost, and the grey gentlemen literally live off the hours people economise. It is The Little Prince 82 written at novel length and with an economic argument underneath, and Animal Farm 78 is the precedent for allegory scoring on its ideas without needing anything else. Where the book asserts precisely - the time-savings bank, the accounting of stolen hours - it holds together as satire; Master Hora and the hour-lilies are left numinous, and the scaling rule says vague magic owes little, so the exemption Narnia 67 got applies here too. The pushback is the lead: Momo's whole characterisation is that she listens, which makes her about as passive as a lead can be, and a flat lead beat strong worldbuilding outright in Artemis 69.

Nothing in this catalogue carries more of the stated earner - higher things to think about - per page: it is the history of Western philosophy delivered inside a novel, and the novel then turns on the discovery that Sofie is a character in a book being written for someone else's daughter, so the idea is enacted rather than only lectured. That turn is what separates it from a textbook. Two honest costs. First, a large share of the pages are Alberto's lectures with the plot suspended, and a thin story spread over many pages is exactly the penalty term that capped LOTR 84 and docked Les Miserables 71 - the length is not the problem, the ratio is. Second, philosophy is the subject in its own right, which brushes the same line that rules out apologetics: the log wants ideas carried inside a story, and here the story is partly a delivery mechanism.

A dying boy and his brother, and the idea is said out loud in the book: there are things you have to do, otherwise you are not a person but a bit of dirt. It is about courage as something done while frightened, which is the heroism-and-friendship material that carried LOTR 84, at 150 pages instead of 1200 - so the sparseness penalty cannot apply. The narrator is both interesting and worth rooting for, the pairing that separates Speaker 90 from Artemis 69, and the two brothers want different things for different reasons. The pushback is real: it is a book about death that ends with the brothers choosing it, so bleakness applies - but bleakness is the mildest recorded objection and only 1984 60 ever triggered it, and this is bleak-with-something-to-take-away in the Animal Farm 78 mould rather than immersion in misery. Worldbuilding owes almost nothing here: Nangijala is asserted, not explained.

t: Ronja, dcera loupeznika (Ronia, the Robber's Daughter)
why: Page time goes on what people want and why, which is the axis with the widest evidence in the log - two robber clans forced to share one fortress, two children who refuse to inherit the feud, and a father who disowns his daughter and then has to climb down from it. Mattis wanting his daughter and his pride at once is the kind of motive conflict that put Mockingjay 91 above Catching Fire 83. Ronja is competent because she is taught and tested, not because the book says she is, which avoids the Divergent 58 unearned-competence turn-off. Against it: the ideas are ordinary compared with the Ende and Lindgren entries above, and the register is squarely children's - the same combination that put Narnia 67 in the B band rather than lower.

The one genuinely affecting thing in it is the frame: a fostered, unwanted boy in Stockholm gets the father and the country he has been longing for, and the reader is left to decide how much of it he is inventing. That is a nameable idea. Everything inside the frame is generic though - a prophesied boy, a black knight, a sword forged for him - and the log's own warning is that clearing the filters is not a reason to propose. Prophecy is present and leaned into, which is a graded deduction rather than a bar, and the reverence test is passed since it is played straight. Lands where Narnia 67 lands and for the same two reasons: child register, not much to think about afterwards.

t: Chlapci z Pavelske ulice (The Paul Street Boys)
why: The idea is that children's play is not play: two gangs run a war over a lumber yard with courts, ranks, oaths and a traitor's trial, and the smallest boy in it dies of an illness he caught doing his duty. The book takes its own premise seriously to the end instead of retreating from it, which is the self-consistency the heaviest axis asks for. Nemecsek is as clear a case as this shelf offers of a lead who is both interesting and worth rooting for - he is despised, he keeps going anyway, and the honours arrive too late. Adult-canonical in Hungary rather than a curiosity. Pushbacks: it ends on a death, and the surrounding register is a boys' adventure story of 1907, so some of the cost of Narnia 67 applies.

t: Ostrov v Ptaci ulici (The Island on Bird Street)
why: One concrete starting situation and immediate investment, which is what the clarity filter actually asks for: Alex is left alone in a ruined house in the Warsaw ghetto and stays there for months because his father said he would come back. He runs it as a survival-engineering problem - water, heat, food, a rope strung to the next building - so the practical work is the text, which is the shape that made The Martian 82 work. The idea is what a promise is worth when nothing supports it. Written by a man who was in the ghetto and then in Bergen-Belsen, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is safe. Two pushbacks: sustained isolation is the specific thing docked in The Martian 82, and a child's inner life inside a testimony frame is the Anne Frank 40 shape - the defence is that this is a novel with a concrete situation and momentum, which is exactly what that diary lacked.

Four boarding-school teenagers walk out into a state that killed their parents for resisting it, and the book spends its pages on why each of them goes and what each is willing to lose - motives over action, the axis four different authors in the log agree on. Two of the strongest strands are an arena fighter who is bred and owned, and a singer whose voice can turn a crowd, so the argument the book makes is about what actually moves people. Told as staggered strands rather than simultaneous ones, which is the configuration confirmed acceptable by LOTR 84 and Golden Son 92 rather than the Guards! Guards! 30 failure. The risk is the one that matters most: this takes a society as its subject, and a subject society must cohere - Divergent 58 is what happens when it does not. The Phalange's politics and economics are sketched impressionistically, and that is unverified.

t: Tim Tolar, aneb, Prodany smich (Timm Thaler)
why: A contract with exact terms and a book that is nothing but its consequences: a poor boy trades his laughter for winning every bet he makes, becomes rich, and discovers that a person who cannot laugh cannot be with anyone. Declaring a resource and then making it behave that way is the form of the heaviest axis the log states most plainly, and the currency here is priced in every scene. The idea states in a sentence, which is what the sharpened short-form rule demands. The cost of the wish is emotional rather than magical, so it earns its allegory the way Animal Farm 78 does. The named risk is the occult one and it is a judgement call rather than a finding: Lefuet is a devil figure, so a reader who treats a devil-pact as occult by source will veto it - but nothing is invoked, no ceremony happens, and no real-world practice is depicted, which is why it is recorded as a risk and not as a block.

The idea is mortality told to children without softening it: a spider spends the only summer she has keeping a pig alive, then dies alone in an empty fairground while the pig lives. Friendship and self-sacrifice beating solo survival is the exact preference that separates Project Hail Mary 92 from The Martian 82, and here it is the whole plot. Male zeny 79 is the new measure of what this register can reach - a childrens-adjacent classic with no premise to work out, clearing the line on character alone - so the top of the range is anchored, not hopeful. The floor drops on re-derivation: Wilbur is passive and Charlotte carries every decision, so the lead the reader spends most time with is not the interesting one, and Artemis 69 now prices that failure mode a band lower than it did. Barnyard register throughout, with the childrens deduction that implies.

Published as adult fiction here, and the idea is stated by its narrator: Death is tired of collecting, and the same words that built the Reich are what saves one girl. Liesel learning to read stolen books while her foster family hides a Jew in the basement is a story where the motives are the content, and Hans, Rosa and Rudy each want different things in different registers - the character differentiation that earned Golden Son 92. The narration is the tell either way: Death interrupts constantly with bulletins and asides, which is a real opening risk in a profile where three books scored 30 for confusion - but the interruptions annotate a single legible thread rather than starting six of them, and the difference between multiplicity and simultaneity is the thing the log already settled. Bleakness is heavy and the ending is announced in advance.

Petr Ginz, the Prague boy who edited the Vedem magazine in Terezin, drew Moon Landscape and was murdered at sixteen - and the reason it belongs on this list is that the book is about a person who kept making things. What earned Seeking Allah 91 and Son of Hamas 75 was insight into how another group experiences the world plus a real examination of what is true, and this is that in Czech and about Czechs. Baobab is a serious literary imprint, not a schools publisher, and the fact face of the heaviest axis is documented history rather than invention. The risks are the obvious ones: it ends in Auschwitz, and it is written for teenage readers, so both the bleakness discount and the childrens-register deduction apply. Neither is a bar.

The single best idea in this whole screen and it is dramatised, not stated: Huck believes helping Jim escape is a sin he will go to hell for, decides all right then, I'll go to hell, and does it anyway. A book whose central act is a boy's conscience being wrong and his instinct being right leaves exactly the kind of thing behind that the log rates highest - and it is the reason this is read as an adult novel with a boy in it rather than a children's book, so the register deduction is near zero. First person, one concrete situation, and the raft keeps it moving. The known cost is structural: the last quarter hands the book back to Tom Sawyer for an elaborate fake rescue that undoes what came before, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that capped LOTR 84 and the dragged ending docked in The Martian 82.

The ancestor of every book in this log that scores on worked-out consequences: a man with a wrecked ship's inventory rebuilds shelter, agriculture, pottery and defence, and the book keeps the ledger honest - which is what the reader means by an author following the rules he lays down, and why both Weir novels are described as awesome on that axis. Nothing is declared that then fails to behave. Two costs, both large enough to keep it out of the A band's top. Long stretches are inventory and spiritual accounting with nothing happening, which is the digression penalty that docked Les Miserables 71; and it is twenty-eight years of one man alone, where sustained isolation was explicitly the thing docked in The Martian 82. Providence is theology carried inside the narrative rather than argued, so it stays on the right side of the no-apologetics line.

A precisely declared mechanism carrying a real argument: a tree that must be fed a lie to bear fruit, and the bigger the lie has spread the more truth the fruit gives back - and Faith, a girl in 1868 who is not allowed to be a naturalist, works it like an instrument. Declared rules add obligation rather than bonus, and this one is kept: the escalating cost of the lies is the plot. Won the Costa Book of the Year against the adult field, which is what crossover means. The risk has to be led with rather than mentioned: the spine of the book is Faith investigating her father's death, so a hard-filtered genre is not a subplot here but the structure - the rule is to watch for investigation-shaped plots inside otherwise eligible books and flag rather than drop, and this is one. Occult passes narrowly; the tree is used, never worshipped.

t: Alenka v kraji divu a za zrcadlem (Alice)
why: Recorded with the risk in front of the case, because this is the one title in the batch that could land in the 30s. The ideas are genuine and adults have argued about them for a century - logic and language taken literally until they break, identity questioned by everything Alice meets, and Looking-Glass built on a chess problem that actually resolves. But the profile's most reliable predictor is the confusing-opening filter, and part of its definition is a long stretch without knowing what the real story is or where it leads: after the fall down the hole there is no goal, no threat and no destination for most of the book, only a sequence of encounters. That is the diagnosis on The Gunslinger 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 almost word for word. Every individual scene is legible, which is why this is a wide range and not a block - but legibility scene by scene is not the test, since Caropisci 30 was legible scene by scene too and was dropped in chapter one for offering nothing the reader could attach to.

t: Dopis pro krale (The Letter for the King)
why: One decision drives 456 pages: Tiuri leaves the chapel on the night of his knighting vigil to answer a stranger's call, and can then tell nobody why, so the whole book is a boy carrying a duty he cannot explain and losing the thing he wanted most in order to keep it. Page time goes on that choice rather than on fights, which is the motives-over-action axis. Fast start, single clean thread, no magic in it at all - so nothing supernatural is declared and nothing binds, and the occult filter has nothing to fire on. Two pushbacks: it is a chivalric adventure for young readers and reads like one, and at 456 pages a single-errand plot risks the thin-story-spread-thin penalty rather than length itself, which was never the objection.

A 160-page novel with one device doing all the work: Felix explains everything he sees in occupied Poland as a story, because stories are what he has, and the reader understands what is happening several pages before he does. The idea is what stories are for and what they cost when they are wrong, and it states in a sentence, which is the test the sharpened short-form rule sets. He is worth rooting for without being noble, and every chapter opens on him wanting something concrete. Bleakness is real and the sequence gets bleaker, but this is bleak-with-an-idea rather than immersion in misery, the Animal Farm 78 distinction. The child's-eye Holocaust narration is also the Anne Frank 40 shape, so that is named rather than waved away; the difference is that this has a plot and momentum.

t: Orel Devate legie (The Eagle of the Ninth)
why: Historical fiction lands in the high 60s to mid 70s in this log - Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66, Monte Cristo 75 - and this is the better-written end of that band. A crippled centurion goes north out of uniform to recover his father's legionary eagle, and the substance is his friendship with Esca, a freed slave who does not owe him it: two men with genuinely different reasons for the same journey, which is the differentiation axis. Research is solid, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is safe, and the reader has already been docked once for false history presented as fact in Ranger's Apprentice 74. What holds it under the A band is that the ideas are modest - loyalty and lost honour, well done rather than new - and Sutcliff's prose slows for landscape, which is where the description penalty sits.

t: Vitr ve vrbach (The Wind in the Willows)
why: Two books stapled together, and only one of them is for adults. The Toad farce is a comic set piece repeated four times; the Mole and Rat chapters are about the pull of home against the pull of the road, and the Piper chapter is a genuine attempt at awe. The problem is structural rather than moral: the parts do not connect to each other, which is exactly the objection that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien and cost the Hitchhiker's sequels 70 their thirteen points. Nothing here is filtered - the Pan scene is awe, not a rite, and there is nothing to object to on content - it simply does not pay much on the axes this reader weights. Lands where Narnia 67 lands: pleasant, animal-nursery register, not enough to think about afterwards.

The thing worth taking away is not in the plot, because there is barely a plot: Petr Bajza narrates his small-town boyhood in a Czech mangled out of newspaper cliche, shop-sign formality and schoolbook grammar, and the comedy is what that language reveals about the adults who taught it to him. Written in 1943 by a Jewish author who was murdered in Auschwitz the next year, and read in Czech that fact is inseparable from the innocence on the page - which is the idea, and it is not one a translation could carry. Comic prose that works is not the risk here; the Pratchett Fs were never about humour, and Hitchhiker's 83 shows comic writing scoring well. The risk is that it is episodic with no story to build, which is the density penalty in its purest form.

t: Chlapec v pruhovanem pyzamu (The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas)
why: Recorded rather than proposed, and recorded low, so that the most famous title in this whole shelf stops resurfacing in every sweep. The failure is on the heaviest axis and it is at the centre of the book, not the edges: a nine-year-old who has lived in Berlin under the Reich does not know what a Jew is, cannot read the word Auschwitz, is unsupervised for a year, and finds an unwatched gap in the wire of an extermination camp he can crawl through repeatedly. Where nothing is declared, reality binds - and here reality is documented history, which the Auschwitz Memorial itself has publicly said this book misrepresents. That is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 objection, false claims stated as fact, except moved from the decoration to the load-bearing premise, and premise implausibility is one of only two things that has ended a book unfinished in the first chapters, at Mortal Engines 55. The prose and the ending are effective; they are effective on top of something that does not stand up.

t: Anna ze Zeleneho domu (Anne of Green Gables)
why: Carried entirely by its lead, which is the axis that beats worldbuilding when they compete: an orphan who talks too much arrives at a farm that wanted a boy, and the book is her wanting to be kept. Anne is interesting rather than merely likeable - the distinction that separates Speaker 90 from Artemis 69 - and Marilla's slow, unstated change is the best-motivated thing in it. Against that, there is very little to think about afterwards: no premise, no consequences, nothing declared, so the heaviest axis has nothing to grade, and the log's most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s is exactly that. The register is a girls' classic of 1908. Sits where Narnia 67 sits, a couple of points higher on the strength of the protagonist alone.

The most-read Czech boys' book there is, and what it actually delivers is momentum and place: the Rychle sipy go into Stinadla, a hostile quarter with its own laws, and every chapter ends on a hook. Fast start and constant momentum is a stated preference with three S-band books behind it. Two things hold it down. First, the engine is a puzzle and a concealed society - a hidden Vont order, a coded manuscript, an object to be found - which is investigation-shaped, and while it is not a detective novel it is close enough that the filter has to be named. Second, there is not much to think about: the appeal is atmosphere and a boys' code of conduct, and the didactic layer Foglar built in has aged into moralising. This is a competent, atmospheric read rather than a book that leaves an idea behind.

t: Kde roste cervene kapradi (Where the Red Fern Grows)
why: The competence is earned, which is the specific thing the log says it wants and Divergent 58 failed: Billy works two years and saves fifty dollars in coins before he gets the two hound pups, and the book shows the work. After that it is a boy, two dogs and the Ozarks, with the training and the night hunts described in enough detail to be the substance rather than the backdrop. The idea is a plain one about what you owe an animal that gives you everything, and the ending is the grief that follows from it - bleak, but purposeful rather than immersive. Two pushbacks: the emotional register is straightforwardly sentimental in a way none of the log's higher scores are, and there is little to think about beyond the loss itself, which is where competent books stall.

One clean declared premise in the middle of Prague: a district where electricity simply does not work, so the block has been abandoned by the modern city and has grown its own economy, its own routes and its own people. That is a capability declared and the society visibly reorganised around it, which is the first and most-cited form of the heaviest axis, and the Czech setting is used properly rather than as scenery. But the same axis is the risk: the book does not explain why the anomaly exists, and the explanation is held back for later volumes - explained later in the same book is a valid defence, a sequel is explicitly not. So the central assertion is left standing on nothing for the length of this volume. Middle-grade register, two children as leads, and the plot is a hunt for a missing person, which is worth naming even though it is not a mystery novel.

Storch was an archaeologist writing to show how people actually lived in the Czech lands before history, and the value is that the material is real: tools, hunts, seasons, a clan's survival economics, illustrated by Burian. Where nothing is declared reality binds, and reality here is the archaeological record the author worked in, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is as safe as it gets. What limits it is the same thing that limits Ranger's Apprentice 74 - it is easy to read and there is not much to think about, and here the didactic purpose is openly the point, so scenes exist to demonstrate rather than to happen. Episodic by design, with a clan rather than a protagonist to follow.

The lowest-confidence line written in this screen, and the range is wide because of that rather than because the book itself is uncertain. What is known is real: a Czech original from Baobab, a serious literary children's imprint rather than a schools publisher, catalogued as an anti-utopian novel at 323 pages - so a society taken as the subject, which is the form the log grades hardest and where Divergent 58 collapsed. A Czech-original dystopia for teenage readers with the consequences worked out would sit in the Hunger Games 89 shape; one that borrows its furniture would sit in the Divergent 58 one, and nothing available here distinguishes the two. Recorded so the title sits in the database with its uncertainty visible rather than being found again by the next sweep; the occult check was not run either.

Recorded rather than proposed. The wit really is aimed over the child's head - Eeyore's self-pity, Owl's fake erudition, Rabbit's officiousness are adult jokes about adult types, and the prose is precise in a way almost nothing else on this shelf is. But that is a register, not an idea: nothing is at stake, nothing is declared, nobody wants anything that costs, and the thing the log rates highest is what a book leaves you thinking about. Narnia 67 was marked down for child leads and not enough to think about while at least having a plot and a war; this has neither. It is also episodic sketches rather than a story, which is the density objection. Two hundred pages of nursery register with excellent jokes in it lands below the B band, not in it.

A declared constraint with a clock on it, and the whole book is the consequences: two brothers find a bag holding 229,370 pounds by the railway embankment seventeen days before sterling is withdrawn for the euro, so the money must be spent or it turns into paper. That is the form of the heaviest axis the log states most plainly - declare a resource and make it behave that way - and it is worked out honestly, including what happens when a nine-year-old tries to give money to the poor and discovers he has no idea who they are. Under the plot, Damian collects the lives of martyrs because his mother has just died, so the page time goes on what he wants and why rather than on the money, which is the motives-over-action axis with the widest evidence in the log. Carnegie Medal, published here by Argo rather than a children's imprint. Three named risks: the narrating voice is a nine-year-old's throughout, which is where the register deduction bites; the saints appear and speak to him, which needs the reader's own ruling; and faith is a thread rather than a subject, which is the stated preference but sits close to the line.

Recorded rather than proposed, and recorded with its uncertainty visible. A seventeen-year-old Czech boy has school, parents, friends and a girlfriend all going fine and is drowning anyway, with the depression written as water rising around him - hence the title. What is genuinely in its favour: a single legible first-person situation, a contemporary Czech voice, and a lead who is rootable without being admirable. What holds it in the C-to-B band is the axis this reader weights most: a state of mind is not an idea you can name in a phrase, and there is no premise whose consequences get worked out - the same reasoning that screens down mood-driven books elsewhere in the log. Sustained low spirits is the 1984 60 objection, which is mild but real, and the lead is close to the reader's own life phase without being it. Stated plainly: this entered the queue on a cheap-model score where the model did not know the book and was reading the library's own blurb, so the range is a flag rather than a finding.

The six leads are individually distinct - a naturalist, a telepath, an illusionist, an empath - which is the positive case reviewers keep giving it credit for even when panning everything else. But 'everything else' is exactly axis:ideas: the recurring, specific complaint across reviews is not that the magic-academy premise is thin but that it is never worked through - 'no plot, barely,' 'no world building, no plot, no tension beyond the sexual/romantic one,' 'there is sadly no story to tell.' That is the C-low question answered directly by sources rather than inferred, so I stopped there. A who-to-trust elimination dynamic runs through the year, which is an investigation-shaped subplot worth flagging rather than a whodunnit the book is actually about, so gate 1 clears. The five abilities read as invented categories (elemental, telepathic, empathic) rather than real-world occult practice, but I did not chase the Depiction question - axis:occult stays open rather than cleared.

t: Buh malickosti (The God of Small Things)
why: A real, examined idea survives contact with the plot: caste as a rule that crushes a forbidden love and the family around it, not a background setting. Ammu is divorced from her husband before the affair with Velutha, so the relationship never crosses a marriage or engagement - axis:infidelity does not fire and is not graded. Two risks pull it toward the line. Chapter one deliberately opens past the ending and jumps as far back as 1876 before the present-day thread is clear; several readers report real disorientation even though most settle in - closer to Anne Frank's testimony-form risk than to the multi-POV chaos of the Gunslinger/Discworld DNFs, but genuinely unresolved rather than dismissible. The bleakness is not the mild, occasional kind the profile mostly discounts - it is sustained and immersive for the whole book, closer to 1984 60 ('too depressing') than to Animal Farm 78, which delivers its bleak idea in short, efficient form.
