Per gate 3 I stop here rather than research each linked story; occult is unexamined at this exit.

t: Mapa Jinozemi Emily Wildove (Emily Wilde's Map of the Otherlands)
why: Reviewers describe the fae magic here as deliberately confusing, to the point that 'even the exceptions to the rules have exceptions', which the book embraces rather than resolves. That is close to the opposite of the self-consistency the reader has rewarded (Project Hail Mary 92) and penalized the absence of (Divergent 58, Harry Potter 51). It is also a sequel, and the log's one measured sequel comparison shows a real fall-off (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 down to the Hitchhiker's sequels 70). A missing-scholar subplot is investigation-shaped but a flag rather than a veto, since the book's core satisfaction is the fae world and romance, not solving a case. Leaning on axis:worldbuilding and axis:sequels rather than a specific idea.

t: Misto na svete (A Place in the World: Finding the Meaning of Home)
why: Reviewers describe this as an eclectic assemblage of essay fragments on home, mixing lyricism, recipes, gardening tips and travel description rather than a single examined thesis. The memoir form the reader has rewarded before needed either genuine examination of what is true (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91) or documented insight into a group's lived experience (Son of Hamas 75); this reads closer to descriptive reminiscence about the author's own homes, without either. Named idea, 'place is fate', is real but stays a mood rather than something worked out, so I would list axis:ideas under risks. Exiting at the default band per the ladder rather than researching further.

t: My vsichni neradi (All of Us Villains)
why: A multi-POV tournament-to-the-death premise praised by reviewers for developed characters, but critical reviews also flag a predictable plot and a death-tournament that delivers surprisingly little death on the page, a declared stake the book does not carry through, the same kind of broken commitment that cost Divergent 58 and, on a plausibility basis, Mortal Engines 55. I would list axis:ideas under risks and take the default band. The occult question is left unexamined at this exit, though the tournament runs on family curses and blood-bound spellcasting, vocabulary close enough to real-world occultism to warrant a real look if revisited.

The annotation's premise, Shadowhunters being murdered while Clary and Jace are bound together by a rival, matches the Mortal Instruments arc where an investigation-shaped subplot (who is behind the killings) runs alongside a romance plot; that is a flag under the detective filter, not a veto, since the reader's satisfaction is the romance and world, not solving the murders. Beyond that the series leans on YA romantic melodrama and plot incident rather than the examined motive that carried Ender's Game to 87 or Speaker for the Dead to 90, so I would list axis:ideas under risks. Default band per the ladder.

t: O cem se nemluvi (Behind a Closed Door)
why: The plot is a couple forced by a gamified app into escalating illegal tasks and then a run from the law, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire, and the satisfaction is not a whodunit either, so the detective filter does not fire. Under the corrected axis, most reviewers describe the sexual content as concentrated early and mostly implied - genuine mitigation on the volume dimension, the same shape as Red Rising (95) staying largely undocked because there was little to affect - but a minority of reviewers flag actual explicit passages and degrading treatment of women, which is a real, if smaller, echo of the crudeness that held Artemis to 69 despite consistent worldbuilding. Nothing in the sources establishes strong interiority or motive-driven characters, so this reads as a plot-mechanics thriller rather than one built on what characters want and why - the axis that tops the log - which caps it below the 'nice read' band even with reviewers praising a coherent, twist-heavy plot. Leaned on sexual-content because that is the axis the new rule changes; motives is a risk because the sources say little about character depth one way or the other.

An epic-fantasy trilogy of political intrigue, revolution and war between empires; reviews describe strong characters and a mechanical-construct magic system but no single premise whose consequences the book is built around, unlike the friendship and ideas that carry The Lord of the Rings 84 despite a plot the reader found thin. It is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Occult status is left unexamined per the C-low rule, since the setting includes a goddess's sword, dark magic and a malevolent being that could fail the source test.

An espionage MacGuffin quest: a prison rescue, a friend's dying words, then a hunt for a lost Tsarist library to stop a dormant Soviet satellite weapon. This is plot-mechanics and globe-trotting incident rather than page time on why characters want what they want, the same imbalance that made even chapters of Golden Son 92 get skimmed when it leaned toward action. Not a whodunit (there is no central puzzle to solve, only a chase), so it clears the detective filter, but I would list axis:ideas under risks: there is no standalone idea beyond the chase itself. Default band per the ladder.

t: Sip a vitr, dyka a more (Opowiesci z meekhanskiego pogranicza (tom 2))
why: The annotation itself describes this as woven from individual stories across the world's regions rather than a single followed plot, matching the series' known linked-story-collection format; the one book in the log that succeeded without a single protagonist did so as a short, dense mythic work (The Silmarillion 80), not a multi-region ensemble serial. It is also a sequel, and the log's one measured sequel comparison shows a real fall-off (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 down to the Hitchhiker's sequels 70). Short-story format suspends the character-and-emotion rules but adds nothing on its own, so leaning on axis:multi-pov and axis:sequels rather than a specific idea. The occult question is left unexamined at this exit, despite the setting's explicit mix of magic, politics and religion/cults.

Senk is an established Czech genre short-fiction writer with fifteen-plus stories published in Ikarie, and this is a themed collection unified loosely by 'gods' across different SF settings rather than a single novel. Reader comments on his other collection describe stories that develop well and then end abruptly on one page, or are barely science fiction at all, an uneven-execution pattern that argues for treating axis:ideas as a risk: a themed collection unified only by a loose motif has nothing to lean on the way Animal Farm 78 does with one idea followed all the way through, and the multi-strand, uneven-quality shape resembles what capped Unfinished Tales at 69 more than a book with a single premise worth trusting. That, plus axis:short-idea-driven suspending rather than earning points, is enough to exit at the below-the-line band without reading each story; occult is unexamined at this exit.

A middle-grade adventure entry praised by reviewers for humor, pacing and friendship, but one reviewer flags that its problems keep getting solved by convenient magical items introduced on the spot (a magic submarine, an enchanted survival kit, a spell-cure for an injured dragon) rather than earned consequences within the world's own declared rules, the kind of shortcut that cost Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55. No idea comparable to what carried The Hobbit to 84 on friendship plus real ideas; here the friendship is present but I would list axis:ideas under risks. Default band per the ladder.

Reviews describe the noir plot explicitly as skipping slow investigation for on-the-fly problem-solving, so this clears the detective filter as a flag rather than a veto. But the same reviews describe the lead, a bodyguard-for-hire in a corporate dystopia, as not particularly charismatic and fairly generic, with little room left for character or psychological development next to the book's descriptive prose. That is the same description-over-character imbalance that kept Artemis at 69 despite consistent worldbuilding, except the lead here is reported thinner still, so I would list axis:ideas and axis:protagonist under risks and take the default band.

Direct sequel to 2001, built on a real, worked-out SF idea - what happened to Bowman, why HAL turned homicidal, and first contact via the monolith and Jupiter's transformation - in the vein of what this reader rewards. Docked because multiple reviews flag flat characterization: Metaphorosis calls the cast 'none of whom are interesting' and the plot 'purposeless' relative to the ambition of the premise, and even the sympathetic Goodreads/Time-praised readings focus on plot over people. That is the same weak-lead problem that sank Artemis to 69 below Project Hail Mary 92 for this reader, so the estimate does not lean up on the strength of the idea alone.

A blind ten-year-old girl steps through a painting and can suddenly see - one clear concrete starting situation, the same trait that carried Hitchhiker's Guide 83. From there she is thrown a century back into interwar Prague and has to track down the painter who caused it, giving the book a real idea to hold onto (what changed and what stayed the same across a century, seen through a girl who only just regained her sight) rather than pure incident. Reviews are consistently enthusiastic about the protagonist specifically, not just the premise, which is what separates this from a book that merely clears the filters. Male zeny 79 sets a ceiling for how far pure character-and-friendship without a worked premise can go; this book adds a genuine idea on top, so it is placed a shade above that.

Opens on one concrete inciting incident - a routine clock repair accidentally triggers a decades-old doomsday device - rather than several unresolved threads at once, the structural trait behind this log's strongest openings. The engine of the book is Joe Spork reckoning with his gangster father's legacy - what he wants and why, not just what he does - the axis this log rewards most. It is billed partly as a detective story, but the pull is a slow-unfolding conspiracy and spy plot rather than a whodunit, so this is a flag under gate 1 rather than a filter. Reviewers repeatedly flag uneven, digressive pacing (dense wit 'occasionally to a fault,' one abandoned-read review comparing the opening to disjointed vignettes), a real risk against momentum. The doomsday device and clockwork automata are mechanical/technological, not occult in the ritual sense.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection together - the combination that sits below the line 81% of the time in this log. Ten stories are united only by a loose mood (the surreal breaking into the everyday) rather than one premise whose consequences are worked out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on, and the short-idea-driven suspension removes penalties without adding points. Reviews are positive on craft (individual stories compared to Poe at his best) but even the coverage of it notes it is not considered the author's strongest work.

Memoirs of an internationally celebrated Czech opera singer's career from the 1920s to 1950s. Available descriptions read as warm anecdote - rehearsal-break sausages at Zofin, career milestones - rather than the truth-examining rigor that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 work for this reader. I would put axis:ideas under risks here, which is the test that exits at C rather than going to full research.

t: Cerveny trpaslik (Red Dwarf: Infinity Welcomes Careful Drivers)
why: Reviewers single out Rimmer as an unusually well-realized comic character - 'the eternal under-achiever... a very sad man' - alongside a sympathetic, believably flawed Lister; that is the axis Hitchhiker's Guide 83 topped the comic-SF slot on, character and want over spectacle. The book opens on one concrete situation (Lister stranded and broke on Mimas, then signing aboard Red Dwarf) rather than fanning out into several threads at once, the same structural trait behind Hitchhiker's Guide's score and behind the DNFs (Gunslinger, Discworld) that lacked it. One review flags the novel cramming in several TV-episode plotlines without a fully solid through-line, a mild density risk, but nothing like the outright incoherence that sank those DNFs.

t: Daleko v srdci (Nobody's Son: A Memoir)
why: A multi-generational family memoir - WWII resistance, escape from Communist Czechoslovakia, a difficult immigrant life in Queens - so infidelity is not the premise (the book survives without it) and does not trigger the reject at gate 2. But it is a real subplot, not incidental: the parents' 1945 marriage is described as one born of desperation rather than love, and the mother's decades-long love for another man, resumed years later and lost again, structures a large share of the book and precipitates the eventual divorce. The framing reads as sympathetic to the mother's one real love rather than condemning it, closer to neutral-to-approving than condemned, which caps the estimate in the mid-40s to mid-50s regardless of the memoir's other real strengths. The same examining-what-is-actually-true quality that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 is present here too (one reviewer calls it 'astounding'), but it cannot lift the number out of the infidelity axis's range.

Reviewers are explicit that this is not a fast-paced whodunit - the killer's reveal is 'swift, almost an afterthought' next to the three interwoven character studies - so axis:detective does not fire. That matches the reader's favorite axis, motives over action: three narrators (an obsessive classmate, a girl who hated the victim, and a cop investigating) are given real interiority instead of clue-dropping, the way Speaker for the Dead 90 and the Collins trilogy score on understanding people over events. Risk: Cameron is an unsettling protagonist (a longtime, secret watcher of the victim), which could cost the way an unrootable lead did elsewhere, and reviewers flag the pacing as slow/overstuffed with flashback, a momentum cost. Leaned on motives and the multi-pov structure, which is not confusing at the chapter-one level - the book opens right after the murder is discovered, one concrete situation, not several unclear plot lines.

t: Dost dobre nenormalni (Nicht normal aber das richtig gut)
why: A first-person humor memoir about living with Asperger's (diagnosed at 22) and ADHD (three years later), covering sensory overload, social misunderstanding and prejudice. It has real insight into a lived, misunderstood experience - the closest analogue to what made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 work - but the material reads as a loose sequence of 'curious incidents' commented on with perspective and humor rather than a single thesis worked through. I would put axis:ideas under risks, which is the test that exits at C rather than going to full research.

Multiple reviewers of this YA debut say the lizard-people (not the dragons the title implies) read as vampire lore with the names changed, and the central romance feels forced rather than earned - the same doubt-the-idea test that sent Divergent 58 down (ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering). One reviewer found the protagonist actively unsympathetic. Other readers enjoyed the pace and action, so this is a competent-but-derivative genre entry rather than a clear miss, hence the default under-the-line band.

t: Dum v blankytne modrem mori (The House in the Cerulean Sea)
why: Linus's arc from a lonely, by-the-book bureaucrat into a found-family advocate who challenges the institution he served is a clear want-driven protagonist arc, the pattern that carries Male zeny (79) and Animal Farm (78) here; the systemic-prejudice allegory gives a real idea to leave with, even though one reviewer flags its handling of the acknowledged residential-schools inspiration as oversimplified. Magic here is confirmed across multiple reviews to be ambient trait/identity (a were-Pomeranian, a sprite, a gnome) rather than spells or rites performed on the page, so it clears the occult test the same way a mechanical system would, just via absence rather than mechanism. Docked lightly for its whimsical, YA-adjacent register and for a magic system reviewers call more a 'nod to canon' than internally worked out, the way Ranger's Apprentice (74) and Narnia (67) were docked.

A short, single-idea SF piece in the same shape as Animal Farm 78 and the [66, 76]-predicted-and-70-landed Labyrint sveta - short-idea-driven work is only ever as good as the idea, and this one is a canonical, frequently-anthologized concept: 'semiotic ghosts,' the idea that a discarded era's imagined future can haunt the present, and that the shiny 1930s retro-futurism being documented turns out to share an uncomfortable aesthetic kinship with fascist propaganda. No occult content (no magic, no ritual) and no protagonist arc to speak of, but the short-idea-driven suspension means that is not a penalty here the way it would be in a novel.

t: Gradiva (Gradiva (with Freud's Delusion and Dream in Jensen's Gradiva))
why: The novella's idea -- a repressed love returning as delusion, resolved through recognition and 'cure by love' -- is real, nameable, and is literally the foundational case study of psychoanalysis; unlike Metamorphosis's bleak dead end (58), it resolves warmly, closer to the romance-as-central-subject pattern that costs nothing in Pride and Prejudice (75). Docked because roughly half the published book is Freud's analytical essay rather than story -- heavy exposition, thin narrative event, the same description-over-story penalty the reader profile flags -- and Hanold is passive and deluded for most of the novella before the late resolution, unlike an actively rootable protagonist.

Teenage Sofie wakes alone in a desert and must find a butterfly for a strange girl she meets, a single concrete starting situation close to what worked for Hitchhiker's Guide 83 (opens on one situation, not several plot lines at once). Reviewers repeatedly compare it to The Little Prince and to Maeterlinck's The Blue Bird - both allegorical growing-up quests - and The Little Prince 82 already shows this reader that a short allegory with a real idea (here: things and beings are not what they first look like, and that realization is what growing up is) clears the line despite a child lead. Docked toward the low end of A for the YA register (12+, illustrated), the same modest discount Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Male zeny 79 carry for audience rather than for any specific flaw.

A WWI love story between two schoolboys that spends its pages on what the leads want and fear rather than on battle set-pieces, the axis that also tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Reviewers describe a real, nameable idea - the gap between the sanitized official record of the dead (school 'in memoriam' notices, many lifted from real WWI papers) and the lived horror behind them. Risk: the romance is 'open door' with sexual content warnings for assault as well, which costs the way Artemis 69 was docked, and sustained wartime trauma costs mildly the way 1984 did. Leaned on ideas and motives rather than plot mechanics, since the book is explicitly interiority-driven and not a war-action novel.

Three widely separated timelines (an 18th-century frontier, a near-future corporate climate dystopia, a far-future ice age) share a symbol - the apple seed - and a manifest-destiny theme, but the library annotation and multiple reviews describe it as a 'meditation' on climate change and responsibility rather than naming one premise whose consequences are worked out; the genre-blending and lyrical prose are praised, but I would put axis:ideas under risks rather than name a single idea I am confident holds up under this reader's rules, so this exits at gate 4.

t: Jak Hitler ukradl ruzoveho kralicka (When Hitler Stole Pink Rabbit)
why: A semi-autobiographical account of a nine-year-old Jewish girl's family fleeing Berlin for Switzerland, France and England, built around family solidarity and Anna's own growing agency rather than passive suffering - closer to Male zeny 79, a domestic story that clears on character alone, than to Diary of a Young Girl 40, which failed as testimony rather than as a shaped narrative. It is squarely a children's book, age 9-12 per multiple sources, but treats real historical persecution with more substance than Narnia 67, so it is not graded down as hard as pure fantasy-children's fare. Small pushback for the child protagonist's age, per the standard life-phase discount.

t: Jak jsme v Teheranu cetly Lolitu (Reading Lolita in Tehran: A Memoir in Books)
why: Examines what is actually true about life under a theocracy and gives real insight into how a specific group - women in post-revolutionary Iran - experiences the world, the same combination that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 the top non-fiction score in this log. It is structured around four literary touchstones and opens in medias res on two photographs of her students, not several unresolved plotlines at once, so the opening filter is clean. The main risk is that a large share of the book is literary criticism of Nabokov, Fitzgerald, James and Austen interleaved with the memoir - denser and more academic than Qureshi's book, which could read as digression rather than lived insight depending on how much a given chapter leans on analysis over testimony.

t: Je matka mrtva (Er mor død (Is Mother Dead))
why: A middle-aged artist returns to Oslo after thirty years and becomes consumed with understanding, then surveilling, the mother she is estranged from. The entire novel is interiority - what Johanna wants, why, and whether her own account can be trusted - the axis that tops this reader's log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Docked because Johanna is genuinely hard to root for at points: reviewers describe an 'ugly aggressiveness' and escalating boundary-crossing (hiding in her mother's building, going through her trash) that several critics say erodes reader sympathy as the book goes on - not the flat unrootability of a villain lead like Coriolanus Snow (The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65), but a real risk in the same family.

Two divorced, lonely people are pushed onto a long walking trip by a mutual friend and the book alternates their POV as they slowly choose to re-engage with each other - the wanting-and-why axis that tops Pyc-a-predsudek 75 and Mockingjay 91, with no infidelity in play since both marriages already ended before the story starts. The opening is one concrete situation, a group walking holiday, rather than several competing lines. Risk: it is a 190-mile walk rendered scene by scene, which is the kind of drawn-out structure that cost Les Miserables 71 against Monte Cristo 75 - terrain description could thin the story if it runs long.

t: Kdo tanci s vodou (The Water Dancer)
why: Conduction is declared precisely -- activated by memory, triggered by loss, tied to a maternal lineage -- and the book follows through on that declaration to its climax (Hiram unlocking full power only after confronting the buried memory of his mother's sale), the same self-consistency that rewards Project Hail Mary (92) and Red Rising (95). It clears axis:occult on the mechanism test: no invocation, ritual or real-world esoteric source, just an internal ability keyed to memory. The central idea -- that memory of what was lost is literally the mechanism of liberation -- is nameable and well-executed, reviewed as the novel's organizing metaphor throughout. Slavery is the backdrop, so bleakness is a real risk, but the throughline is family reconnection and purposeful agency (joining the Underground) rather than sustained despair, closer to Project Hail Mary's companionship discount than to 1984's flat misery.

t: Kdyz neni kral (When There Is No King (selected stories))
why: A curated best-of selection of Thiep's stories -- family sagas, historical vignettes, village folktales, and social satire of post-war communist Vietnam. Literary fiction plus short-story collection triggers gate 4's mechanical exit; the anthology spans too many disparate settings and forms for a single worked idea to carry it, whatever its historical importance to Vietnamese letters.

A solid, well-liked entry in a Czech medieval-set fantasy series (82% on Legie), praised for a relatable, developing squire protagonist and strong atmosphere - but the reviewer who covers it professionally singles out that the book under-develops the supernatural threat at its center, and it is told in four episodic parts that each introduce new characters, closer to a competent genre read than one with a worked idea behind it. That is the doubt gate 4 asks about (I would put axis:ideas under risks), so it lands in the default under-the-line band rather than being pushed lower - readers do not report it as confusing, just modest in ambition.

t: Kniha silenstvi a lecby (The Book of Madness and Cures)
why: A Renaissance quest novel that several reviewers call heavy on invented medical/alchemical detail and light on story - 'revels in alliteration,' 'never met an adjective she didn't like' - the same heavy-description-little-story pattern that cost Les Miserables and Unfinished Tales points in this log. More damaging: the book spends its length establishing Gabriella as an unconventional, independent female physician and then resolves her arc into a conventional marriage-and-childbirth ending that multiple reviewers say the character herself doesn't support - a declared trait the book doesn't carry through, the kind of self-consistency breach that sinks worldbuilding elsewhere. No occult concern: the 'madness and cures' material is period medicine/alchemy theorizing, not a rite enacted on the page. Leaned on density and protagonist-consistency rather than the travelogue plot, which is competently assembled but not more; risk that the historical-detail vehicle crowds out a real idea, per at least one reviewer's read.

Nearly a dozen first-person narrators with no unifying voice, and multiple independent reviewers report real disorientation specifically in the opening third - one calls the narrative choice itself an irritating distraction, another says they had no idea what the characters were doing, or why. That is shape one of the opening filter, several lines running before any is legible, which is what ended Guards! Guards! at 30. Moved down a band 2026-08-28. The old range rested on reviewers reporting that the pieces crystallize into a rewarding whole by the end, and that defence is worthless whatever the shape of the confusion: Caropisci 30 was abandoned in chapter one, so a payoff several hundred pages away is a payoff this reader never collects. What keeps it off the floor rather than at it is that the themes - love, obligation, death, redemption - sit close to what he responds to, and the magic is handled without incantation-and-spellcasting cliches so occult is clear; neither pays if he stops on page twenty.

Reception is genuinely split in a way that raises real doubt about axis:ideas: Kirkus calls it a dramatic, complex imagining of Stonehenge's origins, but the Washington Independent Review calls it 'wildly oversimplified' with a plot that could be jotted on a Post-it note, and multiple reader reviews call the leads 'one-dimensional' and the story 'simply plotted' with 'not enough there' for 700 pages. I can name the premise (a priestess's vision of a stone monument, opposed by drought and tribal mistrust) but not a worked-through idea beyond it, which is exactly the exit test. Stopping at C-low; occult status (Neolithic seasonal/religious ceremonies at the monument) is unexamined at this exit.

A single declared premise - reality itself runs on two-valued logic in Winter and three-valued logic in Summer - is carried through consequences on physics, law, psychology, religion, and even the book's narration, exactly the rule-following-its-own-rules axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. The protagonist, a gambler blackmailed into government service, is given a real arc (he becomes a 'shaper' and declares himself a Mathematician of History), avoiding the passive-lead problem that cost Promena 58 and Oliver Twist 57. Two risks hold this back from a higher band: the political landscape is dense enough that one reader summary found it hard to keep track of who represented what, and a secondary faction is an ice-worshipping cult literally led by the real Rasputin - close enough to real-world occultism to fail the Source test if it is actually enacted on the page. I could not confirm a specific on-page ritual scene, and reviews describe it as a background power-struggle thread next to the main logic-of-reality plot, not the book's focus.

t: Loutkar z Krakova (The Dollmaker of Krakow)
why: Animal Farm 78 shows this reader can accept sustained bleakness when the book gives something to think about rather than just immersing him in misery; this book pairs its Holocaust-era setting with a real, worked idea - the same kind of magic is used by the dollmaker to protect and by a Nazi officer to corrupt, framing power as morally neutral and dependent on the wielder, not a rules-free deus ex machina. Occult is clear: the dollmaker's power is left deliberately folkloric and unexplained rather than modeled on any real ritual, and no rite is enacted on the page. Docked into the high-60s/low-70s for its younger target age (9-11, noticeably younger register than most of the log) the same way Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 pay a modest childrens-axis cost.

t: Mala cviceni v bezohlednosti (Small Exercises in Ruthlessness)
why: Ten stories about introverted women constrained by upbringing and totalitarian-era circumstance, connected loosely like a novel but marketed and reviewed as a story collection -- literary fiction plus short-story form triggers gate 4's mechanical exit; the loose novelistic connection doesn't rescue it since no single premise is worked through end to end.

Pelagia ends her engagement to Mandras outright before anything starts with Corelli, so this is sequential rather than concurrent and axis:infidelity does not fire, matching how romance itself costs nothing in Pyc-a-predsudek 75. What carries the number is Pelagia's arc of wanting and choosing between two men and two futures, the same wanting-and-why axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Risk: reviewers note the unmarked second-chapter switch to a disconnected Mussolini monologue and call the opening a little bit confusing before the perspective shifts settle - not the several-plot-lines failure that sank Guards! Guards! 30, since the Dr Iannis/Pelagia household is legible from chapter one, but real enough to flag. The later massacre of the Italian garrison is a bleak turn, docked only mildly per this reader's standard light treatment of bleakness.

t: Manual pro uklizecky (A Manual for Cleaning Women: Selected Stories)
why: Forty-three autobiographically-rooted stories spanning Berlin's own life across many cities and decades -- widely acclaimed (NYT 100 Best Books of the 21st Century) but literary reputation earns nothing at gate 4. Litfic short-story collection triggers the mechanical exit regardless of quality; no single throughline premise to lean on across 43 independent pieces.

A tie-in Star Trek: Titan novel built around a mysterious object watching over the planet Orisha (the 'Eye of Erykon'). Reader reviews of this specific book say the promised explanation of the Eye and the Orishan civilization never fully lands, the ending is cut off to set up a later crossover, and the back half slides into the series' familiar Orion's-dogs beats rather than following through on the new premise. I would put axis:ideas under risks - the mystery reads as atmosphere the series hasn't cashed in yet, not a premise worked to its consequences - so this exits at gate 4. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 across its sequels.

t: Na konci duhy (At the Rainbow's End (selected stories))
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection - the combination that sits below 68 in 81% of the log's cases. This specific edition is a bilingual English-Czech learner's text (footnoted for vocabulary and grammar) collecting three of London's lesser-known stories, not his canonical Yukon work. Beyond an atmospheric 'love, life and death along the frozen river' framing, I cannot name a specific worked-through idea, which is the lower-band test, so I am using the [42,55] band rather than the default.

New Crobuzon's magic, thaumaturgy, is treated by reviewers as 'just another natural resource to be exploited,' used hand-in-hand with industrial technology and carrying declared consequences that persist - a past 'thaumaturgic atomic bomb' left the land mutated to this day. That is a declared capability whose consequences the book actually carries through, the axis that drove Project Hail Mary to 92. No rite performed on the page turned up in the sources on how thaumaturgy is actually used; it reads as an exploited resource rather than devotion, so I am not treating it as occult. Docked for density: reviewers repeatedly single out the novel's 'amazing and detailed description' and bulk, the same digression tax that cost Les Miserables 71 against The Count of Monte Cristo 75; Isaac's actual research plot is comparatively simple next to the city's texture.

Fifteen whimsical, unconnected fantasy stories riffing on fairy-tale and folklore premises (how stars are born, what the Beauty who does not kiss the Beast pays with, and so on) - a collection with no single premise has no axis:ideas to lean on the way a short idea-driven piece needs, per the short-idea-driven rule: the suspension of character/emotion rules removes penalties but never adds points. Reader reception is genuinely split, from enthusiastic to one reader finishing only 8 of 15 stories and liking just one, which matches a mixed-bag anthology rather than a book with a case for going higher.

t: Neslibovala jsem ti prochazku ruzovym sadem (I Never Promised You a Rose Garden)
why: A completed, semi-autobiographical account of recovery from schizophrenia that examines what is actually true about the experience from the inside - the same rigor that lifted Seeking Allah Finding Jesus to 91. Unlike The Diary of a Young Girl (40, DNF, a child's inner life that did not work), this one finishes, with the protagonist actually recovering and re-entering the world, so the memoir-form bonus should apply rather than the counter-example. Some risk from a 16-year-old protagonist (a small life-phase cost, as with Ender's Game marked down for reading young) and from reviewers calling the prose dense and occasionally melodramatic, a story-density cost. Leaned on the memoir-form/protagonist combination rather than plot, since the book has little external plot to speak of.

Reviewers are consistent that the siblings' relationship develops an explicit sexual and incestuous element as they mature, with reviews specifically flagging the crudeness - lurid, repeated masturbation episodes - alongside the volume, since it recurs across the back half of the book. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. Crudeness is present and sustained here, which is the dimension that actually sinks a book, so the Ready Player One anchor alone supports this range; the withdrawn one was never load-bearing.

t: Nezname veledilo a jine prozy (The Unknown Masterpiece and Other Stories)
why: A collection of Balzac novellas about artists (a painter and composer obsessed with perfection, a sculptor undone by naivety), unified by a shared theme but still a literary-fiction short-story collection, which triggers gate 4's mechanical exit regardless of classic-canon status. The suspension for short idea-driven work removes the character-arc penalty but doesn't add points for the recognizable theme by itself.

The idea (small local conflicts spiralling through tit-for-tat retaliation into a war nobody wants) is real and worked through, not just asserted - reviewers call it 'urgent and fiercely compelling' with a 'sobering' ending, and it is carried by characters making decisions from stated motives (a first-time female president, a spy, a general), the axis that tops this log via Mockingjay and Speaker for the Dead. Docked for the ensemble multi-pov structure that spreads page time across four threads rather than one deep POV, and for a Goodreads-flagged tendency toward overwritten political/domestic chapters - risks that could pull it toward the Silmarillion-style discount for lack of a single throughline, not a confusing-opening problem since each thread is individually legible from the start.

The book's idea is nameable and sustained: who gets to define 'hero' and 'monster,' and how an institution's official story can be false - the same institutional-critique shape that made Golden Son's 92 Fitchner-as-Ares reveal feel earned rather than sprung. Unlike Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, where an unrootable slide into villainy cost 22 points against its own sibling, this book keeps its nominal villain Ballister genuinely sympathetic and wrongly cast as a monster rather than actually becoming one, which is exactly the difference the reader's protagonist rule cares about. No real-world occult: Nimona's shapeshifting and the setting's knights-plus-technology blend read as invented fantasy-SF hybrid rather than anything ritual-based. Held under the mid-80s because the blended magic/tech worldbuilding logic was not independently verified for consistency.

A comic historical novel about a low-status survivor navigating a violent Renaissance court by wit, in the vein of Saturnin (78, liked for voice and character rather than any worked-out idea). Ugo is an engaging, sympathetic lead who survives on cleverness rather than competence handed to him. Risk: Publishers Weekly calls the plotting overstuffed at points, which can cost momentum. Leaned on the protagonist rather than plot or theme, since there is no larger idea beyond the survival-by-wit premise - closer to the Saturnin case than to an idea-driven book.

I cannot cleanly separate premise from subplot here - reviewers and summaries repeatedly call Ned and Margery's relationship 'the most central relationship in the plot,' even though the book carries substantial parallel plotlines (Elizabeth's spy network, Catholic-Protestant war), so I am grading rather than rejecting, per the rule that a wrong reject is unrecoverable. Margery is coerced into marrying Bart, then has a multi-month affair with Ned that produces a son of disputed paternity; the narrative never condemns this - it sympathizes with the separated lovers throughout and resolves with their marriage once both spouses conveniently die, which reads as approving framing (nobody is ruined for it) and multiplies the deduction under the subplot/approving band. Sexual content is a further, well-documented risk: multiple independent reviewers call the series' sex scenes gratuitous or 'cringe-worthy,' and this specific title carries an explicit-sexual-content flag plus a warning for sexual assault.

t: Pameti imaginarniho kamarada (Memoirs of an Imaginary Friend)
why: Budo is an interesting and rootable protagonist -- loyal, resourceful, and facing real stakes (his own existence ends when Max stops believing in him) -- similar to how protagonist quality carried Sunrise on the Reaping 22 points above its sibling prequel. The idea (what makes something real; loyalty and self-sacrifice measured against self-preservation) is nameable and followed through to the climax. The occult signal is a false hit: imaginary friends here are an invented narrative device with no ritual, invocation or real-world esoteric source, clearing axis:occult on the mechanism test. Docked for a YA/children's register (won the Dolly Gray Award for Children's Literature) since the telling leans simple and sentimental rather than on complex ideas, closer to Ranger's Apprentice (74) than to The Little Prince's tighter allegory (82).

t: Pet Cinanu obesenych v Idahu (Four Treasures of the Sky)
why: A trafficking-and-immigration survival story that reviewers say handles its brothel chapters 'delicately but forcefully' rather than gratuitously, examining Chinese Exclusion-era racism the way Son of Hamas 75 and Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 earn credit for examining real history and identity from the inside. Daiyu is a resourceful, reinventing-herself lead worth rooting for. Risk from the sexual-assault content (present within one act of a three-part journey, described as tastefully handled rather than crude) and sustained grimness across the book. Leaned on ideas and protagonist rather than plot mechanics, since the plot itself is mainly a sequence of survival episodes.

t: Pozdni navratilec (Latehomecomer and Other Stories (Czech-curated selection))
why: A curated selection of Gallant's short stories about emigres and exiles in postwar Paris -- 13 disparate pieces from two different English collections, no single premise worked through across them. Literary fiction plus short-story form triggers the gate-4 mechanical exit regardless of Gallant's strong critical reputation (Chekhov/Henry James comparisons); the suspension for short idea-driven work removes the character-arc penalty but does not add points on its own.

After two percent of the world vanishes with no explanation attempted or given, the book spends its time on what the survivors want and believe rather than on the disappearance itself - the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both top this log on. A minor infidelity thread lives entirely in one character's backstory (her ex-husband's affair, publicly exposed and condemned by another character, not the relationship she is currently in) - incidental, not premise, worth only a point or two. A manufactured-prophet subplot (a healer later revealed as exploiting his followers) is played with real cynicism rather than straight, a small further cost on prophecy. The real risk is the ensemble: five-plus character threads across one family and town is denser than this log's best-scoring structures (Hunger Games 89's tight single POV), though the book is organized sequentially by character rather than fragmenting several threads at once in chapter one.

t: Pribeh o lasce a tme (A Tale of Love and Darkness)
why: A literary memoir of growing up in 1940s Jerusalem, examining the author's mother's suicide and his family's history entangled with Israel's founding. It matches the axis that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 work: an adult narrator genuinely examining what happened rather than performing it, giving real insight into an unfamiliar historical experience - unlike The Diary of a Young Girl 40, which failed as a child's raw diary. Leaned on axis:memoir-form for that reason. Docked for a real density risk: critics (Jewish Review of Books, citing Ariana Melamed's review) call the non-chronological structure "structureless," drowning the story in self-indulgent digression - the same kind of digression that cost Les Miserables 71 against The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Also carries mild bleakness, since the mother's suicide is the emotional core.

t: Prvni laska a jine povidky (First Love and Other Stories)
why: A literary-fiction short story collection, the combination this reader's data puts below 68 four times out of five. The title novella does carry a real idea - a sixteen-year-old's first love curdles into disillusionment when he discovers his admired father is secretly involved with the same girl - but that reveal also touches marital infidelity (the father is married to the narrator's mother); at the level of this one novella I cannot cleanly separate premise from subplot, so I am grading rather than rejecting, and the collection as a whole is not built around that thread. Between the collection penalty and the infidelity doubt, this settles at the default C-low band rather than higher.

A graphic-novel adaptation of Capek's 1920 play, not the original text - it keeps the play's central idea (mass-produced artificial labor that ultimately supplants its makers), the same register that carried Animal Farm to 78 on ideas alone. But a play redrawn into a picture-driven format has little room for interior motive, the axis this log weighs above ideas, and the publisher explicitly aimed the adaptation at an audience a hundred years younger than the original, i.e. simplified for accessibility. Reader reviews of this specific edition are split on the artwork, with more than one reviewer saying they would rather reread Capek's original.

This book was originally five separate Hugo-winning stories stitched into a novel, and multiple reviewers say it still feels fragmented - the same shape of penalty that cost Unfinished Tales 69 ('the pieces are not logically connected to each other'). Unlike that book, Hothouse carries one sustained idea across the whole novel (entropy versus fecundity, humanity's biological decline in a jungle-choked far future), closer to how Silmarillion 80 scores well on scope and ideas despite no continuous plot or single protagonist, so it is not pushed as low as Unfinished Tales. Docked further for reviewer-confirmed thin, caricature-level characterization, and because the protagonist Gren becomes markedly less rootable once a parasitic fungus starts manipulating him into threats and violence in the back half - the same shape of penalty that separated Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 from its sibling by 22 points.

Remarque's own late-life reckoning: a Holocaust survivor who spent years hiding in a museum builds a new life in New York, examining survivor's guilt and what it meant to be 'a thinking German' in that era - real interiority about what a character wants and why, not just what happens to him. His relationship with Natasha counters the loneliness, the axis this reader rewards over solo survival (Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82). Docked for bleakness (concentration-camp survival, a friend's death) and because even sympathetic critics admit the plot itself 'wasn't that exciting' and reuses themes from Remarque's earlier, stronger novels - a deliberately quiet, anticlimactic book by design, but one that costs momentum.

Hitchhiker's sequels 70 already show this reader that a sequel is not a safe bet on its own (13 points under book one, 83 to 70), and reviewers of this specific entry, while judging it the more cohesive of the two, still describe the tone as 'a bit less elegant... a bit more on-the-nose' than book one, whose own biggest complaint was reading 'like the outline of a TV show concept.' That is enough to doubt the idea holds up beyond a competent pulp multiverse premise. Occult was checked because it is mandatory: the antagonist faction HEX is styled as 'gothically magical,' but no source found a specific on-page invocation or ritual scene, and the protagonist's own dimension-walking is framed as an inherited trait rather than a cast spell, so this is graded rather than vetoed.

Three boys at the ship's lowest-status table carry the book on their distinct wants and curiosity rather than on plot machinery - the narrator, Cassius and Ramadhin are differentiated the way Darrow, Sevro and Mustang are in Golden Son 92. The opening is one concrete situation, a boy alone boarding a ship, rather than several competing lines, so it clears the confusing-opening test cleanly. What holds it out of the A band: critics flag a missing core to the novel and the fragmented, retrospective structure reads as digressive rather than built around one worked idea, closer to the diffuse payoff of Unfinished Tales 69 than to a book with a single clear thesis - so I lean on the character work rather than crediting an idea I cannot name precisely.

t: Svadlena z Dachau (The Dressmaker of Dachau (US: The Dressmaker's War))
why: The opening is one clear situation, an ambitious young seamstress in 1939 London, then trapped in occupied France, rather than several competing lines. What holds this down is the protagonist herself: reviewers repeatedly describe Ada as an enigma, alternately strong and decisive and naive and frustrating, and one detailed review says the prose is impersonal and disjointed and that the reviewer never felt Ada and her struggle - the same failure to connect with a lead that cost Oliver Twist 57 and, less severely, Artemis 69. The protagonist axis carries the number rather than the wartime survival premise itself, which several reviewers found effectively and even restrainedly handled.

At under 130 pages this is short-idea-driven territory, and the idea names cleanly: a small-town coal merchant chooses to act against the complicit silence protecting a Magdalene laundry, at real cost to himself and his family - a nameable moral premise actually worked through to a decision, the same shape that clears Labyrint sveta 70. Bill Furlong's motive, what he owes the community versus what he owes his conscience, is the whole book, matching what tops the log. Docked only mildly for the bleakness of the institutional-abuse subject matter, per the standard light touch on bleakness, since the book is widely described as ending on hope rather than despair.

t: Takovy prima vek (Such a Fun Age)
why: A social novel about race, class and performative allyship, built on what Emira and Alix each want and refuse to admit - the axis that also carries Pride and Prejudice to 75, where romance/social dynamics as the entire subject cost nothing. Not a mystery despite the initial 'detective' signal: the kidnapping accusation is a single inciting incident, not an ongoing investigation the reader is meant to solve. Emira is sympathetic and worth rooting for; Alix is deliberately less so, but the book is dual-POV, not solely inside her. Risk: reviewers are split on whether the ending resolves too neatly/anticlimactically, a momentum concern. Leaned on ideas and motives.

t: Tehdy jsme zili v letni zemi (A Children's Bible)
why: A bleak climate-collapse allegory close in shape to Animal Farm (78, liked for being short, idea-driven and giving something to think about despite bleakness) - reviewers frame the parents' drug/alcohol/sexual excess as a symbolic device for adult abdication rather than as titillation, and the children (unusually mature for their ages) take over survival once catastrophe hits. That symbolic sexual content, and background 'pointless infidelities' among the parents, still cost on their respective axes even handled at a remove. Leaned on ideas: the generational-betrayal allegory is explicit and nameable, not just bleak events with nothing behind them.

t: The happy prince and other tales (The Happy Prince and Other Tales)
why: The self-sacrifice and social-critique ideas are clear and consistently corroborated across multiple stories in the collection - a statue and a swallow give away everything to relieve poverty, a giant is redeemed by opening his garden to a child, a nightingale's sacrifice is undercut by irony about wasted devotion - the same short-idea-driven pattern that carries The Little Prince (82) and Animal Farm (78) despite the fairy-tale form. The catalogue annotation itself frames this edition as aimed at older readers rather than small children, matching how the life-phase and childrens rules barely touched The Little Prince. Docked a little relative to Little Prince since several of the tales lean more didactic/moralizing (explicit Christ-figure and divine-justice framing) than Saint-Exupery's.

Ten stories, each built on one hard-SF premise pushed through to its consequences - engines to physically relocate Earth out of the solar system, humanity shrinking to survive collapse - and reviewers specifically praise the scientific rigor of the execution (one plot point checked and defended against real neutrino physics). That is exactly what short fiction has to earn in this log: name the idea, and here every story has a nameable one, unlike a themed mood collection with no single premise. No character carries across stories, so the collection can't earn on protagonist or motive, only on ideas, which caps how high it can go next to a novel like Project Hail Mary 92.

The idea - intimacy and dignity found across an unbridgeable difference, set against a Cold War institution's violence and prejudice - is real and reasonably well realized; Booklist calls it 'phenomenally enrapturing,' in the same companionship-over-isolation vein that lifts Project Hail Mary (92) over The Martian. But the interspecies relationship is rendered directly and repeatedly on the page - one reviewer notes the sex scenes are described in 'circumstantial language... not euphemistic' and that 'even the sex is new and strange and different' - which reads as crude by virtue of the pairing itself even where the narrative frames the creature as godlike and reverent. This is closer to Artemis's crudeness dock than to Red Rising's near-zero one, and here the volume is not small. Content warnings for sexual assault, gore and depicted bigotry add further bleakness risk beyond the base estimate.

A multi-POV family novel where the author has stated his goal was making every character's motives legible to the reader in turn - the axis that also carries Speaker for the Dead to 90 and the Collins trilogy generally. The book opens on one concrete situation (a tragedy witnessed during the family's last reunion at the lake house) rather than fanning out into several unclear plot lines, matching what worked in Hitchhiker's Guide 83. Risk: infidelity is one of several long-buried parental secrets revealed (alongside alcoholism and a hidden pregnancy), not the premise, and the resolution favors reconciliation over reward for the affair, so it should cost only modestly - flagged as a risk rather than leaned on because the exact framing (how condemned vs. neutral) isn't fully pinned down from the sources found. Also flagged: some reviewers call the ending too neat/soap-opera-ish, a momentum risk. Leaned on motives, which is what the book is explicitly built around.

Reviewers agree the first part is legible and has momentum, a single starting situation of an English woman traveling to Jachymov in August 1968 to find her father's family, so it does not fail on opening the way Guards! Guards! 30 did. But reception is sharply split on execution: one reviewer calls the back half a senseless string of vile things, another says the plot gets tangled in metaphors and dream elements by the midpoint, which reads as the same worldbuilding-coherence failure that cost Harry Potter 51 and Mortal Engines 55 - a supernatural system tied to the town's uranium mines that is gestured at atmospherically rather than held to consistent rules. Search snippets could not establish whether any specific rite is enacted on the page, so the occult status stays unexamined and is flagged as a risk rather than resolved.

t: Umeni radosti (The Art of Joy (L'arte della gioia))
why: A life-spanning feminist epic, not narrowly a sex plot, so it does not meet the sex-as-the-plot veto - Modesta's ascent also runs through class, politics and crime. But the sexual content is at the extreme end of every dimension this reader grades: sustained across the whole 540-page span, explicit, and including incest and a described collapse of physical pleasure into rape. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected, and the graded-crudeness axis added to deps - this line argued from that rule without depending on it, so a change to the rule would not have reached it. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. Immaterial here: crudeness is at its maximum, which is the dimension that actually sinks a book. Per the axis rule, literary reputation earns nothing - critics themselves cite the transgressive content as the book's defining, deliberate quality rather than incidental.

t: Vecer a jitro (The Evening and the Morning)
why: Ragna's husband Wilf openly keeps other women throughout their marriage, and Ragna herself is drawn to the boatbuilder Edgar once Wilf loses interest, later bearing a son of disputed paternity by a second husband - infidelity runs through the book but as one of three parallel character arcs (Edgar's Viking-raid survival, monk Aldred's abbey ambitions being the other two), not the sole engine of the plot, so I am grading it as a subplot. Framing reads as neutral rather than approving or condemning: one reviewer specifically calls Ragna's passion 'told as a third party might report it' - detached rather than romanticized - landing at the higher end of the subplot/neutral band (45-55) rather than lower. Reviewers describe the book as packed with rape, murder, arson and betrayal 'in nearly every chapter,' which is a real bleakness and sexual-content risk beyond what the base estimate assumes.

Reviews single out the same thing this log rewards: the story is described as well-balanced between military description and the civilian storylines of ordinary people with real influence on events, rather than battle spectacle for its own sake, and reader ratings report it as entertaining from the first page. The catastrophe premise (sudden, drastic 1848 sea-level rise flooding central Europe) is not explained in any source I found, so I cannot confirm the cause is carried through as consistently as, say, Project Hail Mary's astrophage - a real but not disqualifying risk, since an alternate-history catastrophe gets more latitude than a declared hard-SF mechanism.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection, the combination that lands below 68 four times out of five in this log. Fourteen dreamlike, surreal prose pieces (several drawn directly from Kafka's own dream diaries) with no single premise worked through, closer in kind to this same author's Promena 58, the direct Kafka anchor in this log, which was marked down for a passive lead and bleakness that arrives all at once. A collection has no lead at all to root for, so this sits at the lower band rather than the default: no idea to name across the set, and a form (fragmented short prose) that suspends the character rules without anything to replace them.

Content is heavy and recurring: torture, sexual assault, rape and prostitution run through the book. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The old wording called this 'more volume and explicitness than Ready Player One 55 or The Witcher 53, both sunk mainly by volume', which had the mechanism wrong. Restated: depicted sexual violence recurring throughout is the crudeness dimension, not the volume one, so it measures against Ready Player One 55 and lands at least as severe. Range holds on the corrected reasoning.

Reviewers describe this deliberately as a fantasy with no true hero, no true villain and no true quest - episodic and dreamlike rather than resolving what it sets up, which is exactly the doubt gate 4 asks about: I would list axis:ideas under risks. Lead Gwynn works as bodyguard and assassin for a slave-trading magnate and the other lead collects deformed fetuses; neither reads as rootable in the way this reader responds to (the 22-point gap between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 was exactly an unrootable descent-into-darkness lead). A competent, well-regarded literary fantasy, so the default under-the-line band rather than the lower one.

Ed's arc from passive suburban man to a hardened survivor is a real character transformation worth rooting for, and the book follows through on its central idea -- that civilization's veneer over primal instinct is thin -- with genuine consequence (Lewis's readiness to kill, Ed's transformation into a hunter), the kind of worked-out premise the log rewards (Project Hail Mary 92, Red Rising 95). Violence is not an objection for this reader, so the graphic river-trip violence costs nothing directly, but sustained trauma and a grim aftermath is a mild bleakness risk, closer to The Martian's loneliness discount (82) than to 1984's flatly depressing tone (60). A graphic male sexual-assault scene is flagged as a content risk since its treatment is disturbing violence rather than romantic or erotic content, so axis:sexual-content likely does not apply directly, but the intensity could still cost under a general content read.

t: Zakriveny cas v Kremzi (Curved Time in Krems)
why: Five loosely linked stories about aging men confronting the elusive, non-linear nature of time -- literary fiction, explicitly subtitled 'five stories,' and a Czech reviewer found the title story's time-loop conceit too convoluted to follow. Gate 4's mechanical exit applies regardless of Magris's literary reputation; a slim 100-page book with no single worked premise across the set.

A manhunt/revenge thriller, not a whodunit - the twelve masterminds are known from the start and the tension is catching them, so axis:detective does not fire. But reviewers flag exactly the kind of implausibility this reader penalizes under self-consistency - law enforcement's total collapse resolving too smoothly - close to how Mortal Engines 55 was marked down for logic that didn't hold, and there is no idea beyond the revenge/manhunt mechanics the way Red Rising 95 or Project Hail Mary 92 build consequences out of their premise. Leaning on axis:ideas for a below-the-line exit; overspent the gate-1 budget by nothing since the same two sources answered both the detective question and the below-the-line one.

A revenge/uprising story against a systemic, misogynist mecha-piloting system that literally sacrifices girls to save boys' lives; the rigged qi-draining mechanism is a declared, explained capability whose consequences and reveal the plot actually turns on - the self-consistency this reader rewards (Red Rising 95, Project Hail Mary 92). Zetian is driven, vengeful and assertive from a clear motive (avenging her sister), the axis that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Carried as a risk rather than cleared: the mecha system runs on qi and yin-yang, drawn from real Chinese metaphysical tradition rather than a purely invented mechanism, and background dialogue describes 'gods' watching over the setting (their reveal as disguised humans comes only in the sequel); I could not confirm from sources whether any qi- or god-related rite is staged on the page within this specific book, so I am not clearing axis:occult, only flagging the doubt. Sexual content is present (a central F/M/M relationship) but reviewers describe it as implied rather than shown, which mitigates that axis.

Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82 both score on competent, duty-driven problem-solvers under survival pressure, and reviewers describe this book's captain in almost the same terms - 'just does what's necessary, does not care about popularity' - while explicitly praising 'relationship dynamics and minimal action' over spectacle, which is the single axis that tops this reader's whole log (motives over action). One reviewer also credits it with real astrophysics rather than hand-waved setting. Held below Project Hail Mary's range for a reported slow first half and a dissenting review calling the side characters shallow.

t: Ztracena v dobre knize (Lost in a Good Book)
why: The book-jumping mechanism (Jurisfiction, the Prose Portal) is a declared, rule-based system operated like a trade with its own bureaucracy rather than invocation or devotion, so it passes the occult mechanism test the way Allomancy does. Comparisons to Douglas Adams and Wodehouse are direct and earned, the same comic-SF register that scored Hitchhiker's Guide 83, and the identity/existence theme reviewers highlight is a real idea, not just wordplay. Risk: this is book two of a series and reviewers are split on whether it is more linear than book one or a dense transition novel hard to fully grasp on one read - not the several-plot-lines failure that sank Guards! Guards! 30, since the inciting hook (a husband erased from existence) is a single clear situation, but real enough to flag, and Hitchhiker's own sequels fell 13 points from book one, so a sequel is not a safe bet in this log.

A middle-grade novel examining the Holodomor through three interwoven timelines, praised by Kirkus and PW for a 'completely believable, emotionally powerful conclusion' - the kind of genuine historical reckoning that lifted Son of Hamas to 75, pitched here for a younger reader. Register and audience are plainly children's (a 13-year-old stuck at home during COVID is the framing device), the way Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 pay a small cost for audience without being vetoed - the difference is a real, nameable idea (a suppressed atrocity, and what it costs to keep telling the story) doing more work than either of those. Leaned on ideas; risk from the childrens register and the young lead's age.

t: Zvlastni smutek citronoveho kolace (The Particular Sadness of Lemon Cake)
why: The mother's affair is a subplot within a larger magic-realist family story (Rose's gift, a brother who turns into furniture, a grandmother's discarded objects), not the premise, so it is graded rather than vetoed. But the framing lands closer to neutral-to-approving than condemned: the mother is confronted and simply asks whether Rose wants her to stop, then continues the affair for years with no real consequence to her. That subplot-neutral combination costs heavily on its own under this reader's rules. On top of that, reviewers say the book declares magical rules (furniture transformation, a hinted power in the father) it never explains and calls the ending 'slapped together' - the same declare-and-fail-to-carry-through breach that hurt worldbuilding elsewhere in this log (contrast Kafka's Metamorphosis 58, which at least had a legible, if bleak, premise). Leaned on the infidelity-framing and the unexplained magic system rather than the premise itself, which is a real, nameable idea (tasting emotions in food) the execution does not sustain.

This is a short, youth-oriented prose retelling of an inherited myth rather than an original idea worked out -- reviewers are split on whether Nye's version actually carries the original's thematic weight, and one specific innovation (Unferth calling Grendel 'beautiful') is criticized as undermining rather than deepening the moral question, unlike the dense, rewarded mythic prose of the reader's own Silmarillion (80). I would put axis:ideas in risks, so exiting here at the default band rather than researching further. Violence/gore is heavy per reviewers but not an objection for this reader.

Beth Harmon is repeatedly singled out by reviewers as rare-talent-plus-relatable-frailty, the exact combination of interesting-and-rootable the reader's log rewards (Ender's Game 87, Speaker for the Dead 90), and the book is described as page-turning with tension on nearly every page -- the same constant-momentum, single-POV quality that made The Hunger Games a baseline favorite (89). Chess strategy and addiction give real interiority, not just event. Docked from the top because reviewers flag thin supporting-character development (Jolene's late-book return called underdeveloped) and a sudden, professionally-resolved-but-personally-unresolved ending.

Twelve women each get one self-contained chapter, and multiple reviewers describe the book as reading like a linked short-story collection rather than a continuous novel -- the literary-fiction-plus-story-collection combination the reader's own gate flags as landing below 68 in 81% of cases, since the character/emotion rules get suspended without a single premise to lean on instead. Booker Prize co-winner and widely praised, but the structural fragmentation across twelve leads works against the single deeply-rooted protagonist this reader responds to most.

Georgiana's affair with a married colleague is one of three parallel plot threads (alongside Darley's prenup fallout and Sasha's in-law friction), so it is a subplot, not the premise - but the framing sits closer to neutral than condemned: she learns he is married and chooses to keep sleeping with him anyway, and the book resolves the thread through an outside tragedy rather than any real reckoning with the choice. That subplot-neutral combination costs heavily on its own by this reader's rules, on top of reviewers finding Georgiana and Darley hard to root for ('a snob,' 'hard to feel sorry for her') - the same not-rootable failure mode that cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping (65 vs 87, same author and world) on the protagonist axis alone. Leaned on infidelity-framing and protagonist-likability; risk that the multi-thread resolution comes together 'too neatly/fortuitously' per reviewers, a momentum concern.

t: Holka se silicim hlasem (The Girl with the Louding Voice)
why: Adunni's whole arc is want-driven -- she names her own goal (education, a 'louding voice') and actively pursues it through forced marriage, trafficking and domestic servitude to a hopeful ending where she seizes control of her future. That single-minded, active protagonist is exactly what the reader rewards (Hunger Games 89, Sunrise on the Reaping 87), and the book gives genuine insight into a specific lived experience, the same quality that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. Docked for how much real trauma the content carries (child marriage, trafficking, abuse, a co-wife's death) even though nothing here is explicit sexual content.

This is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this reader's log: Hitchhiker's 83 falling to 70 for its sequels. Reader reviews are split, with a recurring complaint that the story is padded with unnecessary flashbacks and leans on action over atmosphere, with pacing that lags. One review credits it with some moral depth, but I cannot state a clear, worked idea beyond a competent monster-fighting adventure in an industrial steampunk setting - the axis:ideas doubt that exits this at C.

t: Julie z vlci smecky (Julie of the Wolves)
why: Miyax/Julie's bond with the wolf pack and her companionship-over-isolation survival arc are the kind of thing that scored well for Project Hail Mary's Rocky, and the opening is one concrete situation (alone on the tundra) rather than several plot lines at once. But the inciting event is a forced child marriage at 13 followed by her child-husband's attempted rape of her -- a Newbery winner, but genuinely dark content that a violence-tolerant, sexual-content-sensitive reader would still register heavily, distinct from ordinary bleakness. Not infidelity (no betrayal, no adultery) and not sex-as-plot (the marriage assault is the inciting incident, not the book's subject), so no hard filter fires.

t: Kocka a mesto (The Cat and the City)
why: A story-cycle novel unifying disparate Tokyo lives through a wandering, shape-shifting cat -- the connective idea ('everyone in the city is secretly linked') is thin and generic rather than a premise worked through in its consequences, unlike Project Hail Mary (92), where astrophage's second-order consequences (space travel, the energy problem) are actually explored. Doubting axis:ideas holds up under scrutiny -- reviews describe the pieces as 'not particularly plot-driven' individually and unified mainly by mood -- so exiting at gate 4 without further research despite the novel form (not a story collection, so bullet 1 does not apply here).

t: Nekde za morem (Somewhere Beyond the Sea)
why: A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70, and Catching Fire (83) lost ground precisely by trading the character-focused stakes that worked for arena-spectacle-for-its-own-sake. The same shape shows up in this book's reviews: multiple reviewers describe 'sequelitis' and characters flattened to 'either very good or very bad,' a loss of moral ambiguity that keeps the protagonist's arc from landing as more than found-family warmth and banter, even though that warmth and banter are still genuinely praised. On-page testimony about childhood abuse in the magical-foster-care system reads as heavier and bleaker than the register this world has otherwise carried, a further risk beyond the sequel discount.

Cora is an independent, curious naturalist and the book's real subject is science-versus-superstition in the Darwin era -- the 'monster' legend is treated skeptically and debunked rather than practiced on the page, so no occult veto. Will Ransome is happily married; multiple reviews confirm his bond with Cora stays an intense intellectual/emotional friendship rather than a consummated affair, and the novel's own ending is ambiguous (letters, not reunion), so infidelity grades as a minor incidental thread at most, not a premise. Docked for meandering, description-heavy Victorian pacing that several reviewers flag, and for splitting attention across Cora, Will, Martha, Luke and Stella rather than one deep POV.

Yale Tishman is consistently praised as kind and magnetic without being a saint, the interesting-and-rootable combination the reader's log rewards, and the whole book is described as a meditation on love and friendship rather than plot events -- motives over action, the axis that tops Speaker for the Dead (90) and Mockingjay (91). The idea it leaves behind (what survives, and who carries memory forward, once the people who made you are gone) is nameable and central. Docked for sustained bleakness -- mass AIDS deaths and the protagonist's own death -- though reviewers call the tone hopeful rather than nihilistic, closer to Project Hail Mary's companionship-over-isolation register than to 1984's despair.

t: Patrick Melrose (Patrick Melrose (Never Mind, Bad News, Some Hope))
why: Never Mind opens as a single-day, single-house novel, one evening at the family chateau, a clear starting situation rather than several competing lines. Patrick's arc moves from abused child to addict to a recovering adult who admits his father's abuse to a friend and begins confronting his past - a real arc of wanting and understanding rather than static suffering, the axis that tops Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91, and unlike Gregor in Promena 58 he is an active agent working toward recovery rather than someone acted upon. What holds it down: the father's abuse of Patrick as a child and the surrounding cruelty are sustained and severe rather than the mild, discounted bleakness of 1984 60, even though reviewers also note real wit and social satire cutting against the darkness.

Sarah/Ursula is resourceful, multilingual, and active by design (a gymnast who turns her training into a survival skill), the interesting-and-rootable combination this reader consistently rewards. Kirkus calls the book powerful and penetrating but flags one specific plausibility problem: the scientist's independent superweapon subplot is 'so James Bond it undercuts the real-world horror' of the setting, which is a worldbuilding self-consistency risk rather than a weak central idea (the identity/survival premise itself holds up). No occult content found in any source -- straight historical spy thriller.

t: Sok z padu (The Shock of the Fall)
why: Matthew is an active narrator processing his brother's death and his own schizophrenia through writing, not a passive victim of events -- reviewers highlight guilt and grief as the engine of the book and praise its authentic, humanizing take on mental illness, the same genuinely-examines-what-is-true quality that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. The ending is described as ambiguous but uplifting, offering real closure, which separates it from The Metamorphosis (58), where the bleakness arrived suddenly on a passive protagonist. Costa Book Award winner.

A fix-up of the original Time Patrol stories, built around one well-worked idea - a policing organization that must repeatedly restore history against travelers who alter it - with each story testing a different edge case of that premise (a merchant's meddling in 5th-century England, restoring history after it is rewritten around Hannibal). That premise-testing structure is exactly what makes short idea-driven work land for this reader when the idea is real - the same mechanism that let Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 land inside its predicted band on axis:ideas plus axis:short-idea-driven, unlike Divergent 58, whose premise reads as pieces borrowed from other books that do not cohere under thought.
