Risk: this is genuinely episodic short fiction stitched into a collection rather than a continuous novel, so recurring agent Manse Everard's characterization is thinner across entries than in a full-length book - closer to Unfinished Tales 69's fragmentation risk than to a tightly continuous narrative.

The Antigone-retelling premise -- radicalization, state power, family loyalty -- is a real, well-worked idea and widely praised (Women's Prize winner). But the book rotates through five narrators, and reviewers specifically criticize the central Aneeka-Eamonn romance, which drives the plot's second half, as unconvincing: one review calls Aneeka 'a cardboard character' and the relationship 'flimsy.' Since the protagonist axis beats worldbuilding/idea quality when they compete, per this reader's clearest rule, that weak center pulls the estimate down from where the premise alone would place it. The ending is a double tragedy with little redemption, closer to the unrelieved bleakness that cost 1984 60 ('too depressing') than to a tragedy the reader has been given reason to feel was earned.

t: Uzdraveni Rose Gold Wattsove (Darling Rose Gold)
why: The Munchausen-by-proxy premise (a mother who faked her daughter's illness for 18 years) is a real, nameable idea and the thriller mechanics are well-reviewed. But both alternating narrators are explicitly described by reviewers as unlikable and deranged -- not one villain lead but two unrootable POVs, a worse case of the same failure that cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping (65 vs 87). Rootability beats worldbuilding/plot craft when they compete, per the reader's own rule, so this is scored low despite the premise being sound.

A surreal, post-apocalyptic commune novella built around the ambiguous substance 'watermelon sugar' that stands in for whatever people value. Reviews describe it as resistant to ordinary rational reading, driven by mood and imagery rather than a worked-out premise. I can gesture at a theme - possessiveness curdling into violence, in inBOIL's self-immolation - but not state it as a clear, developed idea the way Animal Farm's allegory 78 or Red Rising's premise 95 is carried through its consequences. That doubt about axis:ideas is what exits this at C.

Content warnings across reviews are severe for this reader's calibration: extended asylum abuse, hints of rape, and strong implications of a paedophilic relationship from multiple men. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. That material is the crudeness dimension rather than the volume one, so it measures against Ready Player One 55 and sits past it. Range holds.

t: A doggie and a pussycat (A Doggie and a Pussycat)
why: A picture book for the very youngest readers: a dog and a cat keep house together, imitating grown-ups at chores like washing the floor and baking a cake, with the humour built on small domestic mishaps. This is squarely the picture-book case the lower C-low band exists for - short, simple, no idea beyond gentle domestic comedy, the childrens register Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 were docked a little for, and a true picture book costs more.

t: Antropolozka na Marsu (An Anthropologist on Mars)
why: Seven real case studies - a colorblind painter, a surgeon with Tourette's and prosopagnosia, an autistic savant, a formerly blind man learning to see, and Temple Grandin's Asperger's - each rigorously examined for what actually happened and what it reveals about a genuinely different way of experiencing reality, the exact axis that carries Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 above the memoir form earning anything by itself. Sacks frames disorder as paradox rather than tragedy ('latent powers' brought out by the condition), which keeps this reader's mild bleakness discount from firing hard the way it did on Anne Frank 40.

A comedic trivia book for children (age 8+) about the gross history of medicine - no protagonist, no plot, just an illustrated string of historical oddities. There is no idea to name and no story to suspend the character rules on behalf of; it is closer to the picture-book/occasional-piece band than to any narrative this reader has scored, so the harsher C-low band applies.

The catalogue's own annotation describes a 'for the youngest readers' abridged edition, but the verified Czech print route is a different, earlier translation (SNKLHU, 1959, a major literary press), so I am not confident this is the picture-book version the annotation implies - noted in flags. Even so, a fables collection is dozens of short, self-contained animal-and-moral pieces rather than one sustained premise - closer to a diffuse anthology than to a single worked idea like Animal Farm 78 - so I would put axis:ideas in risks regardless of which edition is meant.

A single continuous four-night frame with one dreamer and one woman meeting on a canal bank - one concrete situation, not several plot lines starting at once, the pattern behind Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30 failing unread. The nameable idea is the cost of living inside imagination instead of acting on it, the same territory that lets Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 work as short idea-driven pieces, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends rather than adds. The Dreamer is rootable rather than merely pitiable: he is generous, offering to love Nastenka even knowing she loves another, unlike Gregor in Promena 58 whose passivity (paired with sudden bleakness) sank that book. The ending is a loss, not a devastation - closer to Animal Farm's mild discount than to 1984's 60 'too depressing' - so axis:bleakness costs only a little here.

t: Blazniva nedele a jine povidky (Crazy Sunday and Other Stories)
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection: this exit fires by itself per the ladder (81% of such books land under 68), because axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character rules but a multi-story anthology has no single premise to lean on. Individual pieces do carry real, nameable ideas -- the Benjamin Button story is a clean reverse-aging premise about time, vanity and appearance versus reality -- so the default band applies rather than the lower one, but the collection as a whole (Hollywood satire, high-society portraits, a reverse-aging fable) has no unifying idea for a full pass to anchor on.

A selection of Nemcova's fairy tales adapted and language-simplified for readers from age 4 (Palecek, Smolicek, the gingerbread-house tale, and similar). This is squarely the slight, occasional-piece end of the childrens axis - closer to a picture book than to a worked story - not the register that let Male zeny 79 or The Hobbit 84 clear the line on character and idea alone. No single idea threads the selection, so the number leans on how far toward a childrens book it sits rather than on any premise.

t: Carmen - Skutecny zivot Hany Hegerove (Carmen - The Real Life of Hana Hegerova)
why: Reviews are split, but several single out exactly the failure mode this axis measures rather than praising it: passages 'had to be endured for their dullness,' sensitive material handled 'diplomatically' rather than examined, dwelling on trivia like a concert's song order, and one reader said flatly they would not recommend it despite loving the singer. The memoir/testimony form earns nothing by itself - what earns is examining what is actually true, the axis behind Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 - and a biography criticised for avoiding its subject's hard edges has little there to lean on.

Deserter Inman walks home across a collapsing Confederacy to reach Ada, who is learning self-sufficiency with Ruby's help; both threads are driven by a clearly stated want worked out in concrete scenes, the axis that tops Mockingjay (91) and Speaker for the Dead (90). Publisher copy promises 'witches' among the people Inman meets, but the specific episode that fits (the goat woman) is a herbalist and confessor drawing on folk medicine and myth, not a rite performed on the page - closer to a mechanical, explicable practice than to Havran's (40) real divination. Inman's drive is toward reunion rather than solo survival, the same distinction that separated Project Hail Mary (92) from The Martian (82); the tragic ending costs a little the way sustained bleakness always does here.

Episodic sword-and-sorcery pulp adventure, formula-driven collection of self-contained stories about one wandering barbarian. The reader consistently rewards page time on what characters want and why over what they do (Red Rising 95, Golden Son 92, Speaker for the Dead 90) and docks pure set-piece action (Catching Fire 83, Golden Son itself docked for leaning on action); Howard's stories are built the opposite way, around incident and atmosphere rather than motive. I cannot name a single worked idea the collection pursues to a consequence, so axis:ideas is the doubt that carries this number. Stopping at C-low means the occult question (Howard's Hyborian Age leans heavily on witches and black-magic priests) goes unexamined here; axis:occult stays in deps for that reason.

t: Dar tri kralu (The Gift of the Magi)
why: A single classic short story - Della and Jim each secretly sell their prized possession to buy the other a Christmas gift, rendering both gifts ironically useless - issued here as a 40-page illustrated gift edition. The idea is real and nameable (sacrifice's worth outlasting the object it buys), but it is delivered as an instant twist rather than a premise worked through consequences, and Czech reader reviews of this specific edition note the text itself feels shortened and sparse compared to other printings. At 40 pages of a single vignette this is about as close to an occasional piece as the low band's own definition names, which is why the idea's realness does not lift it into the default band.

Four unrelated high-concept novellas - a camera that steals memories snap by snap, sharp nails falling as rain, a man stranded on a solid cloud, a mall shooting - each carries its own workable idea rather than the collection leaning on voice alone, so this does not read as the thin, idea-free story collection the below-the-line gate warns about. One novella, Loaded, includes an adulterous couple as one part of an ensemble cast around a mall shooting - incidental to that story and to the book as a whole, not a premise, so a small axis:infidelity deduction rather than a veto.

t: Epochalni vylet pana Broucka do XV. stoleti (Mr. Broucek's Excursion to the Fifteenth Century)
why: Broucek, a comfortable Prague landlord with no convictions, falls through a passage into Hussite Prague in 1420 and is confronted with a courage and moral seriousness he cannot match, ending on Vitkov hill too afraid to even watch the battle - a critique-through-contrast structure in the vein of Animal Farm 78, and like Labyrint sveta 70 it is short and idea-driven with a nameable idea (complacent bourgeois cowardice held up against a national struggle) rather than an event sequence. No occult: the passage to another century is unexplained but mechanical (an underground tunnel), with no invocation, ritual or source in real occultism, and the book itself keeps undercutting its own reality by ending on a plausible drunk-dream reading. Risk: as a 19th-century satirical short novel it may carry the kind of narratorial digression that cost Les Miserables pacing relative to Monte Cristo.

The premise - which parent is telling the truth, the father or the mentally ill mother - is a genuinely interesting idea, but reviewers are split and often frustrated by an ending that refuses to resolve it, one calling it 'abrupt and obtuse' and another 'a final incomprehensible chapter.' That is the same premise-not-carried-through problem that sank Mortal Engines 55, applied here to a psychological rather than a worldbuilding claim. Content is heavy too - the mother's backstory involves her own father's abuse of her, and her allegations describe a group preying sexually on young women - closer to 1984's 60 'too depressing' territory than to a book that earns its darkness with a clear payoff.

A two-part novella following idealistic Litomysl gymnasium students from a banned 1847 May festival into the 1848 Prague revolution - a real, worked idea (youthful rebellion against ossified authority, tempered by one friend's death on the barricades) in the vein of what makes Les Miserables 71 and Count of Monte Cristo 75 work as freedom-and-consequence stories, and it opens on one concrete, legible situation (the banned festival) rather than several plot lines at once. Student leads carry a small life-phase pushback the way Ender's Game did, but the friendship-and-idealism material is the same register that carries The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings to 84.

Nineteen independent comic fairy-tale retellings (Czech, Russian, English and Arabic folk material reworked with modern satire), each mocking a single human vice - greed, laziness, and, in the title story, marital infidelity - as a self-contained anecdote rather than a sustained plot. Marital infidelity appears only as the subject of one satirized vignette among nineteen, condemned as folly rather than approved of, so axis:infidelity grades as incidental and costs almost nothing on its own, nowhere near a premise-level concern. The bigger question is axis:ideas: nineteen separate morals is a diffuse anthology rather than one worked-through idea, closer to the picture-book/occasional-piece case than to a single sustained allegory like Animal Farm 78.

The book's core hook is a worked-through consequence of one premise - if everyone could see their own future, would it be fixed - and Lloyd and Michiko's discovery that they aren't married in the future they see pushes the determinism-versus-free-will question further, the kind of idea-forward payoff that carries Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91. The murder-investigation thread (Theo trying to stop his own foreseen killing) gives the book a whodunnit spine, but it is one thread inside a larger societal exploration rather than the point of the book, so it is flagged rather than treated as the detective veto. The ending is the real cost: reviewers describe the closing section as a rushed 21-year summary that reads as if the author didn't know how to close it, the same density/pacing complaint that docked The Martian 82 for a dragging ending, only more severe here.

Cora's affair with Joseph, begun while she is married to Alan, is a subplot rather than the premise - the book's engine is the five-week chaperone trip with Louise Brooks and Cora's search for her birth mother, and that story stands without the affair. But the affair is framed approvingly throughout: it gives her 'the passion her marriage never offered' and becomes a lifelong, celebrated liberation rather than a source of guilt or cost. A subplot-level affair with approving framing is severe on its own per the infidelity axis, well below where Pride and Prejudice (75) sits, since courtship and want inside ordinary bounds cost that book nothing. The genuine coming-of-age material around the trip keeps this off the very bottom of that penalty, but the axis is what carries the number here.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection: this exit fires by itself per the ladder (81% of such books land under 68). A Czech reader summary of this collection describes it as stylistically consistent but bringing nothing new ideologically, with stories that tend to converge on similar endings -- the 'no idea you can name at all' condition for the lower band rather than the default one, since nothing here rises to a stated premise the way a single famous piece might carry an anthology.

A recessive gene surfaces three generations after Cal's great-grandparents married, and the novel works that premise through an immigrant family saga rather than merely asserting it - the same kind of consequence-tracing that makes Project Hail Mary (92) work. Cal narrates as a self-aware adult looking back, and reviewers single out that voice as the book's real strength ('wonderfully engaging', compared to Ishmael and Holden Caulfield), so unlike Artemis (69), where a thin lead undercut strong worldbuilding, the genetics here are not asked to carry a weak protagonist.

Landmark reportage tracing six real Hiroshima survivors from the morning of the blast through the following months (with a 1985 postscript revisiting them decades later) - the same rigorous examination of what actually happened, plus insight into how another group experiences the world, that earns Seeking Allah Finding Jesus its 91 and Son of Hamas its 75, and the clean opposite of Anne Frank's 40, which the log flags as testimony that did not work. It opens on concrete, ordinary morning routines for each survivor rather than a confusing multi-thread start. The six-survivor structure is a multi-pov risk against the log's preference for tight single-POV narration (The Hunger Games 89), and the subject matter is sustained bleakness, though the log treats that as its mildest recorded objection.

A Jewish immigrant family's collapse (father kills the mother, nearly kills the daughter, then himself) followed by the daughter's escape from an abusive marriage and her deliberate self-reinvention under a new name. There is a real idea here - identity as something built rather than given - and the opening and characterization are singled out by reviewers as strong. But the idea's own reviews are split: Kirkus calls the book derivative of the author's earlier work and flags roughly 200 pages of sag while the protagonist is simply on the run, which is exactly the density penalty the reader's log tracks (thin story stretched over pages, not length itself). That doubt about whether the idea is actually carried through, rather than repeated, is what this number leans on. No infidelity premise turned up - her marriage ends through her husband's violence, not an affair - so that axis is examined and clear.

t: Irena Sendlerova. Andel z Varsavy (The Angel of Warsaw)
why: A documentary-grounded account of a real resistance worker who used her ghetto health-administration access to smuggle out and save over two thousand children - the same insight-into-a-persecuted-group axis that carries Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, rather than the memoir/testimony form earning anything by itself. One reader review notes the opening chapters are slower and more descriptive, only gripping once the rescue operations begin - a density risk worth flagging rather than a fatal one - and the Warsaw ghetto and camp setting carries this reader's mild bleakness discount.

t: J jako jestrab (H is for Hawk)
why: After her father's sudden death, Macdonald trains a goshawk while interweaving the biography of T. H. White, and the book is built entirely on the axis that tops this reader's log: an honest, examined interior life rather than events. It is the closest structural match to Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91, 'genuinely examines what is plausible and believable') among nonfiction read so far, and unlike The Diary of a Young Girl (40, first-person testimony that 'did not work'), critical consensus (Costa Book of the Year, Samuel Johnson Prize, NYT's 100 Best Books of the 21st Century) backs that the introspection actually lands rather than just being sincere. Grief is the sustained note throughout, which costs a little the way it costs everywhere else in the log.

A collection of separate short fairy tales, each answering one of a child's questions about the world, rather than one premise worked through - closer to a slight collection than to the single continuous idea that carries The Little Prince 82 as a short allegory. Short-idea-driven only suspends the character-and-emotion penalties, it never adds points, and here there is no one idea to lean on across the book, only many small ones scattered across separate tales - the axis:ideas doubt that decides gate 4. Illustrated and written for reading aloud to young children at bedtime, which pushes it toward the picture-book end of axis:childrens rather than the Male zeny 79 or Ranger's Apprentice 74 end.

t: Jsem Milena z Prahy (I Am Milena from Prague)
why: Reconstructs a real journalist and resistance member's life from her letters and the testimony of those who knew her - the same insight-into-a-real-world axis that carries Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, here into interwar Vienna/Prague journalism, feminism and the Ravensbruck camp. Her marriage and the correspondence with Kafka that contributed to its end sit in the book's first of its four parts as backstory, not the throughline of a book that goes on to cover her journalism, resistance work and imprisonment - incidental rather than premise, and framed as historical fact rather than approved or condemned, so axis:infidelity costs a few points rather than the estimate. The camp ending carries this reader's mild bleakness discount.

Self-published Beat-style prose (1996, no established publisher) by a Prostejov literary figure of the 1970s underground scene; beyond the catalogue's one-line description, no plot summary, review, or reader discussion of this specific title turned up anywhere searched. I cannot name an idea the book works through, which is the gate-4 test itself - I am using the default band rather than the lower one, since nothing found suggests it is a slight or juvenile piece, only that it is unfindable.

A single-narrator memoir of a young officer caught between duty and an unlikely personal bond with the rebel leader who spares his life; the novel's engine is what Pyotr and Pugachev each want and why, not the battles between them, which is the axis that tops this reader's log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). It opens on one concrete situation - a young officer traveling to a remote post, losing his way in a storm - rather than several threads at once. The romance with Maria costs nothing on its own (Pride and Prejudice 75 shows romance as the central subject is not a penalty), and the ending is a genuine happy one for the leads, closer to Count of Monte Cristo 75 than to a bleak resolution. Set slightly above Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 on the strength of a tighter, single-thread narrative and the humanized antagonist relationship the reader's own motives-over-action rule rewards; the civil-war violence and executions around the edges are the only real pushback.

t: Karla a jine povidky (Karla and Other Stories)
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection, the combination the reader's log shows sitting below the 68 line four times out of five. The title story does have a nameable idea (a child dressed as a girl to dodge conscription, disguised again as a soldier to escape, and a love plot resolved through that reversal) and is not a case of no idea at all, but the collection as a whole is unverified beyond that one story, and short-idea-driven work only avoids penalty when the idea is genuinely worked through, not merely present. axis:short-idea-driven is what actually carries the doubt here.

In 1882 Vienna, Josef Breuer secretly tries to treat Friedrich Nietzsche's despair through the therapy that becomes psychoanalysis, and in doing so confronts his own repressed dread. The whole book is interior life examined through dialogue rather than event - the exact axis that tops Speaker for the Dead (90, 'driven by motives and understanding... rather than by action') and Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91) - built on real historical figures and correspondence rather than invented drama, which grounds the ideas instead of just asserting them.

The premise - sin and desire made visible as black Smoke, with the aristocracy hiding theirs behind sweets while ruling the smoke-marked poor - is a real idea about hypocrisy and class, the kind of thing Divergent 58 was faulted for lacking. It is declared as mechanism, not invocation (no witchcraft, spellcasting or devotion on the page), so it clears axis:occult cleanly. But Vyleta explicitly does not explain where Smoke comes from within this book - reviewers confirm the origin is 'never fully defined' here and is instead the hook for the sequel Soot - and a sequel's answer does not count under the worldbuilding rule, so the book undertakes an explanation it does not itself deliver. Three child protagonists open the book together at one school, a mild multi-pov risk short of the confusing-opening filter.

The opening itself clears the reader's sharpest filter: a boy with no memory is raised into a walled Glade in a single third-person-limited thread, one concrete situation rather than several plot lines starting at once, closer to Hitchhiker's 83 than to the Gunslinger/Discworld openings that ended unfinished. But the book declares a capability - an organization built an enormous, mechanically elaborate maze specifically to map immune brains - and does not carry its own consequences: reviewers and fans alike single out the maze's actual purpose as under-explained to the point that one review states the explanation is worse than no explanation at all. This book withholds the fuller account to sequels, which the reader's own worldbuilding rule does not let count. That declared-but-uncarried premise is the same shape of failure that sank Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55, so axis:worldbuilding is what this number leans on rather than the opening, which is clean.

A shipwrecked teenager survives 227 days on a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, then at the end offers investigators a second, darker version of the same events substituting people for the animals - neither is provable, and the book asks which one the reader would rather believe. That is a real worked idea about faith versus reason, not plotless dressing, the sort of idea Animal Farm 78 also leaves behind. Pi's drive is survival plus an examined, three-faith spiritual practice, graded on axis:faith rather than axis:occult - organized worship (Hinduism, Christianity, Islam), not witchcraft, seance or invented ritual, so it is not a veto, the same distinction that let Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus score 91. Risk: the ordeal is sustained and often brutal (starvation, a parent's death, the darker retelling's implied cannibalism), the mild-but-real bleakness discount that cost 1984 and Promena, and Pi is 16 for most of the book, a small life-phase pushback like the one that marked down Ender's Game.

t: Lizni si a hrej (Play It as It Lays)
why: Maria Wyeth drifts through a collapsing marriage and Hollywood career between a mental-hospital stay and her friend BZ's suicide, told in eighty-seven fragmentary chapters built around the idea that nothing means anything. That is heavier and less resolved than 1984 (60, 'too depressing'), the log's own ceiling for sustained bleakness, and Maria is passive throughout in the same way Metamorphosis's Gregor (58) is - acted upon by despair rather than pursuing anything. Casual infidelity appears ('unengaged affairs') but is incidental color inside the numbness, not the source of the doubt here.

t: Mel jsem psa a kocku (I Had a Dog and a Cat)
why: A collection of Capek's newspaper feuilletons about his own dogs and cats - warm, humorous, occasional pieces rather than a worked argument or premise. About half the book is the well-known childrens story Dasenka. There is no idea here to point to the way Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70 have one; this is charm and anecdote, which is exactly the occasional-piece profile the low band exists for.

Fourteen loosely thematic stories (boxing, bullfighting, war, aging) with no through-line premise - the same collection gap that keeps Red Cavalry in this band rather than with Animal Farm's 78 single worked idea. Hemingway's terse style is well regarded but the log has nothing to reward prose style on its own; what carries a score here is a nameable idea, and a story collection has none to point to.

The premise of an unstable empire ruled by a near-immortal, unseen emperor never resolves into a worked idea - reviewers describe the debut as still on a learning curve, with motivations under-realized and the ending not fully satisfying. More costly is that the narrative hands off from its most sympathetic starting viewpoints, the former general Bartellus and the siblings Elija and Emly, to replacement characters reviewers say 'lack the pathos' of the original three. That is a direct hit on the axis this reader weighs above worldbuilding when the two compete - a rootable, interesting lead, the axis that separated Artemis 69 from Project Hail Mary 92 by 23 points.

Confirmed as action-thriller, not classic detective fiction -- sources describe the Reacher franchise as crime/action thriller where Reacher's deduction serves pursuit rather than a whodunit puzzle, so the detective filter does not fire. Reacher detours to find his father's supposed birthplace and learns no one by that name ever lived there, a personal-history hook rather than a worked-out idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). No idea survives to anchor a full pass, so exit here rather than spend a D-full budget confirming a formula entry. Deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

t: Muzeum prazvlastnich veci (The Museum of Extraordinary Things)
why: Coralie, exhibited by her father as a 'living wonder' from childhood, ultimately uses that same tank herself to save the man she loves rather than be used by it - a rootable protagonist working toward something she wants, the axis that separates Mockingjay 91 from Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. A young woman's disappearance, investigated via journalism and photography, runs alongside the romance and the Triangle Shirtwaist fire as an investigation-shaped subplot rather than the book's central whodunit engine, so it is flagged rather than treated as a detective veto. Hoffman writes lushly descriptive prose, a density risk this reader has marked down elsewhere (Les Miserables 71).

Built from disconnected 'routines' that Burroughs deliberately intended to be read in any order, with no throughline and no coordinate system for the reader. This is the exact failure mode that ended The Gunslinger, The Colour of Magic and Guards! Guards! at 30 each - several things happening at once with nothing legible - except here it is the entire book by explicit authorial design rather than a rough opening that later resolves, so the same penalty applies at full force rather than easing off.

t: Nikola Suhaj Loupeznik (Nikola Suhaj the Outlaw)
why: A Robin-Hood-style outlaw novel built on a real Carpathian bandit, deliberately blending documented fact with the folk legend that grew up around him - a genuine worked idea (how legend forms around a real, poor, wronged man) in the vein of what carries Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70. Nikola is a sympathetic, rootable lead who robs the rich for the poor and is killed by betrayal from his own men, the kind of heroism-and-friendship material that carries The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings to 84. The tragic, betrayed ending is a bleakness risk the way it was for The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, though softened by the myth surviving him rather than ending on pure defeat.

Same franchise, same shape: action-thriller where Reacher's investigation exists to set up a confrontation rather than a whodunit -- sources classify the series as crime/action thriller, not deduction-driven mystery, so the detective filter does not fire. Reacher gets off a bus for coffee and stays only because trouble finds the town, a stock setup with nothing to anchor an idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). Exit here rather than spend a D-full budget on a formula entry deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

t: Odlesky ve zlatem oku (Reflections in a Golden Eye)
why: On a peacetime Southern army base, Leonora's affair with Major Langdon is a subplot inside a wider web of repression and alienation among six characters that ends in a murder the novel announces on its opening page. The affair is treated with sympathy rather than approval or clear condemnation, so per the infidelity axis a subplot with neutral framing sits square in the middling penalty band, similar territory to where Metamorphosis (58) landed. Unlike Metamorphosis, which has one passive but sympathetic lead, none of the six interconnected characters here is rootable, which pulls the estimate toward the low end of that territory.

Same franchise pattern: crime/action thriller per genre sources, where Reacher's curiosity about a missing man drives pursuit rather than a whodunit puzzle, so the detective filter does not fire. A curiously named prairie stop and a woman waiting for someone who never arrived is an atmospheric hook, not a worked idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). Exit here rather than spend a D-full budget on a formula entry deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

Testimony of eleven months in the women's orchestra of Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen, and it does deliver what this reader's log rewards in memoir - insight into how a specific group survived an extreme experience, the axis that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91. But this is not a clean repeat of that case: a 2016 scholarly rebuttal drawing on 17 fellow orchestra survivors argues large parts are embellished, and a reader review independently describes the narrator as self-important and hard to warm to, particularly in her account of the conductor. That is a real dent in the examining-what-is-actually-true criterion that carried Qureshi to the top of the log, and it is a protagonist-likability concern on top of it, so I am setting this below the memoir ceiling rather than near it. The camp setting is sustained bleakness but survival-through-companionship (the orchestra itself), which the reader's log treats more gently than solitary bleakness.

t: Pariz ve 20. stoleti (Paris in the Twentieth Century)
why: The predictive dystopia -- cars, elevators, fax machines, a society that has abandoned art for commerce and profit -- is a genuinely nameable idea, so this does not exit at gate 4. But reviews are consistent that the execution around that idea is thin: a Publishers Weekly assessment (via AbeBooks) found little here in the way of either plot or character development, and a LibraryThing review calls the characters flat and one-dimensional in a story with little room left for actual plot, plus a maudlin, tragically pessimistic tone through to a sad, poignant ending. That is close to the failure mode books-read.md already recorded for Promena at 58 -- a real, nameable idea undercut by a thin protagonist and unrelieved bleakness, without the lighter touch that kept Animal Farm at 78 despite its own dystopia. Leaning on protagonist and bleakness rather than the idea itself, since the idea is what earns this book its reputation, not what a reader experiences page to page.

A hacker seizes eight self-driving cars and forces a government jury to vote on who lives, in a mandatory-autonomous-vehicle future. The idea (algorithmic ethics, mob justice broadcast as spectacle) is nameable, but the mechanics needed to sustain it - a jury duty summons that turns into a live-broadcast execution game the authorities cannot simply shut down for two and a half hours - read as convenience rather than a thought-through world, the same doubt that sank Mortal Engines (55, DNF on unaccounted-for logic) and capped Divergent (58, 'ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering'). Below the line on that doubt alone, whatever the twist ending does.

t: Podivuhodny pribeh Benjamina Buttona (The Curious Case of Benjamin Button)
why: The catalogue's own annotation describes this specific edition as a simplified version for intermediate English-language students, not the full original text -- functionally an abridgement even though cz.edition is recorded as print, similar in effect to the adapt-edition case. The original story's reverse-aging premise is a real, nameable idea about time, vanity and appearance versus reality, but a graded-reader abridgement strips a literary novella down to vocabulary-level plot beats; treat it like an occasional piece under axis:short-idea-driven, at the lower band rather than the one the underlying story would otherwise earn.

t: Podzimni mouchy, aneb, Zena z davnych dob (Snow in Autumn)
why: A Chekhov-homage novella following the Karin family's nanny Tatiana as revolution destroys the household and drives them into Parisian exile. The idea of dislocation and lost home is real, but it is delivered as elegy and atmosphere rather than a premise worked through consequences, and Tatiana herself only witnesses and follows rather than wanting anything of her own - the same passivity that held Oliver Twist (57, 'acted upon rather than wanting anything') under the line despite a correctly identified idea.

Same franchise pattern: crime/action thriller per genre sources, built around a military recall and a threat to stop rather than a whodunit puzzle, so the detective filter does not fire. A homeless drifter recalled by the army after an attack on a foreign head of state is plot momentum, not a worked idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). Exit here rather than spend a D-full budget on a formula entry deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

Confirmed as middle-grade (ages 8-12, Lexile 650L) - younger and simpler than Ranger's Apprentice 74, closer to the register that cost Narnia 67. There is a workable premise in peaceful robots who eliminated humanity for the planet's own good meeting the one human girl left, but at this reading level it will be stated plainly rather than worked through, so the default competent-but-under-68 band applies rather than the harsher no-idea band.

Not an infidelity premise despite the medium-tier lexicon hit - the marriage is abusive and controlling, not unfaithful, and the plot is an identity-swap escape thriller: two women meet by chance at an airport and swap tickets, and one flight crashes. The premise has real, worked-through consequences (the survivor must live inside a stranger's dangerous life), but it leans on a large, convenient coincidence to get there, the kind of premise logic that undercut Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58 rather than the tightly held-together plotting of Red Rising 95.

The alien-invasion thread (the Grand Galactics deciding humanity is a threat) reads as bolted onto Ranjit's Fermat-proof plot rather than growing out of it - reviewers describe the novel as lacking a rounded arc and ending precipitously, a declared idea whose consequences are not actually carried through, the same failure mode (if unrelated content) that sank Mortal Engines 55. A genuine idea is named - a young mathematician's proof reshaping his life and drawing world attention - but the larger novel built around it does not cohere, so the doubt sits on axis:ideas.

t: Povidky a mensi prozy (Stories and Shorter Prose)
why: Litfic short-story/prose collection (an omnibus of Vancura's shorter prose, including Luk kralovny Dorotky and Kubula a Kuba Kubikula) - no single premise runs through it, so axis:ideas has nothing to lean on the way Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70 do. Vancura's reputation rests on stylistic experiment (avant-garde, archaic rhythmic prose) rather than a worked-out idea, so this exits at the litfic-plus-collection line rather than being researched further.

An idea-driven satire on a dictatorship, and the ideas are the case for it - the story is the regime, not the marriages. Its four wives and one mistress are noted by reviewers as one-dimensional 'sexual concubines' rather than people, which is undifferentiated, crude treatment layered onto the satire. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. Artemis 69 is the surviving half of the old comparison and it is the right one: a crudeness deduction at small volume, on a book whose plot is about something else. Range holds.

t: Prorok - Zahrada Prorokova (The Prophet / The Garden of the Prophet)
why: Twenty-six poetic-prose addresses by a sage, Almustafa, on love, marriage, work, joy and sorrow, freedom and death, delivered as parting wisdom before he sails home; the sequel gathers further such pieces. Short-idea-driven work has the character rules suspended here since there is no plot and no protagonist to root for, only a mouthpiece, but the suspension only removes penalties, it never adds points - and the axis:ideas test asks for one nameable idea, while this book offers wisdom on two dozen separate topics rather than a single premise worked through, closer to a diffuse anthology than to a book like Labyrint sveta 70, which lands one sustained idea. Faith runs through it as a thread (love, transcendence, the eternal) rather than being the whole subject, so axis:faith does not veto, the same distinction that let Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus score 91.

t: Proti padu noci (Against the Fall of Night)
why: Diaspar's stagnant immortality against Lys's embrace of growth and mortality is a clean, worked idea in the mold of what carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 - critics explicitly note ideas outweigh character work here, the axis:short-idea-driven trade this reader already accepts without penalty. The opening is one concrete situation, one city and one restless citizen (Alvin), the pattern Red Rising 95 and The Hunger Games 89 share and that Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30 both lacked. Characterization is real thin, though - critics say figures are 'identifiable mainly by their names' - closer to the risk profile of Silmarillion's 80 than to a character-forward book, so axis:protagonist is what could pull this down.

A novelization of the Nibelungenlied: Siegfried slays the dragon Fafnir, wins the Nibelung gold and an invulnerability that comes with it, then helps Gunther win Brunhild by trickery, setting up the betrayal and bloodshed that follow - myth-scale stakes in the vein of the dragon-and-treasure plots that worked in The Hobbit 84 and The Silmarillion 80. But reviewers describe it leaning on genre-fantasy and Hollywood beats rather than evoking the saga's own weight, calling it undemanding entertainment rather than a considered reworking - the opposite of what let The Silmarillion 80 hold up without a continuous protagonist. I would put axis:ideas in risks: nothing found suggests the retelling does more with the fate-and-greed material than restate it. The magic here is mythic-artifact fantasy (a cloak of invisibility, dragon blood, a cursed ring) with no rite performed as ritual and no source in real occultism, so it is not a filter concern.

Same franchise pattern: crime/action thriller per genre sources, built around tracing an object to its owner rather than a whodunit puzzle, so the detective filter does not fire. A pawnshop ring prompting a personal quest to find out how a soldier lost it is plot momentum, not a worked idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). Exit here rather than spend a D-full budget on a formula entry deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

t: Ross Poldark (Ross Poldark: A Novel of Cornwall 1783-1787)
why: Reviewers single out exactly what tops books-read.md: extensive internal dialogue revealing what characters think and want, the same quality behind Pride and Prejudice's 75 ('motives and what characters want are the entire book'). Ross returns from war to find his home neglected and his fiancee married to his cousin, then rebuilds a life and eventually a marriage with a servant girl he takes in -- a motive-driven, character-centered story in the same register as that comparison, with no hard-filter content in this opening volume. Held below the top of that band because reader reception is mixed on pacing (some stretches called slow or under-developed), and Graham writes Cornish dialect phonetically, which more than one review flagged as tricky to follow -- a density cost, not a character one.

A collection of standalone Kara ben Nemsi/Old Shatterhand adventure episodes across North Africa, the Middle East and the Boer War - episodic pulp adventure with no premise worked through, and May's 19th-century Orientalist framing of the region trades on the same kind of stated-as-fact ethnic stereotyping that cost Ranger's Apprentice 74 a few points, here without that book's redeeming easy momentum across a single throughline.

t: Sajlok, to jsem ja (Shylock Is My Name)
why: Reimagines The Merchant of Venice: a modern Jewish father, Strulovich, meets an undying Shylock and works through questions of justice, mercy and Jewish identity via a present-day pound-of-flesh plot (forced circumcision instead of a bond) - the idea is developed rather than just gestured at, in the vein of Animal Farm 78. Strulovich is driven by wanting to protect his daughter and defend his heritage rather than by what happens to him - the motives-over-action axis that tops the log at Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. It opens on one concrete scene, a cemetery encounter, the same single-situation opening that worked for Hitchhiker's Guide 83. No occult: Shylock's 400-year persistence is an authorial fantastical device, not a system drawn from real occultism, and no rite is enacted on the page. Risk: reviews describe a dense, 'multidirectional' novel where several storylines develop after the opening, which could cost on the density/momentum axis the way Les Miserables' looser digressions did relative to Monte Cristo.

Naturalist essays adapted from 1950s BBC radio broadcasts about animal-collecting expeditions - entertaining anecdotes and a conservation message, but not an examination of what is actually true the way Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 or Son of Hamas 75 earn their scores; reviewers note it reads as perfunctory radio-script material rather than a worked idea. The memoir/testimony form earns nothing by itself, and there is no single idea to name here beyond animals being interesting and worth protecting.

Same franchise pattern: crime/action thriller per genre sources, opening on Reacher intervening to stop a theft he witnesses rather than a whodunit puzzle, so the detective filter does not fire. An elderly man being watched by a thief on a train is a stock thriller setup, not a worked idea -- the same shortfall that keeps Ranger's Apprentice at 74 ('easy to read, but not much to think about'). Exit here rather than spend a D-full budget on a formula entry deep in a 20+ book series, where books-read.md already shows sequels are not a safe bet (Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 across its sequels).

A chronological cycle of Czech founding legends and later Prague legends - Cech's arrival, Libuse and her prophecy of Prague, the Maidens' War, then Charles-era and Wenceslas-IV-era city tales - carrying an explicit ideological throughline (religious tolerance, coexistence of peoples) that Jirasek wrote into the old material on purpose, a real nameable idea rather than a plain retelling. Like The Silmarillion 80, it has no continuous protagonist and no single plot, yet that structure did not cost Tolkien's mythic collection and need not cost this one on the same grounds. Libuse's founding prophecy is treated with reverence as national myth, not resemblance-for-its-own-sake, so axis:prophecy grades clean. Risk: one late tale, 'Zito the sorcerer,' is a court magician who performs actual transformations for an audience - closer to invented trickster folklore than to a source in real occultism, but the one point in the collection where something resembling a rite could be read as enacted on the page, so I am flagging rather than clearing it outright.

t: The cider house rules (The Cider House Rules)
why: Homer and Candy's affair starts while Wally is presumed dead at war and continues in secret for roughly fifteen years after his crippled return - a sustained subplot, not the premise, since the book is fundamentally Homer's bildungsroman around Dr. Larch, St. Cloud's orphanage, and the abortion debate, all of which stand on their own. The affair is handled with guilt and conflicted loyalty rather than celebration, so per the infidelity axis a subplot with neutral framing lands in the same middling penalty territory as Metamorphosis (58). The orphan's-search-for-a-home idea underneath is real and worked out, which keeps this from falling further, but the axis is what carries the number.

t: The famous stories (Slavne povidky / The Famous Stories)
why: This is a bilingual graded-reader adaptation for English learners (mirror Czech/English text, simplified language, vocabulary notes, MP3 narration by a listed adapter, Sabrina D. Harris) rather than Poe's original prose - exactly the 'slight collection, simplified' case the lower C-low band exists for. Even granting Poe's originals real ideas, a simplification aimed at intermediate language learners does not carry the same weight, so the doubt sits on axis:short-idea-driven rather than any individual story's merit.

Joanna Eberhart moves to a suburb where wives are quietly being replaced by docile robotic duplicates by their husbands' 'Men's Association.' The premise is declared once and then followed through with total consistency, including on Joanna herself, in a single clean POV with a concrete inciting situation - the opposite of a premise that collapses under thought, closer to what Project Hail Mary (92) rewards for working consequences through than to Divergent's (58) unexamined premise. But the ending offers no escape at all, nearer 1984's (60, 'too depressing') totalizing bleakness than Animal Farm's (78) fable distance, which is what keeps this well under the top of the band despite the idea holding up cleanly.

t: Tri legendy o krucifixu a jine baje o lasce (Three Legends of the Crucifix)
why: Three linked novella-legends, each turning on a figure who finds redemption through suffering (an artist's model, a persecutor of Christians, a scorned simpleton) - a real idea in the vein of what makes Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 work as short idea-driven pieces, so this clears the axis:ideas exit that a plain story collection would trigger. But the theology is not a thread here, it is the whole engine of all three plots - miracle, apotheosis, salvation are the point - which sits closer to the apologetics the faith axis penalises than to Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91's honest examination of belief. Ornate 1890s neo-romantic prose is also a density risk, the kind of heavy description that costs elsewhere in the log.

t: Ustrickova smutna smrt a jine pribehy (The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy & Other Stories)
why: Twenty-three brief illustrated rhyming poems about misfit children, each a self-contained mood piece rather than a worked idea - closer to Havran 40, the log's one verse entry, than to any prose the reader has liked. Verse itself carries a penalty independent of subject matter per that entry, and the illustrated, simple-rhyme, YA-marketed format sits close to the picture-book end of axis:childrens, which the log puts in the 30s-40s. There is no single idea beyond a repeated mood of macabre misfit melancholy to lean on the way Animal Farm's 78 allegory can.

This is the fifteenth Cotton Malone book, and this log already has one clean case of a long-running series thinning out - Hitchhiker's dropped from 83 to 70 across its sequels. Reviewers describe the relic hunt (the Arma Christi) here as largely a MacGuffin, meaning the book doesn't actually work out consequences of its own central conceit - the real content is a history lesson on Cold War Poland attached to a conspiracy-thriller chase, not a premise carried through.

t: Vecny Adam (The Eternal Adam and Other Stories)
why: The title story's twist -- a far-future archaeologist deciphering a survivor's journal from a forgotten cataclysm, only to realize his own 'advanced' civilization is just the latest turn of an endless collapse-and-rebirth cycle -- is a strong, nameable idea in the same vein as Animal Farm's 78: a compact premise whose consequences are worked through to a real twist. But this record is a multi-story anthology and most of its contents are far less known than the title piece; the Eternal Adam text itself is credited to Verne but was largely completed by his son from a draft after Verne's death, an authorship complication worth flagging. Leaning on axis:short-idea-driven rather than crediting the whole collection with the title story's idea, since an anthology is judged as a whole and the rest of its contents were not established.

Two unnamed men are stranded by rising water on a Danube island where the willows and unseen forces seem to hunt them; the story is deliberately unresolved about what the forces are or want. Motives here belong to the environment, not the two leads - there is little of what the men themselves want beyond survival, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score highest on and that Unfinished Tales 69 was marked down for lacking (its pieces not logically connected to each other). I would put axis:ideas in risks too: the piece works as mood and dread rather than a premise worked through to consequences. Exiting at C-low per the gate order, so occult status is accordingly unexamined (axis:occult stays in deps for when it is checked).

Winston Graham's Poldark novels are consistently praised for exactly the trait that tops books-read.md: page time on inner motive over event, reviewers noting his frequent use of internal dialogue to reveal what characters think and want, the same axis behind Pride and Prejudice's 75 ('motives and what characters want are the entire book'). Against that baseline, this entry carries a specific cost: a pivotal scene has the married protagonist force a final encounter with his former fiancee on the eve of her second marriage, breaking his own marriage vow -- not incidental, but also not the premise of a book equally concerned with a banking collapse and a mining business, so it grades as a subplot rather than a reject. Framing is condemned rather than approving: the act devastates the protagonist's marriage, plunges him into guilt, and traps the other woman in an unhappy second marriage -- the 'subplot times condemned' cell of the infidelity grid, which costs a few points rather than the more severe cells. That pulls the estimate down from where the motive-driven writing alone would place it.

t: Z Divokeho zapadu (From the Wild West)
why: Ten self-contained Western short stories about lone gunslingers, praised by reviewers for humor, tension and raw atmosphere but not for any single premise carried through. Same doubt as the reader's other episodic-pulp cases: I cannot name a worked idea the collection is building toward, only a mood and a setting, so axis:ideas is what this number leans on. No content concerns turned up (no occult, no detective frame, no romance-as-premise) so nothing else is at risk of collapsing it further.

t: Zazrak v Andach (Miracle in the Andes)
why: A first-person account, written thirty years after a 1972 Andes plane crash, of the 72 days a Uruguayan rugby team spent stranded on a glacier - starvation, an avalanche that killed eight more survivors, and finally Parrado's own trek across the mountains to bring back rescue for those who stayed behind. What earns points on the memoir axis is examining what is actually true rather than just having lived through something, the same rigor that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 - reviewers single out the book's honesty about the survivors' hardest choice (eating the dead) and call it a meditation on love and camaraderie rather than a straight survival thriller. It is a companionship and self-sacrifice story, Parrado trekking to save the others rather than just himself, the same combination that put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82, the latter docked for sustained loneliness. Risk: the ordeal itself is severe and sustained, the mild-but-real bleakness discount the log applies elsewhere.

A retired teacher inherits a house on Ibiza and, investigating clues left by a friend whose diving death looks less than accidental, encounters unexplained paranormal forces and undergoes a personal transformation. The investigation is a real thread but reads as a device for a self-discovery story rather than the book's payoff, so this is a flag rather than the detective veto. What decides the exit is the idea itself: reviewers are split, with at least one describing the themes as delivered like a lecture rather than earned, and the paranormal elements are reportedly left deliberately unexplained rather than worked through - which is the doubt axis:ideas is meant to catch. The 72-year-old lead is a small, not disqualifying, life-phase distance from the reader.

Thirteen-year-old Rose Rivers resents being groomed for a decorative future while her twin brother is sent to boarding school - a real, stated want, the axis this log rewards most. But unlike Little Women (79, 'clears the propose line on characters alone'), reader reviews of this specific book note Rose has 'nothing to really root for' and little that sets her apart, closer to Narnia (67, 'not bad, but... lacks higher things to think about'). A subplot where Rose, thirteen, kisses the adult artist hired to paint her mother is treated as scandal - he is banished - rather than explored, which is a content concern worth flagging even though it is not the book's premise.

Retrospective critics single out the book's late pivot - Falkenberg abruptly marrying Glenda Ruth Horton with an implied kingship, after most of the book followed CoDominium politics through Senator Grant - as a cliched shift rather than a consequence the earlier chapters built toward, the same premise-not-carried-through problem that sank Mortal Engines 55. The political-military worldbuilding up to that point is reasonably well regarded (Poul Anderson called it thought-provoking), but the ending doesn't follow from what the book declared and set up earlier.

A journalist joins an eccentric scientist's expedition to a Brazilian plateau where dinosaurs and ape-men still survive, culminating in public vindication when the team brings back living proof. Reviewers consistently praise the imaginative concept and the plot's pace over more than a century of readers; this is companionship-driven expedition adventure rather than solo survival, closer to the profile the reader rewarded in Project Hail Mary 92 than to The Martian's docked isolation. It sits below the reader's SF ceiling because the leads are drawn with Victorian broad strokes - Challenger arrogant, Malone motivated as much by pride as courage - rather than the deep interiority that wins the top of the log, so axis:protagonist is the one risk that could pull this down; axis:worldbuilding is what actually carries the number, since the lost-world premise is realized vividly and consistently rather than merely asserted.

t: Ruda jizda a jine prozy (Red Cavalry and Other Prose)
why: Thirty-five loosely linked war vignettes narrated by the same outsider - a litfic story collection with no single premise running through it, so axis:ideas has nothing to lean on the way it does in Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70, both of which hang the whole book on one worked idea. Individual stories carry real ideas (an intellectual's attraction to Cossack violence) but nothing sustained across the whole book, so it exits here rather than being researched further.

The central thread is the narrator processing her widowed mother's murder over the following year, not an affair - remove the affair and the book about grief and family still exists, so this does not reach premise level and is not a reject. But a sustained subplot runs the length of the book: the unmarried narrator's year-long affair with a married man who may or may not leave his wife. Framing reads as neutral rather than condemned or celebrated - it is treated as part of her rebellious, black-sheep identity, not punished and not held up as brave. Subplot prominence with neutral framing is the middle cell of the reader's own infidelity matrix, which is what this number leans on. The low end is nudged three points under that cell's floor on purpose: reception is mixed to negative on the book's substance (Kirkus called the premise banal and the novel bloated), which argues for room below the matrix cell rather than a reason to push the range up.

A collection of James novellas headlined by 'In the Cage,' whose plot centers on a telegraphist who becomes obsessed with a married client's secret affair. Infidelity here is a dominant subplot the unmarried protagonist only observes rather than the premise of her own life, and the ending reveals the lovers as mercenary rather than romantic - closer to condemned than approving, well short of premise-level under the reject test. It is still a story collection with no book-wide idea, the same gap that keeps a collection off the pace of an idea-driven allegory like Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70.

A Bierce war-story collection built around the title tale, in which a soldier's celebrated battlefield courage turns out to be driven by a woman's taunting letter rather than honor - real irony-driven ideas within the story, but assembled as a story collection with no single premise across the book, the same gap that keeps a litfic collection off the pace of an idea-driven allegory like Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70.

An episodic collection of autobiographical fishing-and-family stories spanning prewar, wartime and postwar Czechoslovakia (the family, half-Jewish, was deported and returned) - warmly regarded and emotionally textured, but held together by chronology and voice rather than a single premise worked out. No nameable idea the way Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 has one - that book hit precisely because it is a short allegory with a premise you can name, the reasoning axis:ideas plus axis:short-idea-driven was built for; this collection has voice and warmth but no equivalent single idea. The short-idea-driven suspension removes the length penalty but does not add points on its own.

t: Amari a Nocni bratri (Amari and the Night Brothers)
why: A 13-year-old finds a briefcase left by her missing older brother nominating her for tryouts at a secret Bureau of Supernatural Affairs, and must navigate trials while hiding an illegal power to find out what happened to him. Reviews are consistently strong on the protagonist - brave, observant, caring - the trait the log rewards most directly (Mockingjay 91, The Hunger Games 89), enough to offset the modest cost the profile assigns to a middle-grade register, comparable to Ranger's Apprentice 74. The finding-her-brother thread is an investigation-shaped subplot, not the reader's core satisfaction (which is Amari's belonging/found-family arc), so it is a flag rather than the detective veto. The magic is framed as innate 'talents' (mutant-style ability) rather than invoked witchcraft, which would pass the occult mechanism test, but a 'League of Magicians' and references to spellbooks were not conclusively pinned down as ritual-free, so occult is a risk rather than a cleared question. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:childrens.

t: Amari a Velka hra (Amari and the Great Game)
why: Direct sequel: Amari, now a probationary agent, is offered leadership of the secretive League of Magicians and her refusal triggers a power struggle (the titular Great Game) inside magiciankind. The same protagonist strength that carries book one continues here, and the log rewards that trait most directly (Mockingjay 91, The Hunger Games 89); the modest middle-grade cost is unchanged from book one, comparable to Ranger's Apprentice 74. The League of Magicians and spellbook references were not conclusively confirmed as ritual-free on this volume either, so occult carries forward as the same unresolved risk as book one, per the shared author-level research. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:childrens.

A near-future second American civil war told through Sarat Chestnut, whose radicalization from refugee child into an instrument of Southern terrorism is the entire point of the book, not backdrop - reviews stress this is a character study of why ordinary people turn to violence rather than a war-action plot, the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90: motives over what happens). It opens on one concrete, legible situation - one family, one flooding farm, one refugee camp - the shape the log rewards (Hitchhiker's Guide, 83). Risk: Sarat ends the book as the war's chief instrument of mass destruction and the ending is openly cyclical and hopeless ('the whole ugly cycle starts again'), closer to 1984's 60 ('too depressing') than to a redemptive arc, with none of the companionship or self-sacrifice that lifted Project Hail Mary over The Martian. Unlike Coriolanus Snow (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, 65), reviewers say the reader stays attached to Sarat because her descent is earned through victimhood rather than ambition, which should keep this above that floor.

t: Byla jednou jedna reka (Once Upon a River)
why: Set on the 1887 Thames, a drowned girl revives and three families claim her, against local folklore about Quietly, a ferryman who carries the dying across the river. Checked specifically for the occult filter: there is no witchcraft, divination or rite performed on the page - the supernatural is left deliberately ambiguous, filtered through unreliable village storytelling, and the author has said in interview she means it to stay that way. That is a self-consistency choice, not a cheat, and reviewers credit exactly this: a real, sustained tension between Nurse Rita's rational investigation and the folklore that is never resolved either way, the log's 'author must follow his own declared rules' test passed by deliberately committing to ambiguity rather than breaking it. Opens on one concrete situation - a beaten stranger arrives at an inn with a dead child - the shape the opening test rewards. Risk: several reviews independently call it a slow burn with subplots that were not strictly necessary, the density discount the log applies to Les Miserables (71) rather than a bar.

t: Chlapec na moste (The Boy on the Bridge)
why: The series' core idea - that the infected are not simply monsters but a next evolutionary stage worth moral consideration rather than extermination - carries over, and reviewers specifically praise the same ambiguity here ('some zombies are zombies and some are not'), which is the axis:ideas this reader wants a book to leave behind. Stephen's characterization as an anxious, precise thinker gives him real interiority rather than making him a mission-object. Risk: it is an ensemble piece split across a full military-and-science crew rather than one throughline, and it is a prequel rather than the original - this reader's log shows prequels and sequels landing below their originals often enough (Hitchhiker's sequels 70 vs 83, Ballad 65 vs Sunrise 87) that the range should not assume it matches its predecessor.

t: Dalajlamova kocka (The Dalai Lama's Cat and the Claw of Attraction)
why: Sixth book in a long-running series where the cat narrator's function is to deliver Buddhist teaching to visiting characters. One reviewer warns it is worthwhile 'only if you want to learn more about Buddhism' and flags its treatment of Buddhism as the sole path to enlightenment; another calls the plot 'deceptively simple... not complex'. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91) works because it examines what is actually true from inside a real conversion; this instead reads as the theology being the whole of the book rather than a thread within a story, the exact case the reader profile marks as earning nothing on its own.

A 12th-century Cistercian monk's apocryphal journal of building the abbey of Thoronet, written by an architect (Fernand Pouillon) who actually built things for a living, while in prison. The idea it leaves behind is nameable and specific - the relationship between beauty and necessity, human effort and natural order, worked out through real construction problems (deaths on site, material failures) rather than asserted - the same kind of worked premise the log rewards in short idea-driven work (Labyrint sveta a raj srdce, 70). Faith runs through it as the monk-narrator's lens rather than as a standalone theological argument, so it reads as a thread rather than the whole subject. Risk: several readers explicitly recommend reading it in fragments rather than straight through, calling the pace closer to poetry than plot, the same density discount applied to Les Miserables (71); and the faith framing is close enough to the book's whole texture that it is worth tracking rather than dismissing.

Second half of the Flawed duology: a girl branded for moral failure by a judgmental society goes on the run. The branding-as-social-control premise is the same shape as Divergent's engineered-faction society (58), and reviews describe this sequel as leaning on 'preachy' speeches and familiar YA-dystopia beats rather than developing the premise further; none credit it with a worked-through idea beyond the branding conceit. That is the axis:ideas doubt this gate tests for.

t: Dopisy na konec sveta (Love Letters to the Dead)
why: An epistolary YA novel in which Laurel, grieving her sister's death, writes unsent letters to dead celebrities (Kurt Cobain, Amy Winehouse, and others) that gradually reveal a hidden trauma. The core idea - processing guilt and grief through addressing the untouchable dead - is real and nameable, but multiple reviewers call the structure repetitive (the same letter conceit worked over and over) and one flags the narrative voice as actively irritating, plus a direct, repeated comparison to Perks of Being a Wallflower as heavily derivative. That is the story-density problem the log treats as a penalty in its own right - a thin idea stretched thin across the page count - rather than a hard-filter issue, since the sexual content here is a disclosed backstory trauma rather than a plotline built around sexual behaviour.

YA gothic horror: siblings sent to live with secretive grandparents whose house hides old murders and apparitions. Reviews are mixed-positive on atmosphere but call the plot 'forced along' and say it was 'never really genuinely creepy'; one reviewer notes the book 'isn't really about the ghosts' despite the title. No idea beyond family-secrets atmosphere is nameable, closer to Chronicles of Narnia (67) than to a book that leaves something behind. Occult status is left unexamined by exiting here at C; nothing in the reviews describes a performed rite, only ambient hauntings.

t: Dum polamanych andelu (The House of Broken Angels)
why: A Mexican-American family gathers for a mother's funeral and a dying patriarch's last birthday over two frantic days - warm, semi-autobiographical, and consistently praised for heart and voice, but every review's substance is mood and family texture rather than a premise with consequences to trace; there is no single idea here worth writing down the way Animal Farm's or Labyrint's can be. Reviewers also flag a large, easily-confused cast of relatives ('wished for a family tree'), a real risk layered on top of the thin idea. Nothing here hits a hard filter.

t: Fotograf z Mauthausenu (The Photographer of Mauthausen)
why: This is the true story of Francisco Boix, the Mauthausen prisoner who smuggled out negatives an SS officer used to document camp deaths, evidence later used at Nuremberg - exactly the kind of memoir/testimony that earns points under the reader's rule (examining what actually happened, real insight into a group's lived experience), the pattern behind Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. A Goodreads reviewer specifically praises its restraint: 'no purposeful emotional scenes, no forced moral points, just the closest picture of that time'. Risk on axis:protagonist because the comic-panel format necessarily gives less interior monologue than prose memoir, and the reader's strongest preference is page time on what a character wants and why; risk on axis:bleakness for the concentration-camp setting itself. The library's 'detective' signal does not describe a whodunit - it flags Boix's own investigative documentation of Nazi crimes, not a mystery the reader is meant to solve.

t: Jeho kralovstvi (The Secret of the Kingdom)
why: This is not faith as a thread inside a larger story - the entire plot is Marcus's investigation into whether Jesus's claims and kingdom are true, which reviewers describe directly as a book 'if you want to explore your faith' and as dramatizing 'the dilemma of modern man... in gaining and retaining a faith.' That is theology and apologetics as the subject in its own right, which this reader's rules mark down regardless of craft - contrast Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, which scores high as first-person testimony examining what one person actually believes and why, not as a novel built to walk its reader toward a doctrinal claim. The annotation's 'detective-like obsession' pursuing the meaning of Jesus's words is metaphorical, not a whodunit, so axis:detective is a flag here, not a veto.

Opens on one concrete situation - retired mercenary Clay Cooper's old bandmate shows up needing help to save his daughter - which is exactly the legible single-starting-point shape the reader rewards, unlike the several-plot-lines confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Gunslinger. Reviews consistently single out motive over spectacle as the book's strength: a story about aging, friendship and loyalty forcing old bandmates to confront past deeds, with humor used to carry rather than replace emotional weight - the same axis that tops Red Rising and the Collins trilogy in the log. Passes the occult test cleanly: multiple sources describe no defined magic system, with the wizard's tricks played for comedy rather than any invoked or ritual power, so there is no rite on the page to veto. Worldbuilding is a mild risk rather than a strength to lean on - the loose, undefined magic system is the opposite of the declared-and-consequential systems (Sanderson, Bennett) the reader credits. Content tags list infidelity and sexual content only as 'minor', which reads as backstory texture rather than a plot thread; not examined further given budget, so treat as an open flag rather than a graded finding.

A YA horror-thriller about an orphaned girl who discovers her aunt runs a body-snatching syndicate supplying cadavers to a men-only anatomy school in 1850s Philadelphia. Molly's driving want - to be admitted to a world of medical knowledge closed to women, alongside a real class critique of the wealthy's 'performative philanthropy' - gives it a nameable idea and an actively wanting protagonist, the combination the log rewards most (Red Rising, Mockingjay). The subject matter (grave-robbing, anatomy) is medical/scientific rather than occult, so that filter is a clean pass with no rite or real-world religious practice involved. A murder investigation runs through the book too - Booklist calls it 'part mystery, part thriller, part family discovery' - which keeps the whodunit thread as a genuine risk to watch rather than the book's sole engine, since strong reviews (a starred Booklist review, YALSA Best Fiction pick, blurbs from established YA authors) suggest the mystery does not crowd out the character and idea work.

Elizabeth Zott is a determined, competent protagonist whose whole arc is about what she wants (to do real chemistry) and why 1950s-60s institutions won't let her, told in a voice reviewers describe as immediately captivating ('in love with it by the end of chapter one') - the same want-and-why axis that carries Pride and Prejudice to 75. The idea she leaves behind (using a cooking show as covert scientific and feminist re-education) is concrete and namable. Risk on axis:worldbuilding/self-consistency: more than one reviewer notes the plot resolves 'too conveniently' for a story whose own thesis is that science, like life, is messy and rarely goes to plan - exactly the kind of author-declared commitment the reader's rules hold a book to.

A kidnapped 13-year-old chess player, the lonely boy who visits her captivity, and the detective racing to find her, told across shifting POVs and a scrambled week-by-week timeline. The perpetrator is known from early on rather than concealed, so this reads as a survival thriller rather than a whodunit and does not trigger the detective filter. But it is a pure suspense/thriller with no idea to name beyond the tension itself, and even positive reviews note the explanations are 'thin' and the ending 'messy' and 'abrupt' - the same kind of thin-premise signal the log treats as a ceiling (contrast Mortal Engines' unworked premise at 55). Child endangerment content is present throughout, but the reader's rules treat a child protagonist and violence as non-objections in themselves.
