The cost is heavy atmosphere - reader reviews single out the beauty of the setting and emotional tone over incident, the story-density axis this reader dislikes, and the ending is stated as tragic (flight or death), which taps mild bleakness. No infidelity: Djenane's yearning for the visiting novelist reads as unconsummated and she is not shown married or engaged to another man in what I found. No sexual content, no occult, no detective structure.

A rational, science-minded young teacher in 1899 Olomouc hides a family curse and has sworn off love, until a man who risks everything for others enters her life. Consistent reader praise across Goodreads and Databaze knih centers on Dany as a character worth rooting for and on the romance itself, the axis Pycha a predsudek 75 shows 'costs nothing' when what characters want carries the book, plus researched period detail (teacher celibacy rules, period press excerpts) that reads as self-consistent rather than decorative. Docked for the YA ctu (young-adult) imprint and for being a loose sequel, where the log discounts on the Hitchhiker's 83-to-70 pattern. The curse is presented as inherited folk superstition rather than a rite shown on the page, so it is not flagged for the occult filter, though this was not independently sourced.

Middle-grade Czech sci-fi (~112pp, Pikola imprint, Zlata stuha-nominated) about a starship crew searching for a habitable planet. No source establishes a worked-out idea beyond the survival premise itself - unlike Project Hail Mary 92, where astrophage's consequences are actually explored, nothing suggests the habitable-planet search gets developed beyond plot beats (hibernation, a lunar base contact, hostile raiders). Short-idea-driven suspends the character-focused rules but adds nothing on its own, so without a nameable idea this settles under the line like any other thin book. Genre and audience mirror Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67, both of which paid a small childrens-axis cost.

WWII sabotage thriller: SOE agent Felicity 'Flick' Clairet assembles an all-woman team to destroy a German telephone exchange ahead of D-Day, based on real resistance operations. The premise gives real stakes and motive-driven characters (a positive, similar in kind to what the reader liked in Old Man's War), and the opening is a single clear mission objective rather than a confusing multi-thread start. But this grades down hard on axis:sexual-content: reviewers repeatedly flag 'too many' explicit sex scenes and, more seriously, sexualized torture written in explicitly eroticized terms ('they got erections as they inflicted wounds... experienced orgasms during their victims' death throes'), described as recurring across multiple scenes. Violence itself costs nothing under this reader's rules, but this is the sexual-content axis firing on crudeness and explicitness at real volume, which is why the estimate sits below the C-low band rather than in it.

t: Kralovna Tearlingu (The Queen of the Tearling)
why: Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, noted rather than hidden. Multiple reviews independently flag unexplained worldbuilding gaps - a post-collapse society where nobody reads books and there is no medical knowledge, neither ever accounted for - the same kind of unaddressed-consequence breach that cost Harry Potter and Mortal Engines, and one reviewer calls the setup 'very typical, almost Star Wars-like'. That reads as ideas assembled without cohering, the exact language the log already used for Divergent 58. The magic (a protective sapphire, a sorceress villain) is described by reviewers as vague and underdeveloped rather than a worked-out system, so there is no worldbuilding strength to lean on instead.

Reviews are near-uniformly positive on imagination, pace and invention, with no worldbuilding-inconsistency complaints of the kind that cost Tearling or Mortal Engines - the opposite pattern from those two. The opening is a single concrete situation (Twig, raised by trolls in the Deepwoods, sets out to learn his origins), matching the log's favored 'one concrete starting situation' over several plotlines at once. This is the same 'no penalties' shape the log used to explain the Hobbit's 84: friendship and adventure carried competently with nothing that costs points. Held below the Hobbit's ceiling because, unlike the Hobbit's heroism/friendship throughline, no reviewer names a real idea beyond episodic adventure - closer to a thin-ideas case landing in the high 60s/low 70s despite strong craft.

An interactive gamebook, not authored narrative fiction: the reader assembles a party and drives outcomes through skill checks, so there is no single protagonist whose motives the text develops - exactly the axis this reader weighs most heavily. It is genuinely well-regarded as a gamebook (4.55 on Goodreads, compared favorably to Fabled Lands), but reviewers praise it for open-ended replayability and party mechanics, not for character or idea, which is a different kind of achievement than the one being scored here. No fixed ending short of death, and no idea to name.

t: Leva ruka bozi (The Left Hand of God)
why: Cale, raised from age six or seven inside the brutal training of a fanatical religious order (the Redeemers, an inverted mirror of Christianity built around a 'Hanged Redeemer'), is revealed as the prophesied 'Left Hand of God' - the angel meant to end humanity for its unrepented sin. That is a real idea (guilt, free will and destiny inside an apocalyptic theology), but multiple reviewers finish the book with 'no clue as to what Paul Hoffman is trying to achieve,' and a trilogy retrospective calls it 'simultaneously brilliant and original, while also frustratingly lazy,' citing inconsistent world-building (Italian/British/invented names mixed with no apparent logic). I would flag axis:ideas as a real risk to the payoff holding up, which is what exits this at C on the default band. axis:occult is unusually clear here and established rather than deferred: multiple reviewers note the book has no magic at all despite fantasy trappings ('complete lack of magic,' reads 'like an alternate history') - not a concern. Protagonist rootability is a genuine open question: Cale and his fellow trainees are described as 'tough, sociopathic and accomplished liars,' the same shape of concern that cost the villain-adjacent lead in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against a rootable protagonist by the same author in Sunrise on the Reaping 87. Content is dark even by this log's tolerant standard - reviewers flag torture, child abuse and sexual abuse among the mature content - which touches axis:bleakness, the mildest objection in the log but a real one at this concentration.

A geopolitical hacking thriller (Britain weaponizes an autistic teenage hacker against Russia, North Korea and Iran) that reviewers praise for pace and plausible, well-researched topicality. But the central figure is the weak point on exactly the axis this reader weighs most: one critic calls Luke Jennings 'effectively a black box' dramatically, with his hacking feats presented as 'ghost in the machine stuff' that 'just happen' at convenient moments rather than being earned or explained - unearned competence with no consequence-carrying explanation, the opposite of what the reader rewards in Red Rising or Project Hail Mary. Without a protagonist whose motives get real page time, this settles under the line despite strong pacing and topicality.

Dr Rieux, who stays in plague-stricken Oran to work rather than join his sick wife, is exactly the rootable, motive-driven lead the reader rewards - reviewers describe him as persistent rather than heroic-postured, choosing 'a stubborn readiness to do one's work' over despair, the same quality that carries Old Man's War to 87. The idea is explicit and nameable: resistance to the absurd is not one heroic act but repeated ordinary labor, and multiple sources read the whole book as an allegory of occupation and moral choice under it - a real idea left behind, unlike Divergent 58's borrowed-and-unassembled ideas. Risk: sustained death and isolation is the book's whole atmosphere, which the reader discounts mildly (as with 1984 60) rather than penalizes heavily, since Rieux's active resistance, unlike Gregor Samsa's passivity in Metamorphosis 58, keeps the book from reading as merely bleak.

t: Muz, ktery pozoroval nebe (El hombre que miraba al cielo)
why: A minimalist 98-page literary novella built on mood and atmosphere - reviewers describe the prose as precise but note it reads 'as if there were no protagonist, everyone part of one entity,' which works against the protagonist-must-be-interesting-and-rootable rule this log weighs most heavily (the 22-point Snow/Sunrise gap). The mystery-of-the-old-man setup is a genuine hook, but nothing found names a worked idea beyond mood and atmosphere, so I cannot rule out axis:ideas collapsing the estimate - the short-idea-driven suspension only removes penalties, it never substitutes for a nameable idea.

Three Mouse Guard members investigate a missing grain merchant and uncover a conspiracy against their protected territories. Reviews praise the art and distinct character personalities, but reception on engagement splits - one reviewer explicitly 'didn't sense the characters' personalities' and 'didn't care what happened' - and no reviewer names a theme beyond a loyalty-and-duty animal adventure, the missing-idea gap the log docks in the 60s regardless of craft quality.

Second Kingsbridge novel, following four children - Merthin, Ralph, Gwenda, Caris - across four decades (1327-1351) around Kingsbridge cathedral and its two rival monasteries, through a plague epidemic. Plot momentum and density hold up the way they do in Follett's other doorstoppers (Count of Monte Cristo 75 shows length itself isn't a penalty here), and the multi-generational cast gets real page time on what they want. But reviews converge hard on the axis this reader weighs heaviest: sexual content that is frequent, graphic, and, worse, repeatedly treats rape and consensual sex in the same undifferentiated register - multiple reviewers flag 'rape victims... enjoying it' and describe the villain Ralph's rise to power as built substantially on rape used as spectacle rather than consequence. That is volume, explicitness and crudeness all firing together, in the same family as what sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 but by most accounts worse on the crudeness dimension, so the estimate sits below the C-low band rather than in it.

t: Nanook, ledovy netvor (Nanook the Snow Monster)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

t: Nikdo neni ostrov (Niemand ist eine Insel)
why: Not a whodunit - Sylvia's guilt is stated from the outset via her own indictment, so this is a confession-driven melodrama about motive and the treatment of disability rather than a mystery to be solved, which clears the detective filter. But German reader reviews call it 'below average for Simmel' and say it 'drags in circles for too long,' exactly the kind of doubt that belongs under axis:ideas - a social-conscience premise (disability, isolation) is stated but reportedly not carried through tightly enough to trust at full research cost.

t: O cem reka vi (What the River Knows)
why: Dual first-person YA historical fantasy: a Buenos Aires socialite sails to 1880s Cairo to learn what happened to her missing archaeologist parents, sparring and falling for her guardian's associate along the way. The enemies/rivals-to-lovers dynamic carrying two POVs is the same what-characters-want-and-why axis that lifts Pycha a predsudek to 75. Multiple independent reviews (YA Books Central, A Literary Escape, another ARC review) flag a slow, description-heavy first half before the plot accelerates - a density risk rather than a thin-story one, since the source is heavy period detail, not a lack of plot. The touch-activated artifact magic is repeatedly called vague and underdeveloped by reviewers rather than shown as a rite on the page, so it does not trip the occult mechanism test but earns no worldbuilding credit either.

Czech dual-timeline thriller: a modern woman with 'Kafkaesque traits' is betrayed by a lover and crosses between the present and the year 1463, meeting real historical figures. No independent review of this specific book turned up beyond retailer copy repeating the annotation, so the premise doesn't yet resolve into a statable idea from what is findable - the same doubt Divergent 58 earns for 'ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering'. A review of the same author's other novel found its storytelling grows 'increasingly chaotic', which is a genre-level flag on the author rather than evidence about this book, so it goes in flags, not the estimate itself.

Czech YA portal fantasy, openly Harry-Potter-inspired (the author does not deny the influence): three children from a children's home discover a hidden world of wizards, dragons, unicorns, harpies, sirens and genies living alongside ordinary people. Czech reader reviews are positive on execution ('velmi dobra kompozice a hloubka pribehu'), but the premise - orphaned children discover a hidden magic school/world - is the same generic template that sank Harry Potter 51 and Percy Jackson 57 for this reader, and I cannot name an idea beyond it, so axis:ideas is a real risk and this exits at C. axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule: harpies, sirens and genies are drawn from real-world mythology and folklore, the same category that cost Percy Jackson its occult points, so this is a live question for any future full pass, but it does not change today's exit.

Award-winning academic history (National Jewish Book Award, starred Kirkus) whose actual thesis is 'why Auschwitz', tracing the town across seven centuries with architectural plans and survivor testimony to explain how it became the camp, rather than retelling the Holocaust generally. The log's rule that memoir/testimony form earns nothing by itself but examining what is actually true does - the exact praise Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 got - applies directly here, and this is more rigorously sourced than a personal memoir. Held below that ceiling because it is 448 pages of dense archival and architectural detail rather than a single first-person voice, which risks the density penalty, and the subject matter is unrelieved Holocaust history with no companionship/self-sacrifice arc to offset the bleakness the way Project Hail Mary's does. Landed closer to Son of Hamas 75, a rigorous nonfiction examination without Qureshi's personal-narrative pull.

Opens the Psy-Changeling series: Sascha Duncan, a Psy who secretly feels emotion in a society that enforces total emotional 'Silence' on pain of a mind-wipe, is paired with changeling alpha Lucas Hunter to catch a serial killer targeting his pack. The Silence/PsyNet worldbuilding is followed through with real consequences (Sascha's mother disowns her at the end) rather than declared and dropped, and the emotional-repression theme is a genuine idea worked out in the plot, not just a backdrop for romance - both real credits against this reader's core axes. The book is graded down hard for sexual content, though: reviews consistently call it genuinely explicit ('quite explicit... hottest scenes'), and it is a recurring, structurally central genre element, not an incidental scene, so both volume and explicitness cost even though the treatment is called 'appropriate to the story' rather than crude. The serial-killer plot is an investigative subplot, not the book's core satisfaction, so it's a flag rather than a gate-1 filter.

t: Pan Cavendish, jestli se nemylim (Mr. Cavendish, I Presume)
why: Amelia Willoughby, engaged to a duke since infancy, falls for the man contesting his claim to the title - a companion novel that retells The Lost Duke of Wyndham's events from the other couple's viewpoint. Multiple reviewers call the gimmick the weak point: 'probably one of the weakest Quinn books,' 'over 300 pages of deja vu,' predictable because the events are already known from book one. Content is mild (a single, non-crude love scene, per multiple reviews), so sexual content is not the issue - the issue is that the parallel-retelling structure is not a worked idea in its own right, closer to Hitchhiker's sequels' 13-point series decline than to a book that earns its number independently.

t: Pet prani pana Murrayho McBridea (The Five Wishes of Mr. Murray McBride)
why: A 100-year-old widower finds a reason to live by helping a terminally ill 10-year-old boy complete a wish list. Commercially very popular (4.61 on Goodreads) but critical reviews repeatedly flag exactly the doubt this gate asks about: 'realism and plot be damned', 'thrown-together, soap opera ending', 'I just can't suspend belief this much... way beyond any belief'. That is a worked example of the sentimentality-over-plausibility pattern this reader has never rewarded highly; nothing in the reviews names an idea beyond the tearjerker premise itself. The child co-lead is graded on axis:childrens/life-phase rather than vetoed, but it costs a little given the reader's own calibration (Little Women 79 is the ceiling for domestic, character-only stories with no idea to work out, and this one carries a heavier plausibility complaint than that comparison does).

A heavily illustrated children's comic/picture book -- officially catalogued among the 'Best Books for Children 2015/2016' -- with a deliberately naive, simple, pun-driven plot for young readers (two robots exploring a post-human Earth). Reviewers praise it as exactly that: simple, cute, aimed at children who get a strong reading experience from it, with the artwork doing most of the work. This reader's own calibration puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s regardless of charm; there is no idea beyond the gentle premise itself.

Second Psy-Changeling book: F-Psy Faith NightStar, whose precognitive visions have started showing her both murder and desire, is drawn to changeling jaguar Vaughn while a Psy councilor tries to exploit her sight. The PsyNet/Silence worldbuilding keeps expanding with real consequences (the Council 'becoming monsters', the NetMind fracturing), which rewards this reader's worldbuilding axis, and the precognition is framed as an inborn psychic trait rather than any real-world occult practice - no ritual, divination or invocation on the page, so the occult filter does not apply. Same heavy sexual-content penalty as book 1 (same 'high heat' series-wide reputation), compounded here by a subplot where Faith's sister is murdered by the same serial-killer thread, adding a bleakness note; as a sequel it also carries the risk the reader's own log shows for series decline (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Adare, having exposed her father's killer, flees the palace to gather allies against the coup, drawing followers who believe she has been touched by the goddess Intarra. The idea carrying this trilogy is the Csestriim: an antagonist race whose evil is legible only as an absence of human motive, the same 'understand the alien Other' shape of idea that scores well here in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Old Man's War 87. Magic (the 'leach'/'Well' system) is mechanism-based - personal objects, declared rules, no invocation or priesthood - so it passes the occult mechanism escape the way Allomancy does, and an on-page 'trial by fire' miracle earlier in the trilogy is unmasked as a leach's trick rather than real divine power, reinforcing that reading. A real risk worth naming on its own evidence rather than the book's: this is a sequel, and sequels are not automatically safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's dropped from 83 to 70 across its series - so I am not predicting up purely on trilogy momentum.

t: Runy (Runes: The Creature of a Thousand Faces)
why: Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted. This is a heavily illustrated children's comic from Flying Eye Books (the same UK publisher as Hilda), reviewed mainly for its art (pastel colors, Adventure Time/Ghibli comparisons) rather than for any adult-legible idea. The reader-profile scale is explicit that a picture-book-adjacent work 'lands in the 30s or 40s', and at 160 pages aimed at young children this sits closer to that end than to a YA graphic novel like Wynd. The closest thing to a stated theme - deciphering ancient runes / understanding a friend who uses sign language - is a young-reader-level lesson, not a worked-through idea of the kind Labyrint 70 or Animal Farm 78 get credit for.

t: Sepron, morsky plaz (Sepron the Sea Serpent)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

t: Skandar a zlodej jednorozcu (Skandar and the Unicorn Thief)
why: Multiple reviews explicitly state this bestselling MG debut 'does not try to do much of anything new', is built from 'familiar tropes', and warn 'don't expect depth' - the reviewers' own words landing squarely on the log's axis:ideas test. That places it below Ranger's Apprentice 74, the log's ceiling for competent-but-unambitious YA/MG adventure fantasy, and closer to how Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55 read once a reviewer says a fantasy premise is assembled from familiar parts. Character relationships (with his sister and a rival-turned-ally) are praised as the book's strongest element, but not enough on their own to clear the line given the explicit lack-of-originality criticism.

t: Stezka v troskach (The Road Beyond Ruin)
why: A well-regarded (4.06/5, 15k+ ratings) WWII drama about strangers converging in postwar Germany, built on a real idea - that the war doesn't end for ordinary people when it ends for nations - close to what the reader rewards. But the author's own account confirms a back-and-forth timeline device that 'made my own head spin,' and at least one detailed review calls the present-day thread 'painfully slow' next to the past thread and the ending 'disorderly' and rushed - the drawn-out, jumbled-ending pattern that cost points elsewhere in the log (The Martian 82, Les Miserables 71). That doubt about whether the structure holds together keeps this under the line rather than predicting it up on a premise that may not survive its own device.

A real, worked idea - what freedom actually means for the newly emancipated amid persisting hatred - carried mainly through multiple close POVs on what each character wants (George's guilt and hope, Prentiss's wariness, Caleb's fear), the axis this log rewards most (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Booker-longlisted and repeatedly praised for probing beyond genre convention. The opening is a single legible situation - a grieving father meets two men on his land - not several unresolved threads, so this log's strongest predictor is clear. Risk: the book is genuinely bleak (a beating, a shooting, prejudice throughout) though reviewers note 'a tinge of hope,' closer to Old Man's War's mild bleakness discount than to 1984's flat penalty; juggling five-plus POVs also risks diluting the single-protagonist focus this reader prefers, though reviews suggest it is handled cleanly. Caleb's relationship with a fellow soldier is romantic but not depicted with volume or crudeness in anything found, so sexual-content is not a concern. No infidelity, no occult, no detective structure - the plot turns on hiding and revealing a relationship and a killing, not solving one.

Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

A near-future dystopia where infertility has made every birth state-monitored and every parenting slip grounds for a child's removal. Reviewers call the premise 'horrifyingly plausible' (Guardian) and 'entirely plausible' given its starting condition (GeekDad), unlike Divergent 58, which sank on a premise that 'collapses under thought'. Kit's arc is built entirely on what she wants and how far she will go to keep her family, the same axis Mockingjay 91 tops the log on. The consistent complaint is sustained heaviness -- 'The Road levels of parental anxiety', 'not the cheeriest' -- the same objection that was 1984's sole knock at 60, so it is carried as a risk rather than folded into the number; unlike 1984, Kit is actively fighting rather than passively crushed, which the rules treat as mitigating bleakness.

t: The house in the Cerulean Sea (The House in the Cerulean Sea)
why: Linus Baker, a rigid caseworker sent to assess six 'dangerous' magical children, is repeatedly the reason reviewers love this - his warming from bureaucratic fear to found-family devotion is the worth-rooting-for arc the reader rewards, in the spirit of the friendship-and-heroism case that carries The Hobbit to 84. Risk: several reviewers note thin plot tension ('no real huge plot moments,' a mid-book confrontation 'resolved in a snap') and at least one critique calls its allegory (echoing real residential-school history) 'shallow' - doubt about whether the idea is actually worked out rather than gestured at, closer to what stalls competent books in the 60s. The magical children (a gnome, a sprite, a wyvern, a boy prophesied as the Antichrist) are innate traits, not an invoked ritual or real-world occult system - no rite is enacted on the page, so this clears occult on mechanism/absence grounds.

A Texas oil-boom family saga (called 'Dickensian' by reviewers) about twins separated at birth and reunited as adults. The separation stems from their mother's affair while married to another man, but that is backstory the characters uncover, not a present-day marriage being unravelled on the page - exactly the 'betrayal in a backstory' case the rules mark as not-premise, costing a point or two rather than triggering a reject. No source names a worked-out idea beyond 'love, loss and betrayal amid an oil boom' - a family-secrets structure closer to the reviewer's own verdict ('a misnomer for these mostly decent people') than to the motive-driven case that lifts Pride and Prejudice to 75. Without a nameable idea this settles under the line.

t: Tlukot kridel smrti (The Beating of His Wings)
why: The trilogy's close: pursued by Bosco, the Redeemer leader who made him the Angel of Death, Cale's thirst for revenge draws him back to the sanctuary and toward the man he hates most. Same apocalyptic-theology idea as the rest of the trilogy, but with reviewers still reporting no clear sense of what the payoff was building toward and citing lazy, inconsistent world-building across the series, so axis:ideas remains a real risk and this exits at C on the default band, same as the other two volumes. axis:occult established rather than deferred: no real magic in this trilogy despite fantasy trappings. Protagonist rootability stays open - Cale is defined throughout by the 'sociopathic, accomplished liar' training of the Redeemers, the same shape of concern that cost the villain-adjacent lead in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 by the same author, and here the plot is explicitly driven by revenge rather than a clearer redemptive arc. Content stays dark - torture, child abuse and sexual abuse are flagged among the trilogy's mature content - touching axis:bleakness.

Court interpreter Revelle deliberately mistranslates testimony to steer a verdict, then must live with the consequences while a stalker circles closer -- the tension is about her secret and its fallout, not whodunit, so the detective filter does not apply. But the doubt this reader would flag under axis:ideas/worldbuilding is exactly what multiple reviewers name: the plot 'went too far fetched and implausible', with specific unresolved-plausibility complaints (an unrealistic adoption timeline with no social-worker involvement, a severely allergic character accepting unchecked food). That is the same 'does it hold up under thought' failure mode that sank Mortal Engines 55 and capped Divergent 58, just milder -- reception is otherwise mixed-to-positive (a Publishers Weekly starred review) rather than a clear miss.

t: To byl nas dum (We Used to Live Here)
why: House-flippers Eve and Charlie are overrun by a family claiming to have once lived in their new house, and the haunting that follows is praised for sustained dread - Kirkus calls it 'original and extremely scary,' Library Journal gave it a starred review. But the self-consistency test the reader applies (an author who undertakes to explain must make the explanation hold) fails by multiple accounts: one review states plainly that 'nothing is explained - no idea why it's happening, how it's happening, who the people are,' with 'lots of red herrings,' and another found the genre-blending 'left me more confused and bewildered than scared.' That is the same failure mode as Mortal Engines 55 (worldbuilding that doesn't account for itself). The opening itself is reportedly a clear, concrete situation (a house flip disrupted by an uncanny visit), so this doesn't fail the strict opening test the way Foundryside 30 did. Ghosts and ambiguous reality are the genre engine here, not an invoked ritual on the page, so occult is not established as firing, only flagged.

Middle volume of the Relentless trilogy: Sara Grey leaves everything behind to protect her loved ones and struggles to find her place among the Mohiri while a vampire lord hunts her. Same trope-heavy chosen-one/paranormal-romance premise as the rest of the trilogy - no idea beyond that to lean on, so axis:ideas carries a C-low exit despite a likeable, rootable lead and a series readers rate highly (Palmknihy ~89%).

t: Vyhnani Gerty Schnirch (The Expulsion of Gerta Schnirch)
why: Czech literary novel (Magnesia Litera 2010 reader prize) about the 1945 death march of Brno Germans and its aftermath. Sources confirm the book is built on a real idea worth having - collective guilt as a moral problem, the kind of thesis Animal Farm 78 gets credit for - and the opening is a single concrete situation (Gerta on the march), not several plotlines at once, so axis:opening is not a concern. But the content is more severe than any bleak anchor in the log: incest rape by Gerta's own father, plus repeated wartime rape during the march, confirmed by both a literary analysis site and a magazine feature, not just implied. 1984 60 shows sustained bleakness alone already lands right at the C line; this book adds graphic sexual violence on top, which is a heavier pushback than Animal Farm's idea-driven allegory absorbed, so the idea does not lift it back into the A band the way it did there. Some reviewers also call the pacing 'tezkopadna' (clunky), close to the Les Miserables 71 / Quo Vadis 66 territory for slower historical novels, which is the density risk noted.

t: Vyprava za diamantovym mecem (The Quest for the Diamond Sword: An Unofficial Gamer's Adventure, Book One)
why: Unofficial Minecraft tie-in aimed at ages 8-10 (a 2-3 hour read by its own publisher listing); reviewers flag editing errors and inaccuracies against actual game mechanics. There is no idea beyond 'be brave and protect your village' retold through Minecraft's crafting loop - the no-idea-plus-suspended-form combination the log reserves for the lower band, alongside a picture book.

Czech-original SF novel: Sofie Adlerova wakes from cryostasis 160 years late to find her existence reduced to a medical-test subject for a corporation researching android/AI consciousness (bioroids). The idea - what makes a bioroid human, tested through forced experimentation on someone the state has erased - is real and nameable, but reviews raise genuine doubt about whether it holds up: a Slovak Goodreads review says the book 'raises many questions and gives few, mostly unsatisfying, answers,' and a Czech review notes the heroine's defiant attitude 'becomes rather annoying' over time despite an initially sympathetic read. That combination of an unresolved idea and a protagonist risk is exactly gate 4's test, so I exit C-low rather than spend a full pass confirming a doubt already visible in the reviews.

2023 Booker-shortlisted debut about an 11-year-old girl processing her mother's death through competitive squash under her father's increasingly intense coaching. Critical praise is real (Kirkus starred, Booker's own reading guide comparing it to Ishiguro's debut), but it is explicitly praised for operating 'in the gaps outside the plot' -- quiet, restrained, understated. Reader-side reviews are split on whether that restraint pays off: characters described as 'speaking at angles to one another', making it 'tough to follow' and 'hard to get invested', the ending called 'weak' and the plot 'vague'. I cannot name a worked-out idea beyond grief-expressed-through-discipline; this reads as a mood/character study rather than a premise whose consequences are traced, closer to the many competent-but-thin books that settle in the 60s than to Flowers-for-Algernon-style idea-driven work.

t: Wynd (Wynd, Book One: The Flight of the Prince)
why: The book's magic is inherited/biological (a hidden 'weird blood' bloodline that causes involuntary shapeshifting, e.g. into a griffin-like creature) with no invocation, devotion or priesthood shown on the page, so it clears both tests of the occult filter. Multiple reviewers read a clear, nameable idea - hiding one's true self, read explicitly as a queer/trans-coded allegory - which is the kind of idea the log rewards (Animal Farm 78, Little Prince 82). Held well below Little Prince's ceiling because comics have no anchor in this log for the interiority and motive-focused page time the reader consistently rewards over action (violence/spectacle on the page rather than reflection), so the character axis is a real unknown here rather than an established strength.

Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted. English-language coverage of this Norwegian YA-fantasy spinoff is thin; a translated reader review flags 'too many unlikable characters' and says sex is 'used as an odd device', while the plot itself did not hold that reviewer's interest - close to the log's Divergent 58 case of ideas that do not cohere once examined, rather than a worked-out premise. The core idea available from the annotation (a woman who despises the revered but fraudulent seer caste she was raised in) is a real premise but cannot be confirmed as paying off from the sources found. The book's own divination practice is explicitly framed in the annotation as fraud rather than real supernatural power, which would likely clear axis:occult's Source test, but this is not independently confirmed.

t: Zeme tech druhych (Le Pays des autres)
why: A real historical subject rarely covered in French fiction (Moroccan decolonization, versus the much-more-worked Algerian case) and a title that states its own idea - everyone here lives in a 'country of others,' unable to fully belong. But French reader reviews repeatedly flag a confusing chronology that 'makes it hard to attach to the characters' and call the book unresolved ('roman inacheve,' no denouement) because it is the first of a trilogy - that chronology complaint lands directly on this log's single most reliable predictor, a confusing or unclear start, and the lack of a denouement means the book does not stand as its own worked premise. I would put axis:opening under risks if I researched further, the C-low signal.

A German diary-novel of a Latin teacher smuggling Jews to Belgium in beehives in 1944-45, widely and seriously praised (near-miss for the Deutscher Buchpreis, five printings in six weeks). But the diarist is also, by both his own account and reviewers', a married-into-others'-marriages philanderer, and the plot's central late turn is his affair with the wife of the local Nazi district leader (Kreisleiter), whose marriage bed he 'soon ends up in' -- infidelity within someone else's marriage, not the book's premise (remove it and the smuggling story still stands) but a real subplot that precipitates his downfall. Framing reads as neither condemned nor celebrated: reviewers call the narrator a 'love bee' moving flower to flower and note the book answers moral questions 'practically, not through fundamental morality', closer to wry acceptance than judgment -- 'subplot' and 'neutral' on this reader's table, which the reader has ruled severe enough on its own regardless of the book's other literary merits.

Spent 4 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted honestly rather than silently. Sixteenth book of a still-running paranormal-romance series, with none of the earlier 15 volumes in books-read.md - a far steeper version of the sequel penalty the log already records: Hitchhiker's dropped 13 points (83 to 70) between book 1 and its sequels, and that was a reader who had read book 1. Reviews confirm the series' baseline of explicit love scenes plus one villain scene multiple bloggers call unusually intense, which lands in the same territory as Witcher 53 and Ready Player One 55, both sunk mainly by volume. No reviewer names an idea beyond formula war/romance beats resolving across an ensemble cast, so axis:ideas gives nothing to lean on.

A hard military SF debut praised specifically for the author's technical grounding in weapons and transport systems worked into the plot, a real worldbuilding effort. But one reviewer describes the cast as 'sablonovite' (stock/templated) and reports genuine indifference to their fates aside from two side characters, and reviewers broadly frame the book as competent, unoriginal genre comfort reading ('nic noveho ani invence', 'vytecna oddychovka'). That is the same protagonist-thinness pattern that capped Artemis at 69 despite consistent worldbuilding -- worldbuilding never predicts a book up when the lead looks thin.

Starred Kirkus and starred Publishers Weekly reviews both single out real thematic weight - state oppression, forced concealment of identity, reproductive freedom - rather than just atmosphere, the same kind of dystopian-persecution premise that tops the log with Mockingjay 91 and The Hunger Games 89 when the protagonist's stakes stay central. One blog confirms the narrative keeps its center on Lark rather than sprawling across the full cast. Held below the log's dystopian ceiling because one reviewer explicitly calls the POV chapter-ordering 'really confusing' even while rating the book highly, a smaller-scale version of the axis:opening risk that sank Foundryside and The Gunslinger, though most other reviewers say the multi-POV structure reads clearly once you adjust to it.

t: Zverolekar a spol (The Vet: My Wild and Wonderful Friends)
why: Warm, funny, and repeatedly compared to James Herriot in reader reviews, but memoir/testimony earns nothing by itself in this reader's log - what earns points is examining what is actually true or giving insight into how another group experiences the world, the way Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91) does. This is anecdote-driven entertainment about a vet's daily life and courtship, not an examination of a hard truth, so I'd flag axis:ideas as a risk if pushed further - the C-low signal.

Opens on a single concrete scene - a coach travelling into Cornwall - so there is no confusing multi-thread start. Motive and marriage strain again carry the book, the axis that tops this log (Pride and Prejudice 75, Mockingjay 91): Ross and George's old rivalry, and Ross and Demelza's attempt to reconcile, both turn on what each character wants and why. Infidelity - Ross's earlier affair with Elizabeth, now pregnant by him, and Demelza's own past unfaithfulness - is a subplot inside a much larger political and family saga, not the premise: remove it and the parliamentary career, the Warleggan feud, and the Morwenna/Drake romance are all still a book. It is condemned rather than celebrated - Graham has the affair's fallout end in Elizabeth's death, described by reviewers as Ross and George 'effectively' killing her - so per the infidelity axis this is a subplot/condemned deduction of a few points, not a filter. No occult content in a straight historical novel.

t: Ctyri posledni veci (The Last Four Things)
why: After betraying the Redeemers, Cale learns that the order's leader believes mankind must be destroyed to correct God's greatest mistake, and outwardly makes peace with his role as the destroying angel. Same apocalyptic-theology idea as the rest of the trilogy (guilt, free will and destiny), but reviewers of the series overall report finishing 'with no clue as to what Paul Hoffman is trying to achieve' and call the trilogy 'frustratingly lazy' on world-building consistency, so axis:ideas stays a real risk and this exits at C on the default band. axis:occult established rather than deferred: the trilogy is repeatedly described as having no real magic despite its fantasy trappings, closer to alternate history. Protagonist rootability remains open - Cale and the Redeemer-trained boys are described as 'tough, sociopathic and accomplished liars,' the same rootability concern that cost the villain-adjacent lead in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 by the same author. Content stays dark - torture, child abuse and sexual abuse are flagged among the trilogy's mature content - touching axis:bleakness.

Soldier Lee Parker is ordered to bring the rebel Sera back to the Citadel alive, but a deadly storm strands the two of them together for nine days. The annotation-lexicon 'sex' signal appears to be a false positive - every review I found (Databaze knih, Henry's SF&F, kniznidenicek) describes a 'natural' or 'great' romantic line growing out of the captivity premise, with no mention of explicit content, so this does not read as sex-as-plot. The dystopian priests-vs-rebels premise is a familiar faction-dystopia shape (same family as Divergent 58) rather than a worked-out idea of its own, so axis:ideas is why this exits C-low despite strongly positive reader reception (multiple 5-star blog reviews).

In Strachotova's Czech-original dystopian duology Devet dni, Sera and Lee, briefly free, find the Citadel tightening into a crueler dictatorship as energy scarcity drives the population toward desperation. Reviews are consistently positive on pacing and action ('dominuje akcnim scenam') and note the Lee/Sera romance is 'vhodne upozadena' (kept properly in the background), so this does not read as a sex-driven or infidelity book. But one review flags 'a sense of fragmentation from trying to fit too many motifs into one book,' and I can't point to a premise beyond a familiar priests-vs-rebels dystopian-faction setup (the same shape that sank Divergent 58 on premise logic), so axis:ideas carries a C-low exit rather than a fuller pass.

t: Ember a buraceni draku (Ember Spark and the Thunder of Dragons)
why: In Elphinstone's Ember Spark series for younger readers, Ember rescues a hamster-like creature and becomes apprentice to Rusty Fizzbang, vet to magical beasts, then must save a baby dragon from a villain trying to expose the hidden magical world. Reviewed warmly by the Daily Mail ('a joy') and the Telegraph, but it is squarely a younger-reader adventure with no idea beyond friendship-and-wonder to lean on, closest in shape to Narnia 67 - familiar tropes, likeable leads, nothing to think about afterward. The magic (dragons, unicorns, a secret creature-veterinary world) is invented-creature fantasy with no witchcraft, ritual or real-world occult source, so the occult filter does not apply; I record that check rather than defer it, since this task line's lexicon flagged 'occult' off the word 'magickych'.

t: Ember a snezny fenix (Ember Spark and the Frost Phoenix)
why: This Ember Spark book follows Ember and Arno as they trail a baby frost phoenix to the Arctic to save migrating 'neverwhales' from the same recurring villain, Jasper Hornswoggle. The series delivers imaginative younger-reader adventure (Daily Mail/Telegraph praise) but no idea beyond friendship-and-wonder to lean on, and invented creature-magic with no occult source or ritual depiction. C-low on axis:childrens, comparable to Narnia 67 rather than to an idea-driven short work like The Little Prince 82.

t: Grandhotel Schwarzenberg (Grandhotel Schwarzenberg - Der Beginn einer neuen Zeit)
why: This record's annotation centers on a son's dream of building a mountain hotel, his mother's disapproval of his choice of fiancee, and the rise of National Socialism intruding on the family - no infidelity appears in this book's own plot. Reviews describe the series consistently as 'light but intelligent entertainment' with well-researched period detail - competent and readable, but no source names an idea beyond family drama against a historical backdrop, closer to Titans than to the motive-driven case that lifts Pride and Prejudice.

Motive-driven historical drama in the mould this reader rates highest: grief over a dead infant daughter, guilt, and a marriage under strain carry the book more than incident, the same axis that tops Pride and Prejudice 75 and the Hunger Games trilogy in this log. Ross is flawed but rootable - he acts from grief and injustice rather than villainy, unlike the un-rootable leads this reader marks down. No detective engine: the reader already knows what Ross did (inciting a wrecking riot), so the tension is legal jeopardy and marriage rather than who did it, and no infidelity or occult content appears anywhere in the sourced synopsis. Set against Count of Monte Cristo 75 and Quo Vadis 66, the log's other classic historical dramas.

A precise, single-decision premise -- what a mother names her newborn son -- forks into three full 35-year lives, one per name, and reviewers agree the consequences are actually traced through: 'a profound, deeply compassionate examination... startlingly joyful and paced like a thriller', 'Knapp's plotting is skillful'. That is exactly the axis Project Hail Mary 92 tops the log on -- a premise declared precisely, with the whole book working out its consequences rather than just gesturing at them -- and Cora's throughline (what she wants for her son, and the courage or its absence in each branch) is motive-driven in the way Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 are rewarded for. Domestic abuse and one branch's violence are real content (not infidelity -- there is no affair, only Gordon's coercive control), so bleakness is carried as a risk; one reviewer found one of the three timelines slow and the epilogue's necessity questionable, which keeps the estimate short of the very top of the log rather than at it.

In Elphinstone's Unmapped Chronicles (UK title Jungledrop, US title 'The Bickery Twins and the Phoenix Tear'; the Czech catalogue title translates the umbrella series name, not this specific book's title), rival twins Fox and Fibber are swept into the magical kingdom Jungledrop and must find the Forever Fern before the harpy Morg does, learning there are things more important than the inheritance they were fighting over. The sibling-rivalry-to-cooperation arc gives a small motives-over-action credit missing from a pure adventure romp, but it's still a whimsical MG quest with nothing to think about afterward, so it sits with the rest of Elphinstone's work at C-low on axis:childrens, in the Narnia 67 / Ranger's Apprentice 74 range rather than higher. Same invented creature/weather magic as her other books, no occult source or ritual depiction.

On the world of Urth, a decaying moon closing in threatens all life, and four stock companions (soldier, thief, disgraced prince, girl) search the ice for a lost civilization's knowledge of how to stop it - a workable but generic disaster-quest premise rather than a worked-through idea. Czech reader reviews of this specific volume describe the battles as drawn out and not very engaging. As a sequel it takes the sequel discount the log applies elsewhere (Hitchhiker's 83 down to 70 across its follow-ups).

In the Relentless trilogy (Czech catalogue calls the series 'Yoli', the publisher's YA imprint), 17-year-old Sara Grey, still haunted by her father's murder ten years earlier, is revealed to be a Mohiri demon-hunter and meets warrior Nikolas. The annotation-lexicon 'detective' signal is her backstory motive for wanting answers, not the book's satisfaction - the opening (a waterfront confrontation) and the plot are urban-fantasy romance/adventure, not a whodunit, so gate 1 clears. No strong idea beyond standard chosen-one/paranormal-romance tropes ('cliches', a 'derivative' mate concept per a Czech reviewer), so axis:ideas is why this exits C-low despite a well-liked, rootable protagonist.

Military SF opener: humanity's first deep-space voyage lands in the middle of an interstellar war between the Priminae and the Drasin. Reviewers consistently describe it as 'more action than character-driven' though 'characters are viable' -- the opposite tilt of what this reader rewards, the same gap that cost Golden Son 92 points versus Red Rising 95. Old Man's War 87 scored high because the worldbuilding held together consequence by consequence; nothing in the Odyssey One reviews claims that level of follow-through, just a standard, well-executed first-contact-drawn-into-war setup.

Sixth volume of the Harry-Potter-inspired Sedmy smysl series: Hanka has a glowing gem embedded in her skin that unicorns and dragons react to with alarm. Same underlying found-family/magic-school template as the rest of the series with nothing distinctively new introduced at the idea level - I cannot name an idea beyond it, so axis:ideas is a real risk and this exits at C on the default band. axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule.

t: Pamet kosti (An Echo in the Bone)
why: A sequel deep in a long-running series, and this log's sequels are not safe bets - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the Ender saga settled from 92 to 79-81. Reader reviews single this volume out as weaker than the rest of the saga (the one Outlander book one longtime fan wouldn't rate 5 stars) and note large stretches are conveyed through letters rather than direct scenes, working against the momentum the reader rewards. No infidelity in a current marriage is indicated - Jamie's illegitimate son is backstory, not an active affair - so that axis does not fire, but the series is well known for sustained explicit content across its volumes, an unexamined risk for this specific book. Absent a stronger positive case than 'competently continues a beloved saga,' this settles under the line.

Connolly's comedic YA 'Samuel Johnson vs the Devil' series: reviewers describe it as blending Eoin Colfer-style humour with a returning demon cast (Nurd, four dwarfs, Mrs Abernathy) - a good-vs-evil comedy-adventure without a nameable idea beyond its own premise, and it is a sequel, the shape the log discounts (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70 across its follow-ups). Exiting here, the occult question (Hell, demons, the mechanism behind the portal) is left unexamined since nothing under 68 is proposed regardless of the answer.

t: Pet nedel v balonu (Five Weeks in a Balloon)
why: Verne's debut Voyages Extraordinaires novel: three formulaic character types (a know-it-all scientist, a skeptical hunter, a comic manservant) cross Africa by balloon through a chain of small misadventures resolved mostly by convenient coincidence. Reviewers call the plot 'unremittingly linear' and the underlying science 'sketchy.' Beyond generic perseverance-and-exploration, I cannot name an idea I would not list under an axis:ideas risk, which is this gate's test.

t: Posledni smrtelne pouto (The Last Mortal Bond)
why: The trilogy's finale: the empire is consumed by war as the Csestriim - the ancient, near-extinct antagonist race whose evil reads as the absence of human motive rather than a bad one - return to finish their purge of humanity. That is the same 'understand the alien Other' idea that scores well here in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Old Man's War 87, and it pays off directly in this closing volume as gods and Csestriim both act openly. Magic stays mechanism-based (personal-object 'Wells,' declared rules, no invocation or priesthood), so axis:occult clears on the same mechanism grounds. A specific, sourced risk for this volume: a reviewer flags that 'there seems to be a lot of exposition which at times impacted on the plot' in this particular book, a story-density concern - this book's pacing is judged on that evidence alone rather than assumed from general series reputation.

Fifth volume of the Harry-Potter-inspired Sedmy smysl series: twins Tom and Sam attend a school at Airbowan, described as lying on the border between life and death and taught by harpies, while Tom tries to save Sam's soul and reunite it with his body against dark forces. This is the same found-family/magic-school template that already sinks the series on axis:ideas - I cannot name an idea beyond it, so this exits at C on the default band. The setting (a school of harpy teachers 'on the border of life and death' plus a soul/body-separation plot) raises a live axis:occult question, but it is left unexamined per the C-low rule since the book already lands below the line on ideas regardless.

In Smith's Sean Courtney saga, a WWI veteran, Mark Anders, returns to a despoiled family estate and a murdered grandfather, and gets pulled into the Courtney family's violent feud with the corrupt Dirk Courtney. Goodreads and archive.org both flag graphic sexual content running throughout the book (it was banned in South Africa into 1981 over exactly this), which is the axis Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 were sunk by on volume alone - here the content is reported as more pervasive, not a single scene. Reader reception is also split, with more than one review unable to connect with the characters, echoing the thin-lead problem that capped Artemis at 69 despite strong worldbuilding. Neither risk is enough to name a hard filter (this is a revenge/war adventure, not a book about an affair or about sex), so it is graded down rather than rejected.

In Karen Lynch's Relentless trilogy (the Czech catalogue's series label 'Yoli' is the publisher's YA imprint, not the original series name), Sara Grey, now a Mohiri demon-hunter, goes looking for the one person who can explain her past. Reviews (Czech and English) describe a competent, well-liked YA urban-fantasy trilogy - readers root for Sara and Jordan - but call the vampire-mate premise derivative ('trope seen before'), and I cannot name an idea beyond standard chosen-one/mate-bond urban fantasy, so axis:ideas goes to a C-low exit per gate 4. Romance and spice build across the trilogy and peak in this volume ('reaching its full potential in the 3rd'), but are still described as low-to-moderate ('low spice level... not explicit') rather than crude, so this threatens the estimate rather than a filter. A teen lead is a small life-phase cost only.

A 72-page Disney tie-in comic for ages 6+ (Stitch escapes robot kidnappers to protect Lilo), confirmed as a short illustrated children's comic rather than a novel. No idea beyond 'protect the family' is available at this length and audience, and short-idea-driven suspends the character rules without adding points. Unlike The Little Prince 82 and The Hobbit 84 - short, child-adjacent work that still carries a real idea or story - this is a picture-book-adjacent tie-in with nothing to hold onto beyond the premise itself, so it lands well under the 65 line rather than merely a little under it.

Gate 4 exit: a fast, splatterpunk-flavored fantasy where a hunter-of-people tracks a serial killer through a decadent city guarded by a captain and a priest. Reviews credit it for pace, dark humor and fight choreography, not for an idea - one reviewer notes the brutality 'doesn't narrate' the story forward, another says the length should have been cut in half around a fairly simple spectacle. I cannot name an idea I would defend against an axis:ideas risk, which is this gate's test, so I stop here rather than fund a full read. Occult status is deliberately left unexamined, as the gate intends.

German children's fantasy series built on scent-based magic: Lucie chases a stolen magic powder to Amsterdam to free a friend's father from a curse-scent. Aimed squarely at a young children's audience per the catalogue heading, with a plot driven by a mechanism (magic powders) rather than a worked idea. Exiting at C, the occult status of the scent-magic system is left unexamined, since nothing under 68 changes on that answer.

t: Zacatek nove ery (Tochter einer neuen Zeit)
why: A four-woman family saga through 20th-century Hamburg (midwifery training in 1919 through Nazism and WWII). Reception splits sharply on exactly the axis that decides this reader's scores on sagas: one camp likens it favorably to Ferrante's Neapolitan quartet, another dismisses it as 'tanto rumore per nulla' (much ado about nothing) and 'historical romance dressed up', with a recurring critique that the prose and the four women themselves are 'simple'. Compare Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, both mid-B historical novels without a strong idea to lean on; nothing here suggests these four leads are differentiated the way Darrow/Sevro/Mustang are praised for being in Golden Son 92.

t: Zlodejicek z patych hradeb (Zlodejicek z patych hradeb)
why: Seventh volume of the Harry-Potter-inspired Sedmy smysl series: now seventeen, Hanka unexpectedly meets a nanny she doesn't remember, who claims Hanka's father, believed dead, is actually alive. Same underlying found-family/magic-school template as the rest of the series - I cannot name an idea beyond it, so axis:ideas is a real risk and this exits at C on the default band. axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule.

In the dark-academia Atlas trilogy, the surviving Alexandrian Society initiates, bound by a lethal bargain, fracture into rival strategies as their patron Atlas Blakely's real plan comes due. This series is unusually well-matched to this reader's top axis - reviewers describe it as taking place 'primarily in the characters' heads,' with realistically messy, differentiated motives rather than action for its own sake, which is real credit. But the finale is the weak link: multiple reviewers call the ending 'abrupt and anticlimactic' relative to the buildup, one calling it 'one of the worst finales for a trilogy,' and a Czech reader review is bluntly negative ('silene zklamani' - a crazy disappointment). As a sequel in a chain already flagged for uneven pacing, I weigh that momentum risk against the strong motive-driven characterization and land under the line.

Verne states his own aim in the preface: to show what children's intelligence and courage are capable of when tested by real adversity, without the group sliding into savagery. A schooner of boys wrecked on an island must govern themselves, argue over leadership, split into a rival camp over a cheating accusation, and reconcile - a real, statable idea (children can govern themselves capably under pressure), not nothing to think about, so it clears gate 4. Set against Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 in this reader's log - children protagonists, graded on axis:childrens, never vetoed - the self-governance theme and real interpersonal conflict argue for landing at least that well, but reviewers flag one-dimensional, 'irredeemably evil' pirate villains and children written as 'morally perfect,' the same character-differentiation shortfall that never sank Ranger's Apprentice past a B either. Opens on a single clear situation (the ship torn from its moorings in a storm), not a confusing multi-thread start.

Spent 4 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the same series-fatigue shape recorded for Hitchhiker's (83 to 70 across a sequel). Kirkus framed the series' strength as its 'what if' idea-work; multiple later reviews (Recoil Offgrid, a Goodreads-cited critique, and a LiveJournal review) say this later volume leans increasingly into political 'axe-grinding' rather than re-examining that premise, so the core post-EMP-collapse idea is not meaningfully advanced here.

A prose-and-comics hybrid for children (age 10+) where a bullied seventh-grader's video game world and real life collide. A dedicated review from Centrum ceske detske knihy calls the premise of connecting gaming and classic narrative 'remarkable' but says the execution 'falls short of expectations', and describes the comic passages as fragmentary and abbreviated; a reader review separately called the illustration style unappealing. The idea itself (a game world bleeding into reality for an isolated kid) is real but is reported as underdelivered rather than worked through, and about half the book is comic pages, a short suspended-test form in this reader's rules. That combination - a real idea that reviewers say the book does not follow through on, in a partly-comic format - fits the low C-band rather than the default one.

Marketed and reviewed as a youth-aimed action novella (a UK reviewer of the omnibus specifically flags the 'Youth' cover label), the survival-and-training premise (a young gladiator forced to fight for his life) is the kind of situation Ranger's Apprentice 74 also runs on, but the reviews found for this specific series are less flattering than Ranger's Apprentice's 'easy but competent': one detailed critical review names one-dimensional villains, a hero with unrealistic recovery from injury, and dialogue that is mostly insults - exactly the kind of thin idea/execution axis:ideas is meant to flag. Fan reviews call it fun and fast, but nothing found makes a positive case beyond pace. Set below Ranger's Apprentice 74 and near the C-low default band given the doubt about whether the idea and characters actually hold up under scrutiny.

Celie is married to Albert under a forced, abusive marriage, and her transformative relationship develops with Shug Avery - Albert's own mistress - and by the time Celie and Shug become lovers, Shug has separately married a man named Grady. Multiple critics describe this relationship as 'the novel's core' and 'the catalyst' for Celie's whole transformation, so it is a major subplot rather than a bare backstory detail, and it is framed with unambiguous approval throughout - liberating and loving, never condemned or punished. Per the infidelity rule, a subplot with approving framing lands in this band regardless of the book's other literary strengths. It is not premise-level - a full second half is built on Nettie's letters from Africa and Celie's own path to independence, which do not depend on the Shug relationship - so it is graded here rather than rejected. Two sources were spent confirming the prominence and framing, which also settled the below-68 question, exceeding the one-source C-low budget by one.

t: Bezuzdna blahoslavenstvi Baltazara B (The Beastly Beatitudes of Balthazar B)
why: A picaresque following Balthazar from a neglected Parisian childhood through English boarding school to Trinity College Dublin, with a lifelong friend, is not itself a sexual-relationship plot - it is a life-and-friendship arc, so this does not hit the plot-is-mainly-sex filter. But reviewers describe "amorous adventures high and low" running through every phase of the book and sum the whole thing up as "hysterically funny sexual shenanigans... basted in startling amounts of alcohol" - that is high volume sustained across the entire length of the book, the dimension that sank The Witcher 53 in this log regardless of the surrounding book's quality; literary acclaim (the New York Times called it "a triumphant piece of writing") does not buy back points on this axis any more than it does on the infidelity axis for Anna Karenina. One Goodreads reviewer notes Balthazar himself "can only be called sympathetic when compared to" his more caddish friend Beefy - a real risk that the lead is thin or unlikeable on his own terms, not just relative to a worse character.

A medieval-flavoured throne-war fantasy: a scheming regent marries the widowed queen and moves to force her daughter into marriage next, and the prince and princess flee and fight to reclaim what is theirs. Nothing in any source names a worked idea beyond the standard succession-plot mechanics, and one professional-adjacent reader account describes the prose as flowery and convoluted enough that they nearly quit around page 120. Genre adventure fantasy with no idea to name is exactly the C-low case, so I stop here rather than pay for a full read that a competent-but-thin book would not repay.

Testimony/memoir, graded on whether it examines what is actually true - the axis behind the gap between Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40. This continues the same real-life account by the same author: a 2025 investigation disputed the stated cause of the couple's homelessness (reporting it followed accusations she stole from an employer), found they owned a second property in France, reported they used assumed names, and cast doubt on the husband's terminal diagnosis, a thread this book directly continues. Those are the exact claims the memoir axis rewards when verified, and public reporting disputes several load-bearing ones, so I doubt the true-examination axis holds up.

A captured messenger reveals a conspiracy meant to sabotage the campaign against Caratacus - court intrigue layered onto the same war plot that runs through this series. Reviewers describe the draw as the leads' friendship inside a repeating formula rather than a single explored idea, so this sits with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

An orphan enslaved in a cruel matron's match factory rescues an abandoned fairy baby, escapes with the help of its tiny forest-guardian parents, then goes back for the other orphans rather than staying safe - a rescuer's motive that matches the reader's preference for characters defined by what they want to do for others, similar in shape to the self-sacrifice this reader praised in Project Hail Mary 92. It won The Times' children's book of the year and two other awards, evidence of real craft rather than publisher puffery. It is squarely a children's book (target age about 10), the register Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 sit in, and the ecological message named in every summary is closer to incidental flavour than a worked idea, so I would list axis:ideas as a risk rather than lean on it.

A time-traveling teenager from 2012 and a track runner from 1995 fall for each other despite knowing he could be pulled back to his own time at any moment. Reviewers are positive on the romance and secondary characters but repeatedly describe the book as reading like contemporary YA romance wearing a light sci-fi coat - 'more contemporary than science fiction' - rather than a book that works out what time travel actually costs or how it operates; the mechanism is treated as a device for the relationship, not a declared, examined rule set. That leaves no idea beyond a familiar forbidden-romance-against-time premise, which is why this exits here rather than going on, with the thin time-travel logic carried as a worldbuilding risk in case a fuller read surfaces a real rule set underneath.

A sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 across its sequels, the steepest series decline recorded. Here Tom Neave is torn between his wife and son and his loyalty to a divided Parliament during the English Civil War - real motive-driven material - but reception on this entry is mixed, with one review praising the period detail while another found it 'too gung-ho, with too many confusing twists and turns.' Between the sequel risk and the mixed reception on plot clarity, this reads as a book that will probably sit just under the line.

t: Cerna labut (The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable)
why: One idea declared precisely and then worked out at length across finance, history and everyday reasoning - an unpredictable, high-impact event that gets rationalized as obvious only after the fact - which is exactly the kind of premise-with-consequences-worked-out this reader responds to. It is not memoir, but the closest read is Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, praised specifically for rigorously examining what is plausible and believable; Taleb's project is the same rigor turned on financial and historical certainty. No protagonist at all, which is not fatal on its own - The Silmarillion 80 shows this reader can score a book well with no continuous narrative when the content carries it. The genre field is a forced fit (none of the closed options describe argumentative nonfiction); form is nonfiction. Main risk is reviewers repeatedly calling the prose dense, digressive and self-satisfied in tone, which could cost the way heavy description costs elsewhere in the log.

A Booker-longlisted, personally-researched account of a Jewish family's 1939 flight from Nazi-occupied Czechoslovakia, centered on what each character is willing to risk to save the six-year-old son - the axis this reader rewards most (Speaker for the Dead 90, Mockingjay 91). A subplot has the family's nanny in an affair with a married foreman who later betrays them to the Nazis; this is not the book's premise (the family's survival is), and the affair reads as a source of guilt and paralysis rather than anything celebrated, so per the reader's own grid it costs only a few points as a condemned subplot rather than triggering a reject. Sustained WWII bleakness is a further mild, expected discount.

A space elevator sustaining the one immune pocket of humanity on a virus-ravaged Earth, with the practical logistics worked out in real detail - food grown on the stations, water and air trucked up from the ground, the balance tipping into anarchy when the elevator falters - the kind of consequence-tracking this reader rewarded in Valka stareho muze 87 and docked Mortal Engines 55 for lacking. Reception is real but uneven ('good, but not great' alongside 'brilliant debut'), and the protagonist, an immune scavenger largely manipulated into the plot by an industrialist, is not clearly established as rootable, so the estimate sits mid-band rather than higher.

A two-volume, multi-author academic synthesis of Russian 20th-century history, described even by its publisher as dense and citation-heavy ('podrobna, plna citatu, vypisu z deniku, vyhlasek'). Reception is explicitly polarized - some readers call it essential, others accuse the authors of factual sloppiness and bias ('polopravdy a lzi', 'autor by si mal overovat fakty') - which undercuts the one thing that could carry a work this dense for this reader: the rigorous examination of what is actually true that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 land, here explicitly disputed by critics. There is no narrative or protagonist to fall back on, so real doubt about whether the intellectual case holds up is enough to exit at C.

Cato and Macro return from campaign wanting an ordinary soldier's life, but factions fighting for power over the empire drag Cato back in. Some personal-life beats here (Cato's son, Macro's attachment to a nanny) give the leads more to want than pure battle, but the engine is still the recurring political-intrigue formula reviewers describe as this series' real formula rather than a single idea worked through, so it sits with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than climbing past the line - I would list axis:ideas under risks. Deep into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A diary kept between ages ten and fourteen through Terezin and Auschwitz, later expanded with retrospectively written camp sections and a present-day interview layer once Weiss reclaimed the notebooks her uncle hid in a wall. This is the same genre and shape as this reader's one recorded testimony DNF - The Diary of a Young Girl, abandoned at 40 specifically because 'a child's inner life' did not work, with the life-phase rule already docking it before the DNF. The retrospective editing and added adult interview here give more structure and hindsight than Anne Frank's raw diary, which is why this sits above that floor rather than at it, but the core entries remain a child's real-time perspective for most of the book's length - reviewers describe 'penetrating' but still child's-eye observations - so the same mechanism applies. Single first-person narrator, chronological, no confusing opening, and no occult, detective or sexual-plot content.

t: Divka v podivne zemi (Girl in a Strange Land)
why: Teenage Sophia is raised in an isolated valley community that teaches her the outside world is a warzone run by 'Satan's powers'; when a friend flees over the mountains she follows and finds not a battlefield but an advanced, seemingly perfect society, forcing her to question whether her whole upbringing was a lie. That is a real, statable idea - a community controlling its members through a fabricated outside threat - in the vein of the isolated-society reveal this reader has seen work only partway (Divergent 58, whose premise 'collapses under thought'). I found nothing establishing how rigorously the reveal and its consequences are worked out beyond marketing copy calling it a 'suspenseful future-thriller with depth' touching virtual reality and gaming-addiction themes, so I cannot say the idea clearly holds up under scrutiny. Exiting at the default C-low band on that doubt rather than spending further to confirm it either way.

A sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 13 points from book one's 83 to 70 across its sequels, and Catching Fire dropped from 89 to 83 largely because the follow-up premise felt like more of the same rather than a fresh idea. The same worldbuilding (stepping between parallel Earths) already carries a real but contested idea, and reviews of the series already flag meandering pacing as the weak point rather than the concept itself, so a continuation with humanity now spread across many worlds and 'a growing number of critical situations' looks likely to lean further on that same density problem without a comparably strong new idea to offset it.

The core idea is real and worked through in places: a simple stepping device (no cost, no exotic tech, just wiring and a potato) opens an effectively infinite chain of uninhabited parallel Earths, and the book follows the concrete second-order consequences - who controls access, how a species reacts to an open frontier, a spacefaring nation like Kenya taking the lead instead of the US. That is the same kind of thought-out premise the log rewards in Project Hail Mary 92 and Valka stareho muze (Old Man's War) 87. But reviewers repeatedly flag exactly the two things this reader weighs most: the near-omnipotent AI companion Lobsang is widely described as unlikeable and over-explaining rather than someone to root for, and several reviews call the plot meandering with little drive ('a book that went everywhere', 'a slog'), which is the density penalty the reader applies to thin story spread over pages. Leaning on the idea rather than on worldbuilding execution, since reception of the execution itself is split.

Szmaglewska's account of nearly three years as a political prisoner at Auschwitz-Birkenau, written immediately after the war and later entered as evidence at the Nuremberg tribunal. Its examination of what actually happened is as thorough as any testimony in this genre, but its distinguishing choice - writing as 'the prisoner' or 'a prisoner' rather than 'I,' deliberately distancing the account from a single voice to represent hundreds of thousands - cuts against the personal first-person interiority that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 and Son of Hamas to 75, so it is graded a step below those. The task line's 'sex' signal did not turn up any sexual content as a plot element in any source found - the brutality described (hunger, typhus, SS violence) is general camp conditions, not a sexual-content axis hit. No occult, detective or infidelity content; a real-world documentary account.

A biographically-toned account of the author's life from the 1950s to the present against Czechoslovakia's political upheavals. Reception is genuinely split - one reader calls it well-written with real perspective on both political and personal turbulence, but others describe it as unnecessarily long to justify surviving under every regime, and as the confession of a self-pitying man of his age. That is the opposite of what the memoir form needs to earn here: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus scored 91 for genuinely examining what is plausible and true, while The Diary of a Young Girl scored 40 as the counter-example of a first-person account that did not work. The self-justifying framing critics describe reads closer to the second case.

t: Hora v mori (The Mountain in the Sea)
