why: A biologist studies a newly discovered hyper-intelligent octopus species on a corporation-sealed archipelago, alongside a storyline about an AI-crewed fishing vessel and an android built for corporate labor - the book follows the consequences of non-human and machine intelligence with real rigor, winning the Locus Award and reaching the Nebula, Clarke and Bradbury shortlists, the exact kind of worked-through idea this reader rewards in Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87. No occult content in any source. What keeps it off the very top: the prose is repeatedly called dense and demanding, and one reviewer reports a group read that turned to near-universal dislike over pacing, which is the axis:density risk this reader's profile names as the most common reason a competent book stalls; the three interleaved threads (biologist, AI vessel, android) also carry an axis:multi-pov risk I have not confirmed resolves cleanly.

A literary love triangle built almost entirely on what its three leads want and why - Madeleine's reading of Barthes as a model for her own romantic life, Mitchell's religious searching in Calcutta, Leonard's mania - the axis that tops this reader's whole log (Pycha a predsudek 75, Mockingjay 91). It also runs its own explicit thesis about whether the marriage-plot novel can still work in a secular, psychiatrically medicated modern world, a real idea rather than just events. No affair occurs inside the marriage - Leonard's illness and the couple's incompatibility drive the breakup, and Mitchell's feelings only resurface once the marriage is already ending - so the infidelity axis was examined but does not fire, even as a subplot. The one real risk is sustained bleakness from Leonard's mental-illness arc, a mild discount on this reader's own scale.

Cato and Macro are pulled from Britain to Hispania to put down resistance to Roman rule. Same repeating shape reviewers note across this series - camaraderie and a new-posting/new-antagonist formula, not a single explored premise - so this sits with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. Deep into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

In an alternate 1923 London ruled by a human-dragon Peace Agreement and rigid class lines, a rule-following translation student accidentally sparks a civil war, loses her parents to arrest, and takes a wartime code-breaking job to save her family. A Czech reviewer notes the book deliberately declines to let readers root for humans or dragons alone, asking who the real monster is - the dragon or the system exploiting it - which is a genuine idea about structural exploitation, not just a dragon skin on a war story, and Viv is driven by love for her sister rather than by plot mechanics, both traits this reader rewards. Dragons here are a natural sentient species bound by treaty and code-systems, not a magic tradition, so occult does not apply. It is a NYT/Sunday Times bestseller, which raises confidence this clears the line, but I have not verified how the human-dragon treaty's rules hold up under the book's own logic, so I keep worldbuilding as a risk rather than a lean.

A widowed, unemployed father whose son stopped speaking after watching his mother die takes a job as a park street performer in a tattered panda costume - and, without revealing who he is, becomes the one figure who can reach his own withdrawn son. That is a specific, concrete premise (indirect intimacy through disguise) carried through to its emotional payoff, not just a hook - the same shape of premise-worked-through this reader responds to, driven entirely by what the father wants (to reach his son) and why. Reviewers frame it as comedy and grief working together rather than grief alone ("a comedy of sadness and dancing bears"), which argues against it reading as sustained bleakness; still discounted mildly for the underlying dead-wife, mute-child material.

t: Klic k Rebece (The Key to Rebecca)
why: The plotting is well regarded - a tense 1942 Cairo spy-hunt built on a real historical spy and a genuinely clever code gimmick - so this is not a sex-plot reject, the engine of the book is finding the German agent before Rommel breaks through. But multiple independent reviews describe recurring, explicit and crudely-handled sexual content that goes well beyond a subplot: one reader called it 'way too perverted', another singles out a scene that is 'essentially rape' which the book treats as just one more beat, and a third flags a cast built partly around an 'Evil Bisexual' sidekick trope. That hits all three of the reader's sexual-content dimensions at once - volume, explicitness and crudeness - which the log treats as compounding (Ready Player One 55 was sunk mainly by volume alone; this has more going against it than that). One reviewer adds that the handling makes it 'hard to keep rooting for' the characters, which is a direct hit on the axis the reader weighs above almost everything else.

Dual-POV novel following two young men who grew up together in Scottish foster care and have since drifted apart, each trying to rebuild trust and a sense of belonging. Reviewers single out exactly the axis this reader weighs most after motives: distinct voice, calling out that Finlay's chapters carry medical terminology from his nursing training while Banjo's reflect dissociation through fragmented sentence structure - genuine character-differentiation, not just alternating names. Both leads are described as sympathetically drawn ("will make you want to scream at the injustices"), and the book won the 2025 Carnegie Medal plus the Branford Boase Award, indicating unusually strong craft for a debut. Risk is real: content includes abuse, violence and a suicide attempt, which is sustained bleakness this reader discounts mildly rather than rejects; both leads are young adults, a small standard pushback.

A bilingual Czech/English graded reader (A2/B1 level) built around a debut author's simple K-drama-inspired romance and time-travel plot - a young artist inherits a Korean cottage tied to a deck of fortune-telling cards and a temple legend. No idea beyond genre wish-fulfillment romance is nameable, and the language-learner form is explicitly simplified for intermediate readers rather than written for a native adult audience, so it settles at the low band without needing to go further. A deck of fortune cards and a legend-guarding temple are central to the plot, which would normally be worth checking against the occult filter (divination), but since the book already lands below 68 on form and lack of idea alone, that question is left unexamined.

t: Kobky pod Potalou (Les caves du Potala)
why: Set in the Potala Palace in 1968, an old Buddhist painter held prisoner by fanaticized Red Guards recalls his life in sacred art while they destroy everything around him. The theme - beauty and devotion annihilated by ideological fanaticism - is real, but readers report the book alternates documentary passages, heavy footnotes and novelistic scenes so often that, in one reader's words, 'the alternation between these approaches broke up the text too much' and 'readers don't form a real connection to any character.' One reviewer who has read all of Dai Sijie's novels called this his least interesting. That is exactly the kind of digression-heavy, thin-connection pattern this reader's density axis penalizes, so it exits here rather than going on. Occult stays unexamined at this exit - the plot references a search for a reincarnated tulku, which would need a specific check for whether it is enacted on the page rather than recalled as backstory, and that question is left open since nothing under 68 is proposed either way.

A revised omnibus of a classic Czech comic strip serial originally run in ABC magazine, described by reviewers as a Czech cultural landmark 'comparable only to Rychle sipy'. Every review found focuses on the hand-inked artwork and the comic's historical significance - none describes a story idea, just episodic pulp adventure across two linked trilogies about a small god-like figure and his travels. That is a short, suspended-test comic form with no idea I can point to, so it lands in the low C-band rather than the default one.

Two veteran soldiers return to a Britain worn down by Caratacus's continued resistance - the same war-and-politics engine as the rest of the series, which reviewers describe as carried by the leads' camaraderie inside a repeating formula rather than a single worked idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

The external plot is a giant-mantis apocalypse, not a sexual relationship, so this clears the premise-level filter, but reviewers consistently describe the sexual content as constant and crude throughout - 'always circling back to the main theme,' an obsessive genital fixation shared by multiple characters, one graphic scene, and vulgarity flagged by nearly every reviewer found. That is high on all three graded dimensions at once (volume, explicitness, crudeness), the same compounding that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 on volume alone, worsened here by the crudeness that cost Artemis 69. The book does carry a real idea - reviewers credit it with 'mature insights into our relationship with truth and established history' and a sensitively handled account of a teen boy's bisexuality - which keeps this off the bare C-low floor, but the sexual-content axis caps it near the bottom of the graded range regardless.

A former gladiator who led a slave revolt is on the run, and Cato and Macro have personal scores to settle as well as orders to stop him - a manhunt plot that gives the leads a concrete want, but still runs on this series' recurring formula that reviewers describe as camaraderie over a worked-out premise. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. It is well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

t: Leonard a Hladovy Paul (Leonard and Hungry Paul)
why: Two ordinary single men in their thirties - an encyclopedia writer and a substitute postman - move through quiet, low-stakes days (a wedding, a slogan-writing contest, a tentative romance) with almost no external plot pressure; reviewers explicitly note the book treats its characters' happiness as never in doubt and spends its attention on kindness and small resolutions instead of conflict. That is nearly pure motives-and-interiority with almost nothing happening, which is this reader's most-rewarded axis when it is done well - and Saturnin 78 is the log's proof that a book can score well in the A band on voice and character alone, with no idea being worked out, so the absence of a single big idea here is not automatically disqualifying the way it would be for a thinner book. Real risk: there genuinely isn't a nameable idea beyond "ordinary kindness matters," and one reviewer flags an early section as info-dumping and a subplot romance that "didn't quite work" - both point toward this landing nearer the middle of what strong character work alone can earn rather than higher.

An alternate-history series diverging when an 1853 assassination attempt on Emperor Franz Josef I succeeds (in reality it failed), putting his brother Maximilian on the throne instead; this entry follows him defeating France and Italy in the north and now facing pressure from Prussia. Czech reader reviews split on craft: one praises how well it carries complex historical, military and political ideas, but another flags a rushed feel with passages copied word-for-word from Wikipedia in the historical epilogue, and calls the alternate economic-political vision confusing - the kind of declared-but-not-worked-out system the log docks under worldbuilding, similar in kind to what sank Mortal Engines and Divergent. The author's own monarchist politics reportedly dominate the fiction here, which raises real doubt the alternate-history idea is examined rather than simply asserted.

Jam, a selectively-nonverbal girl, pulls a monster called Pet out of her mother's painting and must use it to root out a real abuser hiding inside a trusted family - the book's actual argument is that danger comes from people a community refuses to see as dangerous, a nameable idea in the register that earns points on axis:ideas, and Jam is proactive and worth rooting for rather than merely acted upon. Pet itself is an invented creature born of blood and paint, not drawn from any real-world occult tradition, and no rite is enacted on the page, so it clears the occult test cleanly. The hunt-the-hidden-monster structure is investigation-shaped, which is a flag rather than a filter since the book's satisfaction is moral (who will admit the truth), not whodunit. Kept out of the 80s because it is squarely YA in register and the abuse the plot turns on is handled allegorically rather than examined in the depth the top of this log rewards.

Quinn's debut follows the Boyle family - Declan, Sinead, and their children Owen and Issie - across seven snapshot chapters from 1959 to 2002, each built around what one family member wants: Declan's ambition against his sense of duty, Sinead wondering whether she is allowed ambitions at all in postwar Ireland, Issie repeatedly choosing wrong. That is exactly the axis this reader responds to most - motives over action - and the Irish Times review confirms shifts between perspectives handled 'with empathetic ease' rather than a confusing multi-thread opening. No fantasy or invented-magic content anywhere in the synopsis or reviews, so the occult question closes cleanly. Set below the top of the range because four generations across seven chapters is a lot of ground for one book to cover without diluting any single throughline - Les Miserables settled at 71 for similar breadth with digressions, and this saga adds Cold-War-Europe detours (East Germany, Berlin, Budapest) on top of the family thread.

t: Mnoho smrti Laily Starr (The Many Deaths of Laila Starr)
why: Death, personified and fired from her post the moment a baby is born who will discover immortality, is reincarnated as a mortal woman and repeatedly dies and returns while deciding whether to kill the child. Reviewers consistently single out a real, nameable idea - that death gives life its shape and is not simply a thing to dread - worked through several short, self-contained cycles rather than just asserted, which is what this reader's short-idea-driven allowance is for. Death appears here as a literary personification narrated by a god of life, the device Discworld and Sandman also use, not a rite of witchcraft, divination or prayer enacted by any mortal character on the page, so it does not trip occult. One review found the dialogue not always intentional and some characters underexplained, which I read as a risk to the character axis rather than to the central idea.

A young apprentice Moth Keeper tends the moths that pollinate her nocturnal desert village's sacred tree, and struggles with the loneliness of nights alone away from her friends. Reviews are warm but consistently note this is a lighter, thinner entry next to the same author's other cozy graphic novels, with worldbuilding and character development both called out as shallower than usual - it is a gentle children's graphic novel about duty and community with no idea beyond that, close to the picture-book end of the childrens axis this reader has graded lowest. The Moon-Spirit's gift is an invented village tradition tended as a duty rather than worshipped with any rite, so it clears occult.

A coming-of-age novel narrated by a girl, Eliska, growing into adolescence while the adults and institutions meant to protect her repeatedly fail her. Reader reviews describe it as intense and provocative rather than plot-driven ('you'll want to say enough, leave her alone'), but no reviewer names an idea beyond the general premise of institutional failure, and nothing suggests it is worked through the way Labyrint sveta 70 or Promena 58 work their premises through to a real conclusion - the gap that stalls a competent book in the 60s per the reader's own pattern. Embedded chapters follow two unrelated timeless beings (Theodora, Estrella) seeking harmony with nature, which risks a second thread competing for attention early on rather than one concrete starting situation. Exiting at C on doubt about the idea rather than paying for a fuller read, per the base rate that C is usually right.

The novel runs on want - Catherine's divided passion and Heathcliff's consuming need for revenge are the axis this reader rewards most - but Heathcliff is also the reader's clearest failure mode: his slow curdling into cruelty, including manipulating the next generation to seize their inheritance, makes him hard to root for through much of the book, echoing the 22-point gap this reader's own log records between a rootable and an unrootable lead sharing one world. Catherine's unresolved passion for Heathcliff after marrying Edgar Linton was examined - scholars read it as adulterous longing - but it plays as a condemned subplot inside a larger revenge story, not the premise, and ends in mutual destruction rather than anything approving. Sustained bleakness across two generations is a further mild discount.

t: Nadeje umira posledni (Hope Is the Last to Die)
why: Birenbaum's account of survival through the Warsaw ghetto and Majdanek, Auschwitz, Ravensbruck and Neustadt-Glewe, written roughly two decades later as an adult rather than in real time as a child. That retrospective distance is the key difference from Anne Frank's diary, which this reader DNF'd specifically because a child's real-time inner life 'did not work' - here the account is a considered adult retrospective examining what happened and why, the same quality that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 and Son of Hamas to 75. A review source is candid that the prose itself is not sophisticated - occasionally unstructured, uneven in its descriptive passages - which caps the estimate below those two anchors rather than at them. Bleakness is a real but mild cost here per this reader's own rule, and there is no occult, detective or sexual-plot content in a straightforward survival memoir.

t: Nebe v plamenech (The Sky on Fire)
why: Anahrod, a survivalist raised outside dragon-ruled society, is pulled into a heist against a hostile dragon regent's hoard - reviewers consistently single out the worldbuilding (a society genuinely reorganised around dragon power) and a protagonist whose growth is tracked closely, which is the combination this reader rewards. The dragons' magic is innate to the species rather than drawn from any real-world occult tradition, and no rite is enacted on the page, so it clears occult cleanly. It does not clear as high as the log's worldbuilding leaders because of the sexual content: several reviewers flag an explicit late-book scene and an earlier group encounter as tonally inconsistent with the plot around them, which reads as the crudeness penalty this reader applies even at moderate volume, distinct from Old Man's War 87's single understated chapter.

Teenage Aislinn, who has always seen invisible faeries, is pursued by the Summer King seeking his queen. Reception is split, but the specific complaint that recurs is thin characterization - one reviewer's read is that 'characters range from calm to emotionally volatile but all sound the same' and that the prose is 'terrible at actually invoking emotion,' leaning on a Dark Court gimmick (tasting emotion) rather than earning it on the page. That is a direct hit on the axis this reader weighs above worldbuilding - a protagonist who is both interesting and worth rooting for - and nothing in the premise (a hidden faerie court, a forced-choice romance) offers a distinct idea beyond genre furniture. Fae mythology here reads as invented urban-fantasy court politics (Summer/Dark Courts, glamour, the Sight) rather than real-world witchcraft, seance or prayer to real deities, so it is not disqualifying on sourcing grounds, though whether any rite is enacted on the page was not specifically confirmed and stays unexamined at this exit.

Grace, mid-divorce and grieving, walks out of stalled traffic and across London to reach her estranged teenage daughter's birthday. The separation from her husband turns out to be grief-driven (their younger daughter died), not an affair, so no hard filter fires. But the idea on offer is a familiar one - midlife grief and a fractured mother-daughter bond - worked through a single frantic day rather than examined from a genuinely new angle, and Publishers Weekly's own verdict is that 'the plot can feel undercooked' even while praising the grief writing. I would list axis:ideas under risks if this went further, so it exits here instead. One search spent beyond the one-source budget to confirm the separation was not an affair, since that determination gates the whole reject/grade decision.

A year into the invasion of Britain, the war chief Caratacus keeps harassing the legions while Claudius needs a decisive win to secure his rule back in Rome - the same war-and-politics engine that runs through this series, which reviewers say is carried by the Cato-Macro bond and a repeating formula rather than one explored idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. It is well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Same authors and same action-novella format as this record's Roman Arena entry, examined for this batch: a young captive proving himself among a pirate crew is the kind of forced-survival premise Ranger's Apprentice 74 runs on, but the critical review found for the authors' companion series names one-dimensional villains and thin plotting as recurring weaknesses of the format - exactly the axis:ideas doubt this gate exists to catch. The cruel initiation rite the annotation describes is a hazing/trial-by-combat scene, not a religious or magical practice, so it does not touch the occult filter. Set at the same C-low default band as this author pairing's other entry, absent book-specific reviews to argue otherwise.

A licensed game-tie-in comic explicitly aimed at young children - parent reviewers cite kids aged 6-8 as the target audience, and content guides describe only cartoon-style slapstick with no romantic content. Reviews praise the humor and artwork but name no idea beyond silly time-travel zombie-fighting antics - there is no idea to carry the way Flowers-for-Algernon-style short fiction needs one, so the short-idea-driven suspension does not rescue it and it lands with the other picture-book-tier children's works in this log's lowest band, below Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67. The zombies are a cartoonish game-fantasy trope with no ritual or invocation depicted, so the occult filter is clear.

Testimony/memoir, graded on whether it examines what is actually true - the axis behind the gap between Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40. This is another entry in the same real-life account: the husband's declining health, again central here, is one of the threads a 2025 investigation cast doubt on, alongside the stated reason the couple lost their original home (reported to follow accusations she stole from an employer) and undisclosed property ownership. Those are exactly the claims this form is rewarded for getting right, and public reporting disputes several load-bearing ones, so I doubt the true-examination axis holds up.

Testimony/memoir, and this reader grades the form on whether it examines what is actually true - the axis that separates Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 from The Diary of a Young Girl 40. A 2025 investigative report found the author's account of losing her home, told here as a bad business investment, actually followed accusations that she stole tens of thousands of pounds from an employer; that the couple owned a second house in France while claiming homelessness; that the family used assumed names; and that medical experts have questioned the husband's terminal diagnosis, one of the book's central threads. These are exactly the claims the reader's most-valued memoir axis rewards when they hold up, and public reporting now disputes several of the load-bearing ones, so I doubt the true-examination axis holds up here.

BLOCKED 2026-08-31 by inheritance. Volumes one and two of this same sequence are rejected on the occult filter - a sword-consecration blood sacrifice and a seer's divination, both narrated as they happen - and the sequence is one continuous first-person narration, so no later volume is reachable without them. This is the reader's rule applied outside the author it was raised about, and it is the largest single instance on the shelf: eight live estimates sat in the queue behind two hard-excluded volumes. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: Uhtred is narrated in first person throughout the series and this entry is reviewed as one of its strongest for character - a poignant father-son strand (disowning his Christian-convert son) layered onto his drive to reclaim Bebbanburg, the same want-and-why focus that Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. Reviewers also credit it with a real idea worked through rather than just asserted: Cornwell using the pagan-versus-Christian conflict to examine why and how a pagan land actually became Christian, which is closer to the nameable-idea bar than a generic theme. No enacted rite surfaces in reviews of this entry - the religious material is Uhtred's ongoing belief and rivalry with the Church, not a magic system - so the occult filter does not fire here on the evidence found (unlike Pale Horseman, examined for this same series, where an on-page divination scene is described). Set above Count of Monte Cristo 75's adventure-momentum baseline given the added idea layer, docked slightly for being deep into a long-running series.

An anonymous postcard naming four family members killed at Auschwitz sends Anne Berest to reconstruct her great-grandparents' flight from Russia through Latvia, Palestine and Paris to their deaths, then, fifteen years later, to investigate who sent the card. Reviewers single out its focus on survivors' aftermath and guilt as unusual for Holocaust literature, and the family research reads as a true account rather than invention - Berest calls it 'a true novel.' That combination of examining what actually happened and giving insight into how antisemitism was administratively enforced under Vichy is the same case that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91, though this account is once removed - a granddaughter's investigation rather than a survivor's direct voice - which is why the estimate sits below that anchor rather than at it. The investigation into the postcard's sender (private detective, graphologist) is a genuine mystery-shaped subplot inside an otherwise eligible family history, not the book's premise, so it is flagged under axis:detective rather than rejected. No occult, infidelity-as-premise or sexual-plot content surfaced in any review. Confidence is medium rather than high because only one search was run, even though it returned unusually detailed structural and reception information for a well-covered Goncourt-winning bestseller.

A 24-hour ticking-clock thriller - Ballista alone in Rome racing to stop an assassination before the emperor leaves the Colosseum - built explicitly in the Jack Reacher/24 mode, which reads as pure momentum with little of the motive-driven interiority the log rewards most (Speaker for the Dead's 90, Mockingjay's 91). One reviewer flags the opening physical ordeal as implausible survival even by the author's own admission - a version of the ability-given-rather-than-earned problem that helped hold Divergent's Mary-Sue-style lead to 58. Reads as competent action-thriller filler rather than a book with a strong positive case beyond pace.

t: Posledni ukol Mabel Beaumontove (The Last List of Mabel Beaumont)
why: The task line flags detective, but on checking this is a reunion quest, not a whodunit: a newly widowed 86-year-old follows her late husband's note ("Find D") to track down a childhood best friend she lost touch with sixty years ago, meeting an intergenerational community of women along the way. Not the whodunit satisfaction the detective filter targets. Checked the love story too: Mabel's youthful love for Dot predates her marriage to Arthur and is the reason she chose a conventional marriage under 1950s social pressure - that is backstory, not an affair conducted during the marriage, so it does not touch the infidelity filter either. What is left is a pleasant, competently reviewed grief-and-friendship novel without a strong idea to hold onto - one review calls the central twist predictable and sums the book up as "perfectly pleasant but not memorable," which is exactly the doubt-the-idea-holds-up test this ladder uses to exit here.

A grain shortage and a conspiracy calling itself the Liberators threaten Emperor Claudius in a Rome where betrayal is everywhere - palace-intrigue plotting on the same recurring engine as the rest of the series, which reviewers describe as carried by the leads' friendship inside a formula rather than a single worked idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A Depression-era reporter stages a photograph of children 'for sale' for his career, and the staged lie's real consequences - a desperate mother actually selling her own children after a misdiagnosis - is a nameable idea about the cost of a media fabrication, the kind of premise-worked-into-consequences the reader responds to. But reviews describe the back half fanning out into an orphanage plot, a gangster, a family raid and a search for the family, with one reviewer unsure if it wanted to be historical fiction or mystery, and multiple subplots described as present but shallow. The search for the sold children is a subplot within a broader story, not the book's whole satisfaction, so it is a flag rather than a detective-filter veto.

The world's history has been shattered and reassembled into a patchwork of eras, and this closing entry follows the struggle between a 1900-era British Empire and a Roman Empire led by the returning heroine to control the new Europe that results. Czech reader reception is largely positive and the premise - fragments of history colliding rather than just one alternate timeline - is the kind of consequence-worked idea this reader responds to. It is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, and one detailed review here specifically felt the concept's potential was left unexploited, since the fractured-timeline map implied a wider world than the book actually uses, plus a slower, more political final act that some readers found dragged. That combination - a strong idea only partly cashed in, on a closing volume - keeps this under the line rather than at the level the opening premise alone would suggest.

This is a comic (graphic novel), a short-form work where the character/emotion rules are suspended rather than earned, so the number rests on whether there is an idea to name. Reception is split but the specific complaints line up: The Comics Journal argues the book never shows the regime's actual effects on ordinary people, reducing the plot and characters to 'empty signifiers'; a Goodreads reader found 'no plot point unexpected and no investment in the characters'; another review calls it 'a rather standard rebels versus evil empire storyline'. Praise centers almost entirely on the art rather than the story. Exiting at C rather than researching further: this is a doubt about whether an idea holds up, which is exactly the gate 4 test. Occult status is left unexamined per the ladder rule, despite reviewer mentions of 'ancient mysticism' and grotesque religious ritual imagery tied to the antagonist theocracy - that is why axis:occult stays in deps for a later look if this axis is ever revisited.

Part of an international children's educational comic series recreating prehistoric animal life from the fossil record; this volume follows a Pteranodon fishing and avoiding predators. It is a short, picture-book-style factual recreation for young children rather than a story with a premise to work out - the closest comparison in this log is a picture book, which the reader's own rules place in the 30s-40s. There is a survival narrative here rather than pure captioned facts, so I am not going as low as a bare picture book, but there is no idea beyond that survival framing to lean on.

Set on the eve of the 1956 Hungarian revolution: Csilla's parents were executed by the secret police as Zionist traitors, and she has to decide whether to flee or demand the injustice be acknowledged now that they've been posthumously exonerated. That is a real, worked idea - what it costs to be seen after your family has been erased - carried by a protagonist reviewers repeatedly call worth rooting for. Checked the occult question directly: the magic is a personified river and an angel-of-death character drawing loosely on Jewish folklore (a golem, Azriel), but the one described working scene is Csilla sinking a newspaper into the river and pulling out a flame that won't go out, with a murmured word and a whispered reply - closer to invented magic-realism using folkloric vocabulary as flavor than to an enacted rite of real-world occultism (no invocation, no priesthood, no prayer to a deity). Passing this narrowly, not confidently. Risk: several reviewers found the magic's mechanics genuinely unclear ("it whispers to her, it turns to stone, silver... I just don't understand"), and pacing is criticized as slow to start with too much crammed into the ending.

A charity-run children's book (catalogued under 'publikace pro deti') built around four young friends whose parents work in the rescue services, mixing prevention-education vignettes - bullying, a rafting accident, peer pressure to drink - with retold stories of lesser-known WWII resistance figures. There is no larger idea beyond the safety-education message itself, and no professional literary reception exists to argue otherwise; it reads closer to the picture-book end of the reader's own children's-book scale than to Ranger's Apprentice 74 or Narnia 67, both of which at least carry a continuous adventure plot.

Phoebe watches her friends' bodies corrode into an unexplained body-horror transformation in a dying 1980 Cleveland neighborhood - a real idea (girls' bodies as metaphor for a town and its expectations collapsing), the kind of nameable premise the reader wants. But it is never mechanically explained, and reviewers split hard on whether that pays off: some call the ambiguity the book's real strength, others call the transformation's own description 'vague and unsatisfying' and want the passive Phoebe to 'actually do something to move the plot' - the same passive-protagonist problem that held Oliver Twist to 57, acted upon rather than wanting anything. Two sources were spent settling this, one over the one-source C-low budget.

Macro leaves the legion to help his mother run an inn and manage a veteran's land grant - a quieter, more personal entry than most of the series, which is a point in favour of motive over pure action. Even so, it is still one installment of a series whose reviewers describe the draw as the leads' friendship inside a repeating formula rather than a single worked idea, so it sits with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than climbing past the line; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Cato and Macro escort a client king back to his throne in Armenia, a mission that is really about great-power maneuvering between Rome and Parthia rather than about the two leads' own wants. Same shape as the other entries in this series: reviewers describe the appeal as the leads' friendship carrying a repeating political-intrigue formula, not a single explored idea, so this lands with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 rather than with anything idea-driven in this reader's log - I would put axis:ideas under risks. It is also deep into a long series, and this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A Czech YA original set in a world where magic is an ordinary part of daily life; four girls near their sixteenth birthdays investigate what really happens at the coming-of-age Rite that a mysterious Judge presides over. A reader review describes the book as dragging until the Rite itself finally plays out near the end, and another praises it mainly for playing genre cliches for laughs - between them, no source names an idea worth carrying beyond a coming-of-age mystery-box. This exits on that doubt at one source over budget (a second was needed to locate any review at all), so axis:occult is left unexamined per the C-low rule - the magic and the Rite read as an invented system from the synopses available, not confirmed drawn from real-world practice, and that status should be checked before this title is ever proposed to read.

A comic Czech family chronicle about a household of children and dogs living through renovation mishaps and small dramas, carried by voice and an ensemble of distinct characters rather than by any idea worked out - the same shape as Saturnin 78, which 'scores in the A band on voice and character rather than on any idea worked out, so the humour register carries no penalty here.' Reader reception is consistently warm (83% rating, repeat readers), but nothing in it suggests the sharper wit or lasting reputation Saturnin earned, so the estimate sits a notch under it.

t: Sadako Sasaki a tisic papirovych jerabu (The Complete Story of Sadako Sasaki and the Thousand Paper Cranes)
why: Written by Sadako's own older brother with a co-author, explicitly to correct the contradictory, incomplete versions that had circulated - the same thing that earns points for Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 in this log: an insider genuinely examining what actually happened and giving real understanding of a group's experience (here, Japanese A-bomb survivors and the long tail of radiation sickness). Unlike the Diary of a Young Girl 40, this is not a raw child's own voice but an adult retrospective account, which is the structural feature that separates the memoirs that worked from the one that didn't in this log. Marketed and formatted as a middle-reader biography with a paper-crane craft tutorial at the back, which pulls toward the children's-book register this reader discounts mildly (Male zeny 79 shows that discount has a real ceiling, not a floor). Subject matter - a child dying of leukemia from wartime radiation exposure - is sustained bleakness, discounted the same mild way as elsewhere in the log.

Ten loosely linked stories, washed ashore as ten pipes, each following a different owner across Tsarist Russia, Siberia, pre-war Berlin and South Africa, with recurring figures (a Sand Woman, Amundsen, Rasputin) threading between them. That recurrence is a structural device, not a single premise whose consequences are worked out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on the way a genuine idea-driven short work would need - the same gap that keeps most literary short-story collections under the line in this ladder. Czech reader reception is split ("provazanost postav mne uchvatila" against "zapletky povrchni, nekdy i hloupe"), which reads as competent craft without a governing idea rather than either a standout or a failure.

Reviews describe Sharpe as the reader's kind of lead: a working-class outsider who rises on competence, with a clear code (right and wrong times to kill, elastic honesty toward strangers only) rather than being merely likeable - the kind of want-driven characterization Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. This entry adds a real deduction: Sharpe's wife Jane, still married to him, takes his fortune and falls for Lord Rossendale while hoping Sharpe dies abroad - a marriage betrayal, but one thread among the treasury-theft chase and Sharpe's own arc toward Lucille, not the engine of the book (remove it and the revenge plot against Ducos still stands), so it grades rather than vetoes: a subplot, condemned in its framing (Jane is shown as mercenary, not sympathetic), costing a few points per the axis. The theft-and-frame plot is investigation-shaped but the culprit (Ducos) is known to Sharpe almost immediately, so it reads as a revenge chase, not a whodunit. Landed near Quo Vadis 66 and under Count of Monte Cristo 75 - similar revenge-adventure momentum but without Monte Cristo's structural tightness, and reader reviews of this specific entry call it plot-wise the weakest of the series even while praising the character work.

Three childhood friends each want something different and act on it as fascism and the Nazi occupation close in on Rome - Elisabetta chasing authorship, Marco and Sandro rivals for her heart while their families are pulled toward collaboration or persecution. That is the motive-driven engine that tops the log in Pride and Prejudice's 75 and Mockingjay's 91. Reviews split hard on whether it pays off: some praise 'rich character development,' others call the trio two-dimensional and fault the author for moving characters to where the plot needs them without earning it - a real risk next to a book like Golden Son, where the trio's distinctiveness (Darrow, Sevro, Mustang each thinking and wanting differently) was singled out as a strength. Grounded in a real, well-researched historical event (the 1943 Rome roundup), which the reader responds to when a book actually examines what happened.

t: Sloup do nebe (Pillar to the Sky)
why: A scientist and engineer fight political and financial obstacles to build a working space elevator as a real solution to an energy and water crisis - the premise is worked through with actual engineering consequences, the same trait that carries Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87. No occult (hard SF, no magic system at all) and no detective, infidelity or sex-plot in any source found. What holds it down from that band: reviewers repeatedly flag slow, repetitive pacing and a genuinely messy climax chapter, which reads as the axis:density penalty this reader applies to a thin story stretched long, not present in the higher comparators.

The Iceni queen is captured and several British tribes rise up together, giving Cato and Macro their hardest fight yet - a straightforward escalation of the series' recurring war-and-politics formula, which reviewers describe as carried by the leads' friendship rather than a single worked idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log, not with anything idea-driven; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Deep into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Ben, a bait-shop worker plagued by inexplicable trivia knowledge he can't explain, is kidnapped by an alien bounty hunter who reveals Ben is a 'Stringer' carrying fragments of other lives, and dragged into a hunt across alien factions. Reviewers repeatedly single out the friendship between Ben and his best friend Patton as the book's real emotional core - genuine warmth and stakes when the pair are captured together - which matches this reader's preference for motive-driven pages over pure action, in the comic-SF register that made Hitchhiker's Guide 83 work. The reincarnated-knowledge premise is followed through to an actual answer rather than left as a gimmick. Humor leans on gross-out and crude jokes throughout, which several reviewers call polarizing, but that is a register objection this reader does not penalize, distinct from sexual content, which does not feature here.

A schizophrenic teenager, Will, walks out of a psychiatric hospital into the New York subway, driven by a delusional conviction that he can stop global warming by losing his virginity to a girl he once hurt - almost entirely page time on what he wants and why, which is the axis this reader responds to most. Reviewers with clinical familiarity single out how thoroughly the psychosis itself is researched and internally consistent, not just colorfully written. A detective and Will's mother pursue him in parallel chapters, functioning as an investigation-shaped subplot rather than the book's core satisfaction - it is not a whodunit, and critics actually fault the mystery beat (Violet's secret) for being guessable long before the detective catches up, which argues against reading this as detective/mystery. Two real risks: Will has a violent past against the girl he's chasing, which could make him hard to root for despite the illness framing (the log's clearest parallel for an unrootable-but-sympathetically-drawn lead is Promena 58, where a passive rather than dangerous lead still cost points); and the claustrophobic subway setting and psychiatric subject matter are sustained bleakness, which this reader discounts mildly rather than rejects.

A licensed Marvel/Disney tie-in comic continuing established Star Wars film continuity right after Return of the Jedi, split into three short vignettes for Luke, Han and Leia. Reviews describe it as competently setting up franchise-familiar threats (mercenaries, an underworld mystery, a new political alliance) rather than introducing any standalone idea of its own - it exists to continue the canon, not to work out a premise. As a single comic issue this is also a short, suspended-test form. Han's thread is framed as an investigation ('investigates a deadly underworld mystery'), which is a mystery-shaped subplot inside one of three vignettes, not the book's whole structure, so it is a flag rather than a detective-filter veto.

A long-running Czech pulp SF series: humanity has fought aliens for decades from a ring of orbital cities, and agent John Francis Kovar investigates a weapon threatening the wider setting. Nothing in the available material names a distinguishing idea beyond that generic decades-long-war premise - reader reactions are split between calling it one of the weakest entries ('the aliens don't work, no action, no humor') and praising its internal consistency and tension, with no clear consensus on it standing out. That reads as a competent genre entry rather than one with a nameable idea, landing it at the default C-low band. It is also the twelfth book in a long series, which this log treats as a real but secondary risk on its own (Hitchhikers sequels fell from 83 to 70).

t: Sto roku Lenni a Margot (The One Hundred Years of Lenni and Margot)
why: A terminally ill 17-year-old and an 83-year-old on the same hospital ward decide their combined ages add up to one hundred years, and set out to paint one hundred pictures - one for each year - telling both their life stories. That is a concrete premise carried through to its structural conclusion, the exact shape of book this reader rewards (the same shape, differently applied, that Labyrint sveta 70 hit on). Reviewers consistently describe Lenni herself as the reason it works ("broke through my stony exterior"), and the book is built entirely around companionship rather than solitary suffering, which is the specific thing Project Hail Mary 92 shows this reader rewards on the bleakness axis - Margot is not a device, she is the friendship the book is about. Terminal illness and an approaching death are still sustained bleakness, discounted mildly rather than ignored, and Lenni's age is the standard small life-phase pushback.

t: Strasliva zavrat (When We Cease to Understand the World)
why: Five linked pieces about real 20th-century scientists (Heisenberg, Schrodinger, Grothendieck, Haber, Einstein), blending fact and invention with each successive piece more fictionalized than the last, built around one thesis - that scientific genius and destructive madness are inseparable. It is literary fiction structured as a short-story collection, the pattern this reader's log shows landing under 68 far more often than not even when the pieces are well reviewed (this one was Booker-shortlisted) - the short-idea-driven suspension removes the character-driven penalty but does not add points on its own, and a linked-story structure has no single protagonist to carry the number instead. No occult content - the subject is real historical physics and mathematics, not magic - so that question closes without needing the budget it would cost elsewhere.

Ten stories by ten different Czech authors, unified only by setting and period (the Sudetenland before the German expulsion), not by a single worked-out premise - by construction this is a themed anthology, not a book pursuing one idea to its consequences. Reviews are consistently positive on authenticity and regional texture (Novinky.cz praises how convincingly ordinary lives are rendered; several contributors grew up in the resettled regions themselves), but that is craft and voice, not the idea-driven case this reader's higher scores lean on.

A historical-fantasy reimagining of Vlad III Dracula as a vampire seeking vengeance against those who arranged his death, entangling the Ottoman and Hungarian courts in 1477. The author is praised for historical detail, but a recurring, specific complaint is exactly the kind of self-consistency break this reader's worldbuilding axis penalizes - a Goodreads reader flags modern metric units ('meters and kilometers in 1477?') inside a book that otherwise leans on painstaking period research, and Czech readers separately describe the pacing as dragging in places and the ending as rushed. Vampirism here is a supernatural-creature premise, not witchcraft, seance or prayer to a real deity, so the occult source test is not in play, though whether any specific rite is depicted was not separately confirmed and stays unexamined at this exit.

t: Tajemstvi modrych tresni (A Fistful of Cherries)
why: A post-apocalyptic England where every child collapses into chronic exhaustion on reaching adolescence, and a mismatched pair set out into a mutant-infested wasteland to find a rumoured cure. It had its first publication anywhere in this Czech edition. Reader reception is enthusiastic, but the one professional review found (iLiteratura) flags the book as pulled between inconsistent narrative levels and an ambiguous genre identity, symptoms of a premise not fully thought through rather than a stylistic quirk - the same shape of doubt that sends Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58 below the line in this log. Aimed explicitly at children from age 10, which caps how much weight the premise can be asked to carry.

A Czech blogger's first-person account of a stillbirth followed by a high-risk second pregnancy, written to break the social taboo around losing a child and, by reader accounts, more shaken by the medical system's coldness than by the loss itself. That is the axis that earns points in this reader's memoir rule - not the form itself but examining something actually true and giving insight into an experience most readers avoid thinking about, the same case that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91. Reviewers single out the voice - blunt, funny, unsentimental, each chapter opened with a fantasy-novel quote - as what keeps a heavy subject from becoming purely miserable, which caps the bleakness risk rather than letting it dominate. No occult, detective, infidelity or sexual-plot content in any account found - it is a short, real, continuous first-person narrative with no confusing opening. Only one search was run for a book this well-documented in Czech retailer and reader reviews (91% reader rating on Palmknihy), so confidence stays medium rather than high on source count alone.

Othello transposed onto a single day at a 1970s American schoolyard, with a clean one-to-one character mapping that keeps the play's psychological engine intact: a classmate's manipulation and the new boy Osei's descent into jealous rage are entirely about what each character wants and why, the axis that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead's 90 and Mockingjay's 91. Reviews single out Osei as 'a standout' with a real arc from openness to defiance, not a flat or unrootable lead. The children are eleven, but this is adult literary fiction examining racism through Shakespeare rather than a childish register, so the childrens axis costs little. The real cost is the tragic, ambiguous ending, covered by the mild bleakness discount rather than a bigger penalty given the otherwise strong reception.

A girl is pulled into an unfinished storybook world after its author dies mid-manuscript, and must help set the world's chaos right. It is a Czech children's fantasy (nominated for the Zlata stuha illustration/children's-book award) whose own summaries name only friendship, family bonds and a mother's love as its themes - no idea beyond the standard portal-adventure furniture surfaced in any source, and I would list axis:ideas as a doubt rather than a strength.

Sixteen-year-old Finn dies in the opening pages and narrates from between life and death, watching her family and friends survive the wreck of the accident - a device close to The Lovely Bones. That makes her almost entirely a watcher rather than an actor, the same passive-protagonist problem that held Oliver Twist to 57: acted upon rather than wanting anything. Reviewers also note the afterlife premise is never developed much beyond the device itself, so there is little idea to lean on either. A teen lead adds the small life-phase pushback on top.

Nero exiles his lover, a freed slave, to Sardinia to appease his political rivals, and Cato is ordered to escort her there while carrying a second, separate mission. The infidelity is Nero's, told as a court intrigue happening around Cato rather than to him or about his own marriage - it is incidental to the actual plot and stated neutrally as historical fact, so it costs at most a point or two and does not change the outcome. The book still runs on this series' recurring formula, which reviewers describe as camaraderie over a single worked idea, placing it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

The catalogue's own annotation frames the book around the differences in the motivations of its key characters - Edith Pretty, digger Basil Brown, and archaeologist Peggy Piggott each want something different from the 1939 Sutton Hoo dig, the axis that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead's 90 and Mockingjay's 91. Reception is strong across major outlets, though some reviewers find the restrained prose keeps the three leads 'a bit too far below the surface to be extremely compelling' - a real but secondary risk next to Oliver Twist's 57, where the protagonist problem was severe enough to define the whole book. A minor, mostly implied unhappy-marriage subplot for Peggy appears in the novel itself, incidental rather than the engine of the book, so it costs a little rather than vetoing anything.

t: Vzkaz na zdi zachodku (Words on Bathroom Walls)
why: A teenager newly diagnosed with schizophrenia tries an experimental drug so he can pass as normal at a new school and be with the girl he likes, narrated with heavy interiority - what he wants (to be seen as Adam, not as a diagnosis) and why drives nearly every scene, which is this reader's top-weighted axis. Reception is warm on the lead specifically (YALSA: "hilarious and infinitely lovable"), but there is a real, repeated critique that the illness is softened into "almost a fun personality quirk" to make room for a fairly conventional YA romance - that is a self-consistency concern (declare a serious illness and the book should carry its actual weight) rather than a settled strength, so it is graded down slightly rather than credited fully. Teen lead is a small, standard life-phase pushback, not a real cost.

t: Zariva noc hvezd a ledu (A Brilliant Night of Stars and Ice)
why: Dual real-life POVs - Captain Rostron racing the Carpathia to the wreck, and third-class survivor Kate Connolly - built around a single night's rescue, praised repeatedly for pace. But reviewers explicitly flag it as an 'experience-driven' story with Kate in particular wanting 'a little bit more depth,' and a dropped subplot about a boy in the lifeboats left unresolved. No larger idea beyond the historical event itself to lean on, so the number rests on pacing and the real-event grounding, with thin protagonist depth as the risk that could pull it down.

t: Zil jsem mezi malomocnymi (In the Sanctuary of Outcasts)
why: A journalist serving time for bank fraud is imprisoned in a facility that shares grounds with America's last leprosy colony, and his growing friendship with patients like Ella Bounds, exiled from her own family as a girl for a disease rather than a crime, gives him - and the reader - real insight into a stigmatized group most people never think about, the axis that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 and Son of Hamas to 75. Set below those because one reviewer's specific complaint is a rootability problem this reader weighs heavily: White reads as 'charmingly unsympathetic,' with self-justifying passages that sit oddly in a redemption memoir even though the same reviewer praises how vividly he renders the people around him. No occult, detective or sexual-plot content in a straightforward memoir with a linear structure.

t: Zlata sbirka pohadek (Peter Pan (Zlata sbirka pohadek))
why: This volume belongs to a Disney-branded weekly collectible fascicle series (87 issues, sold at newsstands from 2021) that retells classic fairy tales for young children in simplified, illustrated form. Per the reader's own scale a picture book lands in the 30s-40s, and this is exactly that register - no idea beyond the familiar Peter Pan story, well below Hobbit 84 or Little Prince 82, which pay nothing for their child audience only because real ideas carry them.

A dual-timeline reimagining of the real 18th-century thief Jack Sheppard as trans, framed as a manuscript being annotated by a present-day academic whose footnotes gradually take over the book. The premise (who gets to tell history, and what it costs to "liberate" a text or a body from the record) is genuinely worked through, not just gestured at - a positive case in the reader's own terms. But by the author's own description the book is "pretty dirty" and reviewers independently describe erotic content in nearly every chapter and most scenes, in an explicit register - that is volume and explicitness both landing high, which is the axis that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 in this log regardless of how well-regarded the surrounding book is. The footnote-within-manuscript structure and a late-book reveal about "radical librarians" tampering with the text add real structural complexity; one reviewer called it a book that "may push away the average reader" with its layering, so the opening is a genuine risk rather than a settled pass.

Military-political adventure: Cato is sent as an envoy to negotiate with the Parthian king while Corbulo stalls for time before a real campaign. Reviewers of the wider series frame its appeal around the Cato-Macro camaraderie and a repeating formula of new posting, new antagonist, political intrigue from above, rather than a single worked-out premise - closer to Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log than to an idea-driven book, and I would list axis:ideas under risks if I pushed further. It sits deep in a long-running series, and this reader's log shows sequels settling lower than openers (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), which does not raise the case for going on. Competent, grounded in real Roman politics, but nothing here argues past the line.

Thomas of Hookton has a clear want - complete an urgent task before he can rejoin the Black Prince's campaign, while a rival churchman hunts the same relic for his own ambition - the axis Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. The central relic, La Malice (said to be the sword of Saint Peter), is deliberately kept ambiguous rather than shown working: reviewers and TV Tropes both note Cornwell never confirms real supernatural power, and the book ends with the sword indistinguishable from scrap metal on a smith's discard pile - the same restraint the series uses for the Grail itself, where the danger is what people believe about the relic, not magic it performs. That keeps the book clear of the occult filter: no rite is shown functioning on the page. Reviews single out the climactic Poitiers battle as an unusually strong set piece. Estimated close to Count of Monte Cristo 75's adventure-momentum baseline, docked slightly for being a sequel - sequels are not a safe bet in this log, per Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70.

A Czech children's space-adventure series by a Magnesia Litera-winning author, warmly reviewed as an accessible read for roughly ages 11-15 with 'an interesting idea and a well thought-out story' and no occult or mechanism-magic content (a hibernation-sleep space academy premise, not fantasy). A single clear mission carries the book: 18-year-old Harald Olufsen discovers a secret German radar site in occupied Denmark and must get the evidence to Britain in a barely-flyable biplane, joining the fledgling Danish resistance along the way.
