This is assembled entirely from deleted scenes, alternate drafts, and a production journal - fragments left over from a screenwriting process, not a narrative with a premise of its own. Reviewers themselves call it inessential outside fandom ('not a necessary addition... but kind of a must have' for fans specifically), which is a tell that there is no standalone idea here to weigh. The fragmentary, notes-plus-deleted-scenes shape is close to what cost Unfinished Tales 69 its footing in this reader's own log - 'the pieces aren't logically connected to each other' - only here there is no finished novel sitting alongside the fragments to anchor them, so it settles below even that.

OPENING VERDICT, and it is the reason this sits at the top of the Zemeplocha screen: one lead and one concrete situation on page one, which the reader has all the context he needs to read - a convicted confidence man is hanged, does not quite die, and is offered a choice between the drop and a derelict post office. That is the structural opposite of the roughly six thread starts inside fifteen pages that produced two abandoned reads at 30 in this same setting, and Mort 83 already established that the prose and the comic register are not the objection. WORLD VERDICT: form one of the heaviest axis at close to its best. A communication technology is declared, priced, and Ankh-Morpork visibly reorganises around who owns it - a rival semaphore monopoly, a labour dispute, a stock swindle and a postal service that had stopped working all follow from the declaration rather than being decorated onto it, which is the Hunger Games 89 and Project Hail Mary 92 shape rather than the Harry Potter 51 one. Motives are the content: he wants to stay alive, then unexpectedly wants the job. RISK is an investigation-shaped strand, a midnight killer and a fraud being uncovered; that is a flag under the hard genre filter rather than the filtered genre itself, because the engine is building an institution and not solving a crime - say it when proposing. Set above the level Mort 83 occupies because there is a worked-out idea here that Mort does not carry, and held under S because nothing in it reaches the interiority of Red Rising 95.

LEANS ON THE IDEA, and it is nameable in one sentence: a god's power is exactly the number of people who actually believe in him, and the whole book is that arithmetic worked out - a church, an inquisition and a holy war are all consequences of it, and the god of the state religion has one believer left. That is the earner behind Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, at novel length, and it is the axis Narnia 67 and Rangeruv ucen 74 were marked down for lacking. OPENING VERDICT: one thread, one lead, a novice in a garden - but the book enters through a short authorial passage about the nature of gods rather than through the situation, so the entry is essayistic for a few pages. That is legible and single-stranded, which is what the filter actually asks for; it is not the many-threads-at-once shape that scored 30 twice in this setting. WORLD VERDICT: the premise IS the theology and it is followed through to the end, including the cost to the believer, so form one and form two both hold. RISKS: faith as the subject rather than a thread, which is the Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 exposure - mitigated because this is a story about the mechanics of belief and not devotional writing; and the library's own annotation says the boy 'je vyvoleny', a chosen one, which is a graded deduction scaled by prominence and is played straight rather than for cynicism. Occult passes: the god is invented and no real deity is petitioned.

LEANS ON THE LEAD, the axis that outranks worldbuilding. A girl cuts her hair and enlists in her country's army under a false name to find her brother; she is interesting and worth rooting for from the first chapter, which is the pairing that separates Speaker for the Dead 90 from Artemis 69, and her want is stated rather than implied. OPENING VERDICT: single thread, one recruit, one recruiting sergeant, no invented vocabulary to decode - the concrete starting situation the filter demands. This is also a standalone with its own print edition, so nothing has to be read first. WORLD VERDICT: the declared thing is a state religion that keeps adding to a list of Abominations, and the book prices it - the country is starving and at war with everyone because of what it has forbidden, which is the society-as-subject face the Divergent 58 factions failed. Real ideas on top: atrocity propaganda and what a nation tells itself, the register that earned Animal Farm 78. RISK is bleakness, the mildest recorded objection, and it is bleak-with-ideas rather than immersion in misery.

LEANS ON THE PREMISE plus a now-scored author. Declared premise, and the library's annotation states it outright: Death is dismissed from his post, so nothing on the disc dies properly and the unclaimed life force has to go somewhere. The consequences are then worked out rather than asserted, which is form one, and one of the two strands is a man who has never had a life discovering he now has a finite one - motives as content, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 above Catching Fire 83. OPENING VERDICT and the reason for the risk: TWO plots start close together, the dismissed reaper taking work on a farm and Ankh-Morpork filling up with surplus vitality. Two staggered threads are explicitly fine on this profile - LOTR 84 and Golden Son 92 both anchor one before the next arrives - and roughly six at once is what scored 30 twice here, so two is the tolerated end of the axis and not the filtered end. If they open simultaneously rather than staggered, this is a 30 and not a 70; that is what the risk means. WORLD VERDICT: the rules of the declared mechanism are obeyed and the urban strand is where they are tested, though the second strand is closer to a running joke than to a worked-out system. Occult passes: a personified death is not a rite.

LEANS ON THE WORLD, and the guard against doing that applies and is cleared: the lead is not thin - he is a stated confidence trickster with a want and a nerve problem, so this is not the Artemis 69 configuration where a strong premise was carrying a flat protagonist. Declared premise, straight out of the library's annotation: he is handed a royal mint that loses money on every coin it strikes, and the plot is paper currency being introduced into a metal economy - a bank run, the question of what actually backs a promise, and a vault that no longer holds what everyone thinks it holds. That is form four of the heaviest axis, a resource declared and then made to behave that way, and it is the face the Divergent 58 premise failed at. OPENING VERDICT: one lead, one situation, he is summoned and given the job - legible from the first page and nothing like the many-threads start that scored 30 twice in this setting. RISKS: it continues a lead established in an earlier volume, and sequels are not safe bets on this profile - Stopaduv pruvodce fell thirteen points to its own sequels, the steepest series decline in the log - so read the earlier volume first; and the lead being carried over means his want is partly already spent. Occult passes: an undead accountant is a character, not a rite.

LEANS ON THE IDEA, and it is the strongest one in this author's Death strand: belief is load-bearing, you learn to believe the small untruths so that you can believe the large ones that a civilisation actually runs on. Declared premise, which the annotation gives obliquely - the fat man who brings the presents has been removed by going after the belief in him rather than the man, and the reaper takes over the round to keep the sun coming up. The consequences are followed through, which is form one. OPENING VERDICT, and it is the reason the range is not higher: FOUR strands start close together - the granddaughter, the reaper, the assassin and the auditors - and that is the failure shape that produced two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting, only at four rather than six. WORLD VERDICT: the belief mechanic is declared precisely and obeyed, and the book leans on it in every scene, so the obligation is high and it is met. A second risk is the lead: the granddaughter is competent and sardonic but the reaper takes the best scenes, and a divided centre is not the interesting-and-rootable pairing that earns the top of the log. Faith appears as a mechanism rather than as devotion, so it is a listed dep and not a live risk.

t: Uzasny Mauric (The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents)
why: LEANS ON THE IDEA. Declared premise, from the annotation: a cat and a troop of rats have become self-aware, and the book is about what awareness costs them - they take names, argue about a story they have inherited, and have to decide whether they are still allowed to run a confidence trick on human beings. That is a nameable idea in a phrase, which the sharpened short-form rule demands, and the rats are differentiated the way Golden Son 92 differentiates its cast. OPENING VERDICT: one situation and a small legible cast, a talking cat and a boy with a pipe walking into a town to work the trick - concrete, and no invented vocabulary. WORLD VERDICT: the mechanism is a wizarding university's rubbish heap and the book does not undertake to explain it, so little binds; what it does declare - that these rats think - it then honours in every scene. RISK is the register, graded and never a filter: an audience-childrens book pays nothing when there is an adult layer for the deduction to grade, which is why Hobit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing and a nursery-register book lands in the 60s, and the layer here is real. Occult passes: no rite, no invocation.

LEANS ON THE IDEA: belief and mass, with pyramids declared as structures that dam up time and a kingdom that has spent seven thousand years paying for them. One lead, a boy sent away to be trained as an assassin and recalled to be a god-king, and the annotation frames it exactly that way - being a pharaoh in adolescence. OPENING VERDICT: an examination at a school of assassins is a single concrete situation with a clear goal, which clears the filter; the mild pushback is that the book then jumps to a second setting. WORLD VERDICT: the declared resource behaves as declared and the consequences arrive, so form four holds. RISK, and it is the one that could collapse this: OCCULT. The kingdom's priesthood, embalming and pantheon are modelled closely on documented ancient Egyptian religion rather than invented, and rites are performed on the page - the source test and the depiction test are both in play, and Percy Jackson 57 is what it costs when a real pantheon is prayed to and sacrificed to on the page. Anyone proposing this must run the depiction check first and lead with it, not with the idea. A second, small risk is the lead's age reading young from the inside, the Ender's Game 87 pushback.

LEANS ON THE IDEA and the lean is honestly weak, which is why the range sits in the B band. Declared premise: a kind of music arrives that is itself alive and possesses the people who play it, and a granddaughter inherits the reaper's round. The consequences are followed through in places, but a large share of the book is a sustained joke about rock and roll history rather than a premise worked out, and a running gag is voice rather than an idea you can name in a phrase - Saturnin 78 shows that voice and character alone still reach the A band, so this is not a failure, it is a ceiling. OPENING VERDICT and the live risk: two strands start close together, the possessed band and the inherited duty, which is the tolerated end of the multi-thread axis rather than the filtered end, but this book has less to compensate with if the entry does not hold. WORLD VERDICT: the mechanism is declared loosely, so little binds and little is breached; the deduction is that nothing much is built on it either. Occult passes.

STATED CONFIDENCE: MEDIUM-HIGH, and the reason is on the record - the library's annotation for this volume is pure publisher boilerplate with no premise in it, so everything below rests on outside knowledge of the book rather than on the catalogue. LEANS ON THE WORLD: a printing press arrives in a city that had no news, and the consequences are the plot - a trade guild's monopoly broken, a readership invented, a competitor selling invented stories that sell better than real ones. That is form one, and it is the same face that the good worldbuilding rows in the log are praised for. OPENING VERDICT: one lead, a gentleman's son who writes a newsletter, and one situation - the press literally runs him down in the street. Legible, single-thread, the opposite of the shape that scored 30 twice here. RISK, and it must be stated first when proposing: the SPINE of the plot is the lead investigating who framed Ankh-Morpork's ruler for attempted murder, and that is the hard-filtered genre as the book's structure and not as a subplot. The profile says an investigation-shaped strand inside an eligible book is a flag rather than a drop, but here the strand is the engine, so this is recorded and flagged rather than proposed clean.

LEANS ON THE WORLD, and this is the purest example of form one in the whole holding: a locomotive is declared, and the annotation itself describes the consequence rather than the machine - steam rising over a continent, a technology that reorganises trade, war and who can reach whom. Declared capability then society visibly different for it, which is the reader's own formulation of the axis. OPENING VERDICT: single situation, an engineer and an engine, legible from page one. RISKS are what hold this in the B band. First, story density: this is widely reported as thin on plot for its length, with long stretches of speech-making about progress rather than events, and a thin story spread over many pages is precisely the penalty term - Monte Cristo 75 and Les Miserables 71 were both docked for digression and they are far better plotted than this is reported to be. Second, it continues a lead established two volumes earlier and is late in a long run, and sequels are not safe bets here. Access note lives in the cache and not in this field. Occult passes.

LEANS ON THE WORLD and then is pulled back down by the lead, which is the Artemis 69 guard applying rather than being cleared. Declared premise: a place is found where the barrier between what is imagined and what is real has worn thin, and an entertainment industry grows on it - the consequences are worked out, an economy, a labour market and a hazard all following from the declaration, so form one holds. But the profile is explicit that a flat lead beats a strong world, and the two young protagonists here are vehicles for the joke rather than people who want things; the wizards and the supporting cast take the best material. OPENING VERDICT and the second risk: the cast fans out early across several locations with no single figure carrying the entry, which is the shape the filter names, and the two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting are what it costs. Recorded rather than proposed. Occult passes: the mechanism is a thinning of reality, not a rite.

BLOCKED 2026-08-31 by inheritance. The commander, his watch and his marriage are all established in the volume read and abandoned at 30, and the book assumes every one of them. Its own detective risk was already the second-heaviest thing against it. Was recorded at a low range. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: LEANS ON THE IDEA, which is real: how two cities talk themselves into a war over an uninhabited rock that has just surfaced, and what patriotism looks like from inside the machinery - the register that earned Animal Farm 78, though carried much more lightly. RISKS are two and they compound. First, the spine opens as an inquiry into the first casualty and the lead is a police commander running it, so the hard-filtered genre is the structure; the profile flags an investigation-shaped strand rather than dropping it, but here the strand is the frame. Second, the entry: the disputed island, the two governments, the commander's watch and a diplomatic party all start close together, which is the many-threads shape that produced two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting - and one of those two is this same lead's first volume, so the closest read comparator is a 30. WORLD VERDICT: nothing much is declared beyond a plausible pseudo-Mediterranean politics, so little binds and little breaches; there is no worldbuilding case to predict up on. Recorded, not proposed. Occult passes.

The library's own annotation is the diagnosis: it announces that the book introduces a fresh set of protagonists - a barbarian hairdresser and a reluctant destroyer - inside a save-the-world plot that is already under way, with the wizard carried over from the volume abandoned at 30. This is the sub-series whose FIRST volume the reader read and abandoned at 30 on an unclear, confusing start, and the objection is now correctly scoped: Mort 83 proved the author and the comic register are fine, so what is being priced here is this strand's structure and not Pratchett. The strand is picaresque - a cowardly wizard is carried through a sequence of set pieces with no single declared situation, and new protagonists are introduced into a plot already running. OPENING VERDICT: that is the filtered shape, arrived at from the read score on volume one rather than from a fresh reading of this volume's first chapter, so it is inference and is labelled as such. WORLD VERDICT: almost nothing is declared and the magic is deliberately unsystematised, so the obligation is low and nothing is breached - but by the same rule there is no worldbuilding case to predict up on either, and rules add obligation and never bonus. Occult passes: comic invented spellcasting with no rite in the historical mould. RECORDED, NOT PROPOSED - a low range so that the title stops resurfacing as an unscreened find, which is the whole point of writing it down.

A guardian angel falls for the boy she is assigned to protect and has to hide it from strict superiors. That is one clean situation rather than a confusing fan-out, which is the thing this reader most needs, but it is also the whole of the book: a forbidden-love complication, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and I can name no thought it leaves behind. Doubt on that axis is what decides the exit and the band. The risk is the declared setup - once you assert a supervised angelic order with rules about contact, the rules bind, and Harry Potter 51 is in the log partly because a concretely declared system was never followed through into how the world would actually work. What reader comment exists is about repetitive phrasing and a quick read rather than about anything the book achieves. Occult status unexamined at this exit; the angelic apparatus is what would need checking there. One source, within budget.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a military-adventure SF novel opening a six-book run - and the idea is a conspiracy hook rather than a premise worked out: three unexplained zones on the map, an invading Shadow that destroyed Atlantis ten thousand years ago and is back. That is a machine for producing set pieces, and set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader; it is what pulled Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 even where the writing was strong. I would list axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. The larger danger is the opening: reviewers describe the author's habitual method as two to four sets of characters introduced in parallel and followed across different eras, which is the shape that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 unfinished. That risk is what could take it well under the range rather than what sets it. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

A standalone with its own lead and premise; the excluded books by this author are a different sequence set in Anglo-Saxon England and nothing here continues them, so no inheritance - decided on the book's own plot summary, not on the hint. It then exits at the below-the-line gate. The positive is a legible single-situation opening, one archer under sentence of the noose in 1414, which is exactly the concrete start this reader wants and the opposite of the failures at 30. But I would put axis:ideas in risks: the last quarter is the battle, the bulk before it is siege and campaign detail, and reviewers repeatedly describe the characters as two-dimensional and hard to build rapport with - a thin lead outranks strong research here, which is the whole lesson of Artemis 69. Set against Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68, the historical band in this log, that lands under the line. Two smaller deductions are already visible and neither changes the exit: the lead has an affair with a married woman, which is incidental rather than the premise and costs a point or two, and his patron saints speak to him on the page. That second thing is a live occult question which I deliberately did not examine, because the book is already below the line either way.

The hook is genuinely promising - the tyrant is dead and the hero of the book is the tyrant's son, hunted by the good queen's soldiers - and a lead who has to find out whether he is his father is a real want to follow. What sinks the estimate is self-consistency: the one substantive reader account describes valkyries, vampires, trolls and assorted magicians assembled into a world that does not cohere, characters who alternately fight like lions and inexplicably give up only to be rescued anyway, and convoluted explanations. That is the Divergent 58 failure exactly - ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering, with the plot saved when it suits the author - and it is the axis carrying the number down. Ideas are the risk rather than the lean: I cannot name a thought the book would leave behind beyond the premise's own irony, and doubt on that axis is what sends this out at the gate. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

I examined the infidelity axis first, within its two-source budget, and decided not to reject. Removing the adultery does not remove the book: the engine is the Japanese invasion of Malaya, the flight south by yacht, the poisoning plot pursued by a servant girl carrying out her mother's curse, and the pirates - so this is a prominent subplot, not the premise, and where the doubt is real the rule says grade rather than reject. The doubt is real here and I am recording it: a married woman's attraction to another man is the emotional centre of the middle of the book even though it is not its plot. What the axis then costs is severe, and it is the framing that does it. The marriage is written as loveless with the husband at fault, and the publisher's own copy presents the new attachment as a discovery of freedom - approving framing, which the measured table puts at thirty to forty for a subplot and which the log says bites even when brief. There is a second, consummated adultery in the recent past as well, so this is not a single moment. Against that I can name no idea the book leaves behind: it is a wartime escape story with a romance inside it, and colonial complacency shattered is a setting rather than a premise worked out. That is the below-the-line exit, and between the two bands the lower one is the honest one, because the axis table would place it lower still. Note that I spent the gate-two budget of two sources before exiting, and nothing further. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Exits at the below-the-line gate. Form is a novel of about 592 pages, genre a procedural war thriller built on a real weapons programme. I would put axis:ideas in risks and that is the exit: the satisfaction on offer is whether the weapon is found in time, and reviewers converge on the same complaint, that the research swamps the story and the reader wanting deep psychological characterisation is in the wrong book. That is the log's heaviest objection stated plainly - page time on what characters want and why beats page time on what they do - and it is joined here by the density penalty, a plot embedded in a hundred pages of hardware detail, which is what cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its difference over The Hobbit and what the reader named against The Martian 82. Two things I checked and neither fires: the reader's satisfaction is a hunt for an object rather than finding out who did it, so this is not a detective novel, though the intelligence-gathering is investigation-shaped and worth flagging; and the opening is reported as strong rather than confusing, so the several-plot-lines-at-once filter that sank three books at 30 does not apply even though the narrative cuts between Washington, London, Baghdad and the desert. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

t: Bud jako reka (Go as a River)
why: Form and genre settled at one source: a historical novel, autumn 1948, one point of view, opening on a single concrete situation - a seventeen-year-old carrying late peaches into town is stopped by a stranger asking directions. That is the opening shape The Hunger Games 89 rests on, and it is a genuine positive. Where I doubt it is what it leaves behind. The material is atmosphere and endurance: a chance meeting, a tragedy, then a long stretch alone in the mountains while the valley is flooded for a reservoir, and reviewers describe the pacing as meandering and several significant events as touched only lightly. Solo survival as the sustained theme is also the specific thing the reader marked The Martian 82 down for and that companionship beats. No premise is being worked out, so I stopped at the idea question rather than research the graded axes. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

The opening situation is concrete and legible, which is worth saying because that is the one thing that has ended books unfinished in this log: one boy, one night, one errand in a named landscape, and the trouble arrives to him. Past that I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - it is marketed as a funny story full of romance and mystery, a Czech young-adult fantasy whose interest is the adventure rather than a premise whose consequences get traced. Reception supports the doubt rather than settling it: readers praise the readability and repeatedly call the writing beginnerish and the ending unclosed, and the log punishes exactly that shape, an open or unresolved close costing The Martian 82 and pieces that do not connect costing Unfinished Tales 69. Worldbuilding obligation is a further exposure, since a system named and used is binding and it is what took Harry Potter 51 down alongside its other objection. So I would put axis:ideas under risks, which is the below-the-line gate's own test, and I stopped there on one source. Occult status is unexamined and is a live question: the book turns on Walpurgis Night and three figures met in a wood, which is real-world folklore rather than an invented mechanism.

Form and genre settled at one source: a multi-generational family-saga novel with a dual timeline and several points of view, built on a dead mother's recorded account of a life her children never knew about. A domestic story with no premise to work out is not itself a problem here - Pride and Prejudice 75 and Little Women 79 both clear the line on motives and character alone. What I doubt is whether anything is left behind: migration, class, race and the inheritance of secrets are the book's subject matter rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, and the engine is a sequence of revelations about the past. That is the reason a competent book most often stalls in the 60s, so I stopped there rather than research further. The non-linear structure across two timelines and several viewpoints also puts the opening under some load, the axis behind the log's four abandoned books. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Infidelity was checked first, because the catalogue calls her his mistress and the screen bound the needle to the first sentence, and it does not fire at premise level. The relationship begins before he marries, is set aside because Roman law forbids a senator to marry a freedwoman, and resumes after his wife's death; the obstacle the book is constructed on is statute, not adultery. Doubt remains about how the novel handles the married middle years, so this is recorded as a subplot-or-less grading with that doubt stated rather than a clean sheet - a wrong reject is unrecoverable and a wrong grading is not. The detective hint attached to this author does not reach here either: this is a standalone with its own lead, written before and separate from her investigator novels, and nothing about their exclusions depends on or propagates to it. The positive case is genuine and sits on the reader's heaviest axis - two people over forty years, each wanting something specific, with imperial politics seen from close range, and Pride and Prejudice 75 shows romance as the central subject costs nothing when motives are the whole book. What stops it here is that a climb through four reigns is a chronicle, and this log puts well-textured historical novels with no worked-out idea at Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because Caenis is by every account the interesting part. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

There is a real claim on seriousness here. The author called this the most important thing he wrote and said it was written in his own blood, and the subject - an adolescent Czech Jew working out an identity between marxism and zionism while the century closes on him - is one the reader has rewarded highly when a book actually examines what is true rather than merely feeling it. The trouble is that everything sourceable about this book praises the writing and not a proposition: painful and beautiful in Orten's manner, comparable to Peroutka and Hostovsky, an almost ruralist-zionist motif of work on the land. Beautifully written is not an idea, and the reader's literary record punishes precisely that: 58 for a canonical short novel whose idea was real but whose lead was passive, and a DNF at 40 for first-person wartime witness that examined nothing. So axis:ideas is nameable in outline and not trusted to hold, which is the gate, and the file stops at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:bleakness because the war is background here rather than the subject, and rather than axis:life-phase because a teenage lead is only ever a couple of points. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and it is a live question: the publisher's own copy mentions a mysterious farm where both Germans and witches figure, and whether anything is enacted on the page is unchecked.

A runner steps sideways out of our world while fleeing danger, finds an Order of travellers, learns the knack and uncovers why her father vanished. The opening is one concrete situation, which is the thing that matters most here, but the book is a discovery plot - learn the power, meet the villain, solve the family secret - and I can name no thought it would leave behind. That doubt is the exit. Worldbuilding is the risk and the readers point at it themselves: an infinity of worlds is a capability declared broadly, one reviewer says things stay under-explained and the book should have been longer, and unexplained declared capability is what put Mortal Engines at 55 as a DNF. The lead is a teenager and the log prices that at a couple of points at most, so it is not doing any work in this number. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

t: Chasidske povidky z doby holocaustu (Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust)
why: Eighty-nine short self-contained tales gathered from oral testimony and told in the traditional tale form, each a rebbe or a disciple and a reversal. Form and genre settled, and that is what decides it: the suspension for short idea-driven work removes the character and emotion penalties but adds nothing, and there is no single premise to work out across eighty-nine pieces. Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 are the short books that score, and both score because one nameable idea is carried the whole way; Unfinished Tales 69 is what the log gives to a book whose pieces are not logically connected to each other, and that is the shape here. The subject also puts the faith axis under load - the reader wants faith as a thread inside a story rather than as the whole of it, and here the religious response is the whole of it. I doubt what the collection leaves behind, so I stopped at that question. Occult status is unexamined at this exit: the tales include miracles and supernatural intervention, and whether any rite is performed on the page was not checked.

There is a real idea and the readers who liked it name the same one I would: a being that knows nothing of our world comes alive and has to work out what it is for, with a girl showing it the humanity in a stone heart. That is a premise, not just a setting. What holds the number down is the register - 120 illustrated pages published for children, one situation and one journey through Prague legends - which is graded and costs a little, the Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 position of easy reading with not much to think about rather than the picture-book end of the scale. Ideas are the risk and the reason for the gate exit rather than the lean: the idea is announced but one reader reports the ending turns sanctimonious, so whether it is carried through is exactly what I would doubt. Occult status is unexamined here and the ghosts and apparitions of old Prague are what would need checking. One source, within budget.

Exits at the below-the-line gate, and the axes carrying the number are axis:ideas and axis:multi-pov. Form is a novel, genre historical panorama - roughly 800 pages tracking Chinese, British and American families from the First Opium War to the present. The opening deals the reader several strands at once, a Chinese official's secretary and a British merchant among them, with no single starting situation to be invested in, and that is the log's most reliable predictor of a bad outcome: The Colour of Magic 30, Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30 all died on exactly that. Panoramic history is not automatically fatal - The Silmarillion 80 scored well with no single protagonist and no continuous plot - but that book had mythic ideas behind it, whereas here the thing the book leaves behind is historical information about how the West humiliated the Qing, which is education rather than a premise worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit condition. Reviewers also report organisational problems and a contrived recurring character. The reader's own historical-novel results cluster right at this line: Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68. The positive case is genuine, and it is the axis that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - the book gives the Chinese side its own viewpoint rather than the foreign one only. Length itself is not counted against it; the concern is thin story per page. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

A Norse-legend adventure a century after Siegfried: the gods are talked into bending time, the young prince and his betrothed wake in a black century under an immortal tyrant, and they have to unwind it. The lean is self-consistency, because time being rewound by divine favour is a capability declared loudly, and the log is unforgiving where a declared capability is not carried through - the one concrete complaint on record here is precisely that, a sword turning into Excalibur on a timeline that does not add up, which is the Divergent 58 shape. Ideas are the second doubt and the reason for the gate exit: readers describe an overcooked finale counted down page by page rather than anything left behind. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70 is the steepest decline recorded. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the gods intervening directly is exactly what would need checking, given the Greek pantheon is what put Percy Jackson at 57. One source, within budget.

Checked the detective gate first because the catalogue flagged it, and it does not fire: reviewers describe the book as detective-shaped in manner only, and the satisfaction on offer is recovering what happened to a girl and her Jewish friend under the occupation, not identifying a culprit. That is a flag rather than a veto. The positive case is genuine - two time layers braided together, a lead reviewers call believable and dryly funny, and a subject worth having. But the number is carried by how juvenile the telling is and by how much of the idea is borrowed rather than made: a hundred and twelve illustrated pages that introduce the Holocaust to children, where the reader's objection to Narnia 67 was precisely children as leads plus nothing higher to think about, and where first-person testimony about the same period produced the log's joint-lowest score at 40. A reviewer's complaint that the girl uncovers every detail of the past quickly and easily is the unearned-competence cost on top. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined.

The infidelity axis was examined despite no screen hit on the task line, and it does not veto: the lead marries the diplomat only after the man she loved is killed in a plane crash, so the marriage is one of convenience entered in grief, not an affair, and no adultery is the engine of the plot. The espionage plot that follows sends her back to Poland to find a traitor. I could not establish how the marriage resolves, and a novel with this title and a lost love kept alive in it can turn that way, so the axis sits in risks rather than in the number. On form and genre the exit is clear: a commercial wartime historical novel with one point of view opening on a single concrete situation, a survivor at liberation, which is a genuine positive - but I cannot name what it leaves behind beyond the setting, and that is the axis that stalls competent books in the 60s. Exodus 68 is the log's anchor for the historical novel that is carried by its subject rather than by an idea, and Quo Vadis 66 sits just under it. Leaned on the idea question, which is what the exit turned on.

The detective question was asked first and answered no: this is a dual-timeline family novel in which a wartime secret surfaces, not a novel whose satisfaction is identifying a culprit, so the filter does not fire and the buried-crime strand is a flag rather than a veto. It then exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas, which is the axis carrying the number. Form is a novel, genre historical and contemporary women's fiction. I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - the material is family secrets, a house to be restored and a wartime romance, and reviewers report a slow start with unattractive characters, a one-dimensional boyfriend subplot and a rushed, anticlimactic ending - so axis:ideas belongs in risks, which is the exit condition. That is the pattern the log records for competent books with nothing to think about: Ranger's Apprentice 74 with its stronger momentum, and lower here because the reader also flags drawn-out and unsatisfying endings, which cost The Martian 82 points it had earned. The positive case is a concrete opening situation - one woman, one letter, one house - which is the shape this reader wants, and Rebecca's practical restoration work gives her something she actively wants. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

t: Holky z Detroitu (A Matter of Happiness)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a dual-timeline commercial historical novel, 2018 Kentucky against 1920s Detroit, joined by a journal found in an inherited car - and the question it puts is whether a woman must trade her freedom to marry. That is a theme the book restates in two eras rather than an idea it works out, and restating a contrast across timelines is what the genre does; I would list axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. Pride and Prejudice 75 shows that romance as the central subject costs nothing here when what characters want and why is the whole book, so the ceiling is not the subject matter - it is that the journal frame keeps the reader at one remove from the earlier woman's motives, and page time on what she does in speakeasies is not page time on what she wants. axis:multi-pov is the risk rather than the lean: two timelines opened together is the fanning-out shape this reader has abandoned books over, though a journal handoff is a legible way to do it. On the infidelity axis, examined because it is mandatory: the modern lead has a broken engagement behind her and the historical lead's question is whether to marry at all, so no marriage or engagement is betrayed. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

t: Hrichy rodu Borgiu (Sins of the House of Borgia (originally The Book of Love))
why: Both hard-filter questions were examined and neither fires, then the book exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas and axis:sexual-content, which are the axes carrying the number. On infidelity: the central attachment is an unmarried lady-in-waiting's obsession with Cesare Borgia, so the reader's marriage-or-engagement scope is not clearly engaged - his own political marriage is offstage and unwritten - and the affairs of a fellow lady-in-waiting with two brothers of Lucrezia's husband are one thread of court colour rather than the plot; that is a subplot grading with the doubt stated, not a reject, because a wrong reject is unrecoverable. On sex as the plot: the book is a court chronicle of Ferrara and Lucrezia's household, so removing the romance leaves a book, and the veto does not fire. What is left is graded and costs. Reviewers report crude sex scenes, and crudeness is the one dimension the log anchors cleanly - Ready Player One 55 was sunk by the kind of sexual content rather than the amount, and Artemis 69 was docked for exactly this at small volume. Form is a novel, genre historical fiction; the idea I can name is a converted Jewish girl watching Christian power from inside it, but reviewers describe a slick soap opera that drags in the middle with a narrator they found frustrating and acted-upon, so axis:ideas goes in risks, which is the exit condition - the Oliver Twist 57 shape, a lead who is moved rather than wanting. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

This is a bound-up run of ten short comics episodes first printed in a children's magazine, about a father-and-son climbing pair who meet weather, prehistoric creatures and family history in a few pages each. Craft is not the question - it took a Muriel for best children's comic - but there is no idea I can name, and there is no room for one: each episode restarts, so nothing accumulates and no premise gets its consequences worked out, which is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 and is exactly what is absent here. The episodic comics form also suspends the character tests rather than passing them, and the suspension removes penalties without adding points. That combination - no nameable idea plus a form that cannot earn on character - is the lower of the two below-the-line bands. Register is squarely juvenile, which the log costs at Narnia 67 and more steeply as a book moves toward picture-book territory. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined.

Exited at the below-the-line gate: literary fiction and a collection of short pieces at once, which is the mandated stop. The pieces are routines written for magazines over several years, not a book with one premise, so there is no single idea to name and the short form suspends the character rules without putting anything in their place - the suspension removes penalties, it never adds points, and Animal Farm 78 earns its place by having an idea, not by being short. Kirkus's verdict that the parts are better than the whole is the same finding. The heavier reason for the low band is the reader's most reliable negative predictor: he ended The Gunslinger, The Colour of Magic and Foundryside in their first pages at 30 apiece for openings where a lot happens and none of it is yet legible, and hallucinatory discontinuity is the declared method here rather than an accident of the first chapter. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

There is a real subject here - four generations of Philippine history under the Spanish, the Americans and Filipinos themselves, and what the country's educated class is actually for - and the book does open on one concrete situation: a body pulled from the Hudson and a student setting out for Manila. That is why this is not scored at the floor. What sinks it is how the telling arrives. From the start the reader is tracking the narrator's story, his unfinished biography of the dead man, excerpts of that man's poems, novels, interviews and memoirs, a critic's blog, a running series of jokes, and meta-narrative commenting on the narrator, in both first and third person, with a fictional apparatus presented as real. Reviewers consistently report it as exasperating to enter and ask the reader to trust that the pieces will cohere. That is the reader's most reliable predictor and it has three separate 30s behind it - the diagnosis the reader himself settled on was 'lots happening, none of it meant anything yet', and an incident-rich opening is no defence against it. Unfinished Tales 69 is the mild end of the same complaint, pieces not logically connected to each other, and it is the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin. Leaned on the opening rather than on ideas because the ideas are only reached by a reader who gets past the structure, and this reader has twice not.

t: In the lives of puppets (In the Lives of Puppets)
why: The positive case is that this is a premise with a question in it and the ending actually answers it: the boy raised by machines saves his inventor father by wiping the memories of the machines who love him, doing to them what was done to humanity, so the title's question of who the puppet is gets turned back on the protagonist. That is an idea left behind rather than a theme announced, which is the axis Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 both score on. The telling is also motive-heavy: the page time goes on what Victor and Hap each want from the other and what they are willing to accept, and that is what tops the log at Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Two filters cleared on sources: the opening is one concrete situation in a single point of view, Victor twenty feet up a scrap heap on a home-made pulley salvaging a circuit board, which is the opposite of the confusion that sank three books at 30; and the powers are machines, with no rite and no invocation anywhere. Now the deductions. The nurse robot's running joke is bodily and sexual - explicit exchanges about genitalia, whether androids have them, and whether the protagonist is aroused - and that is the crudeness dimension at low volume and low explicitness, which is exactly the Artemis 69 docking and the kind rather than the amount that took Ready Player One to 55. The world is also the weaker half: reviewers read it as assembled from other robot books, and a post-human society whose Authority and history are asserted rather than worked out will not hold up under the scrutiny that Valka stareho muze 87 passed and Divergent 58 failed. I leaned on the idea and the motives rather than on the worldbuilding, because the log's clearest lesson is never to predict up on a world when the human material is what is carrying the book.

Roman military adventure done with confident period detail, and the opening situation is exactly the shape the reader wants: one man, one legible task, escort a deposed king to a town and put him back on his throne. Reviewers credit seamless co-writing, solid research and well-drawn military detail. Beyond that it is battles. The five-part serial origin shows in the pacing, the army-life material is reported as thinner than in the authors' main sequence, and the appeal reviewers name is the crescendo of action towards the end. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the ceiling in this log for easy, well-made adventure with not much to think about, and that book had fourteen volumes of character to lean on where this has one campaign; so axis:ideas is the doubt that closes the file at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:momentum because the pacing seam is a minor complaint and the missing idea is not. One live hazard sits above the range rather than inside it: a druidic sect drives the second half, druids are real historical pagan priests, and whether any rite is enacted on the page is unexamined at this exit - if it is, the number goes well below this band.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. There is a real premise - a boy on a colony ship learning to cook, meaning to gene-engineer, living creatures, and wanting to build a dragon - and one reviewer says the small details are planted and pay off, which is genuine credit on the axis that Golden Son 92 scores on. But it is a short illustrated adventure for children and the appeal reported by readers is excitement, friendship and pictures, not something to think about afterwards; that puts axis:ideas in the doubts and is what the below-the-line gate asks. Register sits below The Hobbit 84 and nearer Narnia 67, which the reader marked down precisely for lacking higher things to think about. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, on the lower band, and the form is what decides it. This is a forty-page illustrated picture book for preschool and first-year children, written as a practical aid for telling a child that someone has died and usable as a methodical handbook in kindergartens - the profile puts a picture book in the thirties or forties outright. There is no idea I can name in the sense that earns here: the animal allegory carries a purpose, not a thought, and the recorded complaint from readers is exactly that it states the fact of death without answering the child's why, where he went or what death is. The Little Prince 82 shows a short allegory can score high, but it scores on the thoughts it leaves behind, and that is what is missing; the suspension of the character rules that comes with this form removes penalties without adding anything. Bleakness is the risk that could take it lower - readers report stalling with children at the picture of the dead brother lying on the rock. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

t: Kdo odejde, uz se nevraci (All Who Go Do Not Return)
why: This is the closest thing in the log to Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and for the same reasons: honest first-person, a closed religious world made legible from inside, and above all a man testing what he was raised to believe against what he can actually credit - the rigour the reader singled out as the thing that earns high tiers. The idea is nameable in a phrase: what it costs to find out whether the thing you were forbidden to question is true. The opening is a single concrete situation with one point of view - a boy of thirteen taken to a village he did not want to visit - so the failure that ended four books in their first chapters is not in play. Held below Qureshi 91 because the movement here is out of belief rather than toward a settled position, so what the book arrives at is loss, exile and a custody fight rather than a resolved case, and because the reader wants faith as a thread inside a story rather than as its whole subject; that is the risk, not the lean. Son of Hamas 75 sets the floor for the same form with less self-examination in it. Leaned on the memoir form and the idea rather than the protagonist, since the narrator's interest is entirely in what he is working out.

Exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas and axis:density, which are the axes carrying the number. Form is a novel of about 520 pages, genre historical romance set on Cyprus around the 1974 Turkish invasion, with a present-day frame in which a young woman wants the truth about her soldier father. The infidelity axis was examined because it is mandatory: the central relationship is between an unmarried sixteen-year-old emigre and a British soldier, so the marriage-or-engagement scope is not engaged by anything I can source, and the frame narrative's withheld paternity is not evidence of an affair inside a marriage - graded as not applicable rather than rejected, with the doubt stated. The reason for the exit is that the idea does not hold: a Czech reviewer reports substantial padding, repeated situations and weak dialogue, and complains of learning almost nothing about the period or the place while being given the heroine's entire wardrobe. That is the reader's density objection exactly - a thin story spread over many pages, which cost The Lord of the Rings 84 the ground its ideas had won - and it puts axis:ideas in risks, the exit condition. Positive case: the exchanged letters give page time to what the two want and why, which is the axis the log rates highest, and readers do credit the book with reflections on war, totalitarianism and freedom. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

Detective was the first question and it does not fire. This is reportage, not a whodunnit: the killing and the conviction of the ex-wife who ordered it are public record, the author covered the five-month trial from the courtroom, and readers report that the murder occupies roughly the opening and closing chapters while the body of the book is boardroom fights, family lawsuits and an investment bank's eighteen-month buyout. The satisfaction on offer is not finding out who did it. What is on offer is three generations wrecking what they built, with real access behind it - and that is events, not an idea. The reader's non-fiction record is unambiguous about which half earns: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scores because it examines what is actually true and shows how another group experiences the world, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows the form itself earns nothing at all. Corporate history of a fashion dynasty offers neither, and there is nobody in it to root for. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:density because what the book is for, not its length, sets the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:faith and axis:ideas, which are the axes carrying the number. Form is a mosaic of autobiographical stories rather than a novel with one plot line, genre reflective testimony. Two things put it under the line. First, the reader's stated position is that faith works as a thread inside a story but not as the subject in its own right, and a Databaze knih reviewer reports the book is strongly organised around the author's newly found belief in God and is markedly esoteric and spiritual throughout - that is the whole subject, not a thread. Second, a collection assembled from whoever the author happened to meet has no single premise to work out, so there is nothing for axis:ideas to lean on; the short-idea-driven suspension removes penalties but never adds points, and the log's short books that scored - Animal Farm 78, The Little Prince 82, Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 - are all carried by one nameable idea, which this is not. So axis:ideas belongs in risks, which is the exit condition. Positive case is real: a warm Czech storytelling voice, and Saturnin 78 shows voice and character alone can reach the A band here. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits, and the esoteric register is the specific thing to check if it is ever reopened.

t: Kniha ztracenych jmen (The Book of Lost Names)
why: First the inherited-exclusion question, because the task flagged an already-excluded book by this author. It does not carry: that book is a separate standalone with different characters, a different setting and no shared plot, this novel introduces its own lead and its own premise from scratch, and there is nothing here to depend on - the exclusion propagates only through dependency, never through an author or a shelf. On its own infidelity axis, examined independently, both people in the central relationship are unmarried and no marriage or engagement is betrayed, so nothing fires. That leaves the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a dual-timeline WWII novel - and the idea is more nearly present here than the genre usually manages: forged papers erase children's real names, so someone has to keep a record of who they were, and identity kept against erasure is a thing to think about rather than only a thing to feel. The lead is also active and worth rooting for, risking herself for others, which is the combination the profile puts above worldbuilding. What keeps it under the line is that the record is used as a plot object and a frame for a love story rather than pressed for what it means; Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 mark where a solid historical novel settles when the thinking is not the point, so I would still list axis:ideas in risks and the gate fires. axis:multi-pov is the risk, not the lean: a present-day frame opened before the wartime story is a mild version of the fanning-out shape, mild because the frame hands over quickly. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

The premise is a real one - Alexander does not die in Babylon in 323 BC and turns his Indian war elephants on Carthage - and it is carried by an outsider, an elephant handler raised into the Macedonian command, watching power corrupt the man who raised him. That is a motive-shaped spine, the axis that tops the log in Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. But I doubt the idea is actually worked out: the book is sold and reviewed as a fast battle adventure, the alternate history is a setting rather than a consequence traced, and the second lead is a captured general's daughter whose thread is romance rather than argument. Set-piece action without character revelation is dead weight for this reader - it is what docked Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 and what sank the second arena in Catching Fire 83. Historical fiction that entertains without leaving an idea behind sits at Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68, and that is the band I expect. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the gate's own test, so I did not research the graded axes. Occult status is therefore unexamined here.

This book asks the reader to spend four occupied years inside a woman whose entire project is keeping her money, and who collaborates with the Reich and then spies for it to do so. The reader's clearest recorded verdict on that shape is 65 for a book by an author he otherwise tops the log with, on the single ground of a lead descending into evil with nobody to root for - and reviewers here say Ewen walks a fine line between humanising Chanel and empathising with her, while another credits her with not sugarcoating the actions or the personality. Interesting is not the problem; rootable is, and those are two separate failure modes in this log. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than the period detail because the strongest single case in the log is that a lead the reader cannot back outranks everything well built around them. What the book leaves behind beyond a portrait is the further doubt, hence one source and a stop. Infidelity was examined and does not fire: the lead is unmarried and the engine is the fight for control of the perfume company plus the collaboration, not an affair. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The opening is the reader's single most reliable predictor and here it is clean rather than a hazard: 1593, one viewpoint, an Edinburgh goldsmith with a pregnant wife summoned again and again to a teenage queen who loves jewels. One concrete situation, nothing fanning out, and an outsider lead who is both interesting and easy to back - reviewers specifically praise the choice to tell the union of the crowns through the money man instead of through the king, Shakespeare and Jonson. Against that, at just over 200 pages one reviewer reports it reading as a set of fictionalised episodes rather than a continuous novel, and what the book is for is atmosphere and court intrigue rather than a proposition worked out; the praise it draws is for economy, sensory detail and viewpoint. That is the doubt about axis:ideas the gate asks for, and Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 mark where well-textured historical fiction without one settles in this log. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:opening precisely because the opening is a positive here and cannot be what holds the number down. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. A near-future surveillance dystopia with a walled rich quarter, drones, implants and a mafia underworld, and a parent who takes an untested offer to let a dying child continue in a virtual world. The premise is nameable, but the reader's bar is that a declared premise has its consequences worked out - that is what separates Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 from Divergent 58, where the engineered society did not cohere - and this is a debut from an author-services press with no critical reception at all to indicate the second-order questions get answered. So axis:ideas belongs in the doubts, which is the gate's own test. The dystopian setting itself costs nothing; the reader said as much about Divergent. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Nine unconnected stories with no single premise, so there is no idea to name that the book as a whole leaves behind - and the short form suspends the character rules without adding anything, which is why Animal Farm 78 earns its score on its idea rather than on its length. Unfinished Tales 69 is the closest thing in the log to this shape and it is the reader's lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other. Genre readers rate this below the same author's better-regarded books and no critical reception exists. The murderous angels in the blurb are a comic conceit rather than an investigation, so the detective filter does not fire. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits, and would be worth checking if the axis is ever bumped - vampires and angels appear in the descriptions.

t: Legenda o Brokenu (The Legend of Broken)
why: There is a real idea here and it is nameable - a fortress society dooms itself through the corruption of its merchant and priestly classes while a banished philosopher beats it with what amounts to science - and the worldbuilding is worked, thirty years of it, down to an invented language. That is the sort of thing that earns points, and it is why this got full research rather than an early exit. The number is nevertheless low, and it is density and the opening that carry it. The main text runs past 650 pages with 80 more of notes that several readers report are effectively mandatory in the early chapters to know who and what anything is, the prose is a deliberate pseudo-archaic translation, and the narrative alternates between two peoples from the start. This reader's most reliable failure is exactly that - not slowness, which is forgiven, but arriving in a world whose context is withheld while material piles up, the diagnosis that produced three separate scores of 30. Reviewers also report the pace stays slow past the opening and that the confrontation the whole book is built toward deflates into everyone sitting down and agreeing, which is the drawn-out ending that cost The Martian its position at 82. I leaned on those two rather than on the ideas because the log shows an idea cannot rescue a book that is not got through. Occult is a live risk not resolved: the sorcery is reported to have natural explanations, but both peoples have priesthoods and one character practises moon-worship and healing, and devotions performed on the page are a veto regardless of the deity being invented. The plague investigation is an investigation-shaped thread, flagged rather than treated as the book's satisfaction.

No inheritance applies: the already-excluded book by this author is a separate standalone novel with its own cast, nothing here continues it, and the exclusion there was a detective heading rather than anything this book depends on - so I judged this volume on its own. Both content gates were examined and neither fires. The love the annotation names is between two unattached people meeting late in life; there is no marriage or engagement in evidence being betrayed, so the infidelity axis does not reach premise level, and I am recording that as a non-hit rather than an unrecoverable reject. Nor is the plot sexual: the erotic thread is one strand beside a camp past, a death, Jerusalem politics and a divination motif. The positive case is that the material is real and hard-won - a Czech-Israeli writer's late book on farewell, on the past dissolving into the present in one city. What I doubt is that it resolves into an idea worked out rather than a mosaic of motifs recapitulating a life, and the critical account of this author's prose supports the doubt: a sensitive, meditative narrator taking stock, not a premise whose consequences are traced. That is the shape the log settles in the high sixties - Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 earned its place on one nameable idea, while pieces that do not connect to each other cost Unfinished Tales 69. Add a mild bleakness discount for death and farewell as the register and a small life-phase pushback for leads far past the reader's age. Exited at the below-the-line gate; occult status is unexamined, and the publisher's own copy naming a divination secret makes that a live question rather than a formality.

The catalogue flagged this as possibly a detective book and it is not: reviewers state plainly that the identity of the hunted woman is known and the book is not built as a whodunnit, so the satisfaction is a pursuit and a reckoning, not an investigation. That clears the cheap gate but leaves the below-the-line one. Form and genre are settled - a post-war manhunt novel - and the strongest thing in it is one lead, a Siberian night bomber pilot with a wholly distinctive way of wanting things, which is the character-differentiation earner that Golden Son 92 was praised for. Against that, what the book leaves behind is a situation rather than an idea: that Nazi hunters were left to private individuals once the world's attention moved to communism is interesting history, not a thought the novel works out, so I would list axis:ideas in risks and the gate fires. The larger danger is structural. Three points of view are started at different moments in different countries and different years and reviewers note how long they take to converge; several plot lines beginning at once before any is legible is the most reliable predictor of failure in this log, the cause of Guards! Guards! 30. That is the risk that could take it under the range, not the thing setting it. Two sources were spent against a budget of one at this exit, because clearing the flagged detective question came first. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. A short post-apocalyptic novella with one clear starting situation - Karel wakes in a fallout shelter under Prague and every person and animal is gone - so the opening is not the risk. The idea is the problem: readers report the philosophical passages read as duty rather than as consequence, and that the short form kept the premise from being developed or closed. That is the failure the reader punishes hardest, since Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 both score on consequences actually being worked out, and it puts axis:ideas squarely in the doubts. Sustained emptiness and solitude is also the objection that held The Martian to 82 against Project Hail Mary's 92. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

A painted comic told by an old man looking back on being born in an alien zoo to a human mother and a godlike ball of light, then surviving a war across the galaxy. There is a theme - a search for enlightenment, and a religious authority who took power by owning the economy - but a theme is not the same as a premise whose consequences get worked out, and reviewers themselves say there is no antagonist to speak of and that the narrator is deliberately unreliable and romantic. That is the case where I would list axis:ideas under risks, and the rules say exit when I would. Sexual content is the leading risk on the number rather than the lean: the recurring companion is written as lecherous and readers list sex and debauchery among the registers the book runs through, and crudeness at small volume is what docked Artemis to 69 without any other objection needing to fire. Density is the second risk - an episodic picaresque with no single line to follow is the sparseness that cost Unfinished Tales its 69. Sex is plainly not what the plot is for, so no filter fires there. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

The positive is concrete and better than the packaging suggests: a man comes home from the war on a wooden leg in 1864 wanting to build steel-framed apartment houses uptown, and the book follows that want through Tweed-era corruption, tenement money and Wall Street. Page time on what a character wants is the reader's heaviest axis and there is a real want at the centre here. What there is not is anything to think about afterwards. Trade reviews call it competent enough with flat dialogue and contrived scenes, note that the pace often lags across the sprawl, and the warmest of them sells it as a page-turning guilty pleasure plus a history lesson. Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 are where historical novels with real texture and no worked-out idea land in this log, and that doubt about axis:ideas is what closes the file at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:density because length has never been the objection on its own - what costs is a thin story spread wide, and the sprawl only compounds a book that was not going to leave an idea anyway. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

One idea is declared and carried the whole way: a story survives because each generation copies it out again. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score on, and it is genuinely worked out here, not decoration. Against it sits the reader's most reliable negative predictor, and this book walks straight into it. The prologue opens inside a sealed vault on a generation ship in mission year 65 with a girl and an AI; then a fake ancient text arrives with its own dedication to an ailing niece; then chapter one alternates an octogenarian Greek translator rehearsing children in a library with a boy carrying a bomb into it. Six characters over five timelines in non-chronological order, with the connective context withheld by design. That is the Foundryside 30 failure exactly - plenty happening, none of it meaning anything yet - and the reader settled that diagnosis himself: an action opening is no defence against missing context. Leaned on axis:opening rather than axis:ideas because the log shows the opening decides whether the ideas are ever reached; four books scored 30 on it and none got far enough for their premises to matter. Density at over 600 pages and the bleakness of the bomber thread are further costs but neither is doing the work here. The range is wide because the outcome is bimodal: an abandonment near 40, or a book he finishes and rates on its idea.

The infidelity screen flagged the word for lovers in the title, but the axis is marriage or engagement only and the relationship here is between two unmarried students, which is ordinary relationship material and does not touch it; no marriage appears anywhere in what I found, so no filter fires and the axis grades at nothing. Exited instead at the below-the-line gate on one source. The premise is a political one - a Directive on religious correctness has made Islam part of Europe, and a Czech doctor falls for a devout Muslim student - and a premise of that kind is binding: the reader marks a book down when a society taken as its subject does not cohere, which is most of why Divergent sits at 58. There is no critical reception at all on a book by a retired regulator writing outside his usual line, so I would put axis:ideas in the doubts rather than bet the argument holds together. Faith as the subject rather than as a thread inside a story is the second discount. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

An illustrated adventure written for eight-to-ten-year-olds and deliberately typeset to be easy for dyslexic readers: twins get a cat with a medallion and travel through fantasy landscapes. The register is what carries the number, and this axis is graded rather than a veto - but it is graded by how far toward a children's book the thing actually sits, and this one is squarely inside that audience rather than adjacent to it, which is the end of the scale where a picture book lands in the forties, not the end where The Hobbit pays 84 and Little Women 79 clear the line on characters. There is no idea I can name that would be left behind - the stated purpose is to awaken imagination and a love of reading - and the form suspends the character tests without adding anything in their place, which is what puts this in the lower of the two bands rather than the default. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

There is a genuine idea here and it is why the number is not lower: descendants of an advanced human civilisation come back to a sixteenth century of slave-hunting and Catholic-Protestant hatred, and the book argues for human greatness reached without weapons. On ideas alone this could have sat with Animal Farm 78. What sinks it is the opening, and this is the most reliable predictor in the whole log. Readers independently describe the start as extremely sprawling and overcrowded, with many elements that do not mean anything yet, several time planes cut against each other, and so many protagonists that they are numbered - and they report losing track of them and abandoning the book. That is exactly the diagnosis the reader settled on for the three books he stopped in the first chapters at 30 apiece: lots happening, none of it meaning anything yet. I leaned on the opening rather than on the ideas because the ideas cannot be reached from behind it, which is the whole lesson of those failures. Two novels bound as one volume also invites the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cost The Lord of the Rings 84. Occult status is left unexamined at this range: the second novel's title refers to wizards, and at an estimate this far under the line the distinction would change no decision.

t: Na prvni pohled (You Had Me at Hello)
why: The infidelity axis was examined and it does not veto. The lead's own engagement ends early and of her own doing, and the man she reconnects with is married - but reviewers who specifically avoid books with married leads report that the thread never becomes an affair, so infidelity is the obstacle rather than the premise: remove the marriage and there is still a reunited-friends novel. It is not clean either. Much of the book is a woman waiting for a married man's marriage to fail, there are two further adultery threads, and nothing in what I found suggests the treatment condemns any of it - prominence I could establish, framing I could not, so this belongs in risks rather than in the number. On the exit itself: Pride and Prejudice 75 shows that romance as the central subject costs nothing when what characters want and why is the entire book, but there the wanting is examined and here I cannot name anything the book leaves behind. That is the axis that most often stalls a competent book in the 60s, so I stopped.

The memoir form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same shelf holds Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 - so the number rests on what this particular account delivers, and it delivers the thing the log rewards: insight into how a group nobody can interview experiences the world. A conscious mind sat inside a body treated as empty for years and heard what people say in front of someone they believe is not there; that is an idea, statable in a phrase, and it is why axis:memoir-form and axis:ideas carry the number rather than the prose, which several reviewers call ordinary and which is a real ceiling on the range. It also sits on the right side of the reader's companionship rule: the arc ends in being recognised, communicating, marrying and working, so it is not the sustained solitude that cost The Martian 82 its ground against Project Hail Mary 92. Deductions: the middle of the book is institutional confinement plus physical and sexual abuse by carers, and bleakness is a real if mild discount here - 1984 60 was disliked for being depressing - which is why bleakness and content sit in risks rather than in the lean. The subject is twelve to twenty-three across the confinement, so a child's inner life occupies a good part of it, which is the small life-phase pushback and part of what sank the one memoir in the log that failed. Anchored between Son of Hamas 75 and Seeking Allah 91: stronger material than the former, without the analytical rigour that earned the latter. Occult does not arise. Opening structure is not sourced, so this is medium, not high.

The premise is nameable - a miracle-worker turns up in the worst part of a city and the woman who shelters him has to work out what he is - and it opens on one concrete situation, a drug-dependent woman needing a fix and dodging the pimp she ran from, which is the single-situation start this reader needs. But the retailer material describes the payoff as a dark world of strange people, blood, madness and magic plus a powerful secret society taking an interest, which is a genre machine rather than a premise worked out, and there is not one review anywhere to say the idea is carried through. That doubt about axis:ideas is what sends it out here. Protagonist is a risk on the rooting half rather than the interest half: an addict who is chiefly pushed by need and pursued by others is the Oliver Twist 57 pattern of a lead acted upon. The messiah figure is the second risk, since the log prices this axis on reverence and a careless resonance costs. Sexual content was examined and is not the plot - her work is background to the boy's story. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and the miracles are what would need checking. One source, within budget.

The positive case is the lead. Addison is told in one first-person voice from one concrete starting situation - a man who cannot be looked at, living under the city - and he is both interesting and easy to root for, which is the axis that separates Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 and that Oliver Twist 57 failed on.
